Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:44:11 GMT

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine

Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.

Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.

In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.

He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."

He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.

In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.

And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".

"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.

"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."

BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:02:02 GMT

This judgement that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017.

In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict.

He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since the Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes.

The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent.

They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation.

The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.

The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.

Lawyers will study the way in which the Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.

Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough.

The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group".

The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.

That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.

In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.

Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.

According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.

"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."

In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.

The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.

The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".

The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.

"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.

"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."

The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.

The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.

That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.

The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".

It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.

Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".

Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.

He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.

She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago.

It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel.

"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University.

"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:16:21 GMT

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

US President Donald Trump's envoys were also there, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner said Trump wanted to make a deal with Russia "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia has never accepted the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but Article Five-style guarantees could theoretically be offered to Kyiv without being part of the Western defensive alliance.

Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukraine sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And today, Putin vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready for making compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said.

England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:11:03 GMT

The match between Spain and England took place at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano stadium

England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:55:52 GMT

Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said.

The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing.

The prime minister's spokesman said that if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Burnham's spokesman said Brexit had done "more harm than good".

"The choice over the coming days is clear: stand with Boris Johnson and Kemi Badenoch defending a broken status quo, or with Andy Burnham delivering change, cutting costs for business, helping with the costs of the weekly shop and creating opportunities for young people," he added.

One of the deals expected to be reached on Friday includes a new youth mobility scheme, which would make it easier for young people to work and travel in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:45:56 GMT

New Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (right) worked with his full squad for the first time on Thursday

Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (second right) hugs forward Bryan Mbeumo

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:59:16 GMT

More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.

The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.

Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.

He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.

McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".

Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.

The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.

Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.

He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.

He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.

He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.

Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".

Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.

"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.

"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."

A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".

"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.

Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".

But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".

When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.

He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."

He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."

The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".

"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.

"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."

The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.

The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).

ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.

GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.

The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.

Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.

"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.

"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.

"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."

A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.

"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.

"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:55:15 GMT

Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and it appears that he left with little in return.

In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.

The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.

That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.

So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.

While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.

On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.

For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".

That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.

"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.

A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.

If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.

While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.

But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.

"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.

"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."

Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.

"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.

Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.

In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.

Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:49:24 GMT

A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.

Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.

West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.

The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.

A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.

Ahmed said Ali was undergoing emergency surgery at Leeds General Infirmary after being stabbed in the leg. He said Ali was in a stable condition but had lost a lot of blood.

"My thoughts are with him and his family and loved ones. It's an extremely distressing time," said Ahmed.

"We shouldn't have to fear for our personal safety because we have chosen to serve the public.

"There should be no normalisation of violence in our democratic life."

Responding to the incident in his Bradford East constituency, Labour MP Imran Hussain described the incident as "horrific" and "deeply disturbing".

"My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family," said Hussain.

"No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community."

Ch Supt Richard Padwell urged anyone with information to contact police.

"This is a serious incident where a local councillor has been stabbed in the street and our thoughts are with him, his family and colleagues at this difficult time," he said.

"Whilst the investigation is in the early stages, there is nothing to suggest that this incident is politically motivated at this time."

Ali is a community development manager at charity The Leap.

He has worked with community organisations Bradford Moor Pass and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

He was first elected as a councillor in the May local election, replacing the previous Labour representatives.

Men guilty of abusing woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:42:25 GMT

Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.

"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.

"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."

She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".

She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".

Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.

She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.

The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.

Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.

The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".

One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.

As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.

Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.

Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.

Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.

The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.

Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.

They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".

Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.

"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

Joanne Young was drugged and raped by strangers after her husband offered her online

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:18:24 GMT

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

When Joanne Young awoke tied to her bed, she had no idea about the horror that had been unfolding while she was unconscious.

After hearing her then-husband Philip Young calling for someone else to "get down", she quickly realised another person was in the bedroom with them.

Unbeknown to Joanne, Young had advertised online for other men to abuse her. He then drugged her and invited a series of strangers into their bedroom to sexually assault her.

This had been going on for 13 years.

On Thursday, four men were convicted of a number of offences including raping and assaulting her. Her ex-husband had already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges.

Young, a former Conservative councillor, and another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing.

The group came from a variety of backgrounds. One of the men worked on Ministry of Defence nuclear defence projects while another drove Red Cross trucks to Romania in the 1980s.

Speaking outside court after the verdicts earlier, Joanne said "silence is not an option if we are serious about preventing abuse" - you can read her statement in full here.

Her case has striking comparisons with the repeated rape of Gisèle Pelicot in France, with experts saying the crime was "deeply abusive".

Online, Young portrayed the abuse as a shared sexual kink known as "cuckolding". The photographs used in the adverts posted on sites like Craigslist and Grindr showed Joanne inanimate and tied to the bed.

James Foster, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Young "would drug her so that he could then sexually abuse her and record that sexual abuse and also arrange for other men to attend the address to sexually abuse her".

One of the men who answered the advert was Dean Hamilton, 46, who admitted to raping Joanne and abusing her in 2015.

The other men who were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne were Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48 and Mohammed Hassan, 38 - the man Young told to "get down" when Joanne woke.

They told the court they believed they had the consent of both Joanne and Young and were told Joanne was pretending to be asleep - when in fact she was heavily sedated.

"But not once during any of this abuse did they ask Joanne Young what she wanted or show any interest in what her wishes were," Foster said.

The law states the sexual consent can only be given if the person involved "agrees by choice ... and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

Investigators are told to establish "what steps, if any, the suspect took to obtain the complainant's consent".

Professor Marianne Hester, emeritus professor at the University of Bristol, said Joanne "clearly" had no capacity to say no, adding a "women cannot consent if they are asleep".

"So it's the same if they are completely drugged. They cannot make the decision to agree to sex," she added.

Hester, who has researched gender-based violence for years, said those cases raise broader questions about attitudes towards women and sex.

"We have to question the men, the way men think it's okay to do sex and how they keep normalising, we keep normalising all these very abusive acts within sex and that's really problematic," she said.

Hester added: "We know that investigations have now started on certain websites and that individuals have been identified in a number of different countries who have been up to exactly the same kind of thing.

"So I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline."

The case has also reignited questions about the role of websites used to facilitate abuse.

Lisa Sugiura, Professor of Cyber Crime and Gender at the University of Portsmouth, argued online platforms have a responsibility to address content that normalises violence against women.

"Often these sites are accompanied by image-based abuse and deeply violent language and rhetoric about women anyway," she said.

"You think, how are these forums allowed to act with impunity without oversight and accountability?

"Before we even get to the question of whether we should simply accept the word of a man claiming to speak on behalf of himself and his wife."

Data shows hundreds of similar potential crimes are currently being investigated across the UK.

The National Crime Agency said there was an "urgent need" to deal with the problem as an international issue.

NCA investigators have identified more than 270 individuals linked to one online forum and successor groups.

The CPS describes this type of offending as an emerging challenge for investigators.

"This particular type of offending, where a husband is drugging and abusing his wife and arranging for other men to abuse her, does seem to be a new type of offending," said Foster.

A spokesman for Wiltshire Police explained the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

He said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

Sugiura disagrees the offending itself is new.

She believes technology has made it easier to facilitate and conceal abuse that may have existed for years.

"The use of technology enables anonymity, it enables that division of identity, the protection of the respectable face offline, and these heinous deeds online," she said, adding offenders often operate within wider online communities where misogynistic attitudes are encouraged and abusive material is shared.

"These are not always isolated incidents," she said.

"They can be part of larger networks where people are swapping tips, encouraging one another and sharing material that is deeply abusive towards women."

"I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline," she added.

Why fibbing about stolen snacks is an important part of childhood

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:36:33 GMT

When drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.

Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development.

"It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast.

Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.

Young children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one.

One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are 10 months old.

Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own.

"As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be.

"Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."

Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.

"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."

By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.

She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.

These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".

"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains.

"This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."

Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent.

"All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."

Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth.

"[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."

This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast that she has been trying to do.

The mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened.

"I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space.

"And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."

Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically.

"My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."

She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly.

"I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."

Dutch watchdog tells people not to buy AI smart glasses

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:33:17 GMT

The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.

While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.

The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.

Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.

It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.

The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.

Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.

Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.

The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.

But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.

AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.

It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.

One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.

The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.

And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.

It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.

Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.

It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.

In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses

Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI.

It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.

The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument around smart glasses.

"They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.

But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 15:05:21 GMT

Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United head coach will be at Liverpool on 22 November

"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

There is a clear non-negotiable.

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

Matheus Cunha's injury-time goal against Roma on 3 November sealed one of only three Manchester United victories in 15 games this season

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

Diogo Dalot is consoled by Manchester United team-mate Joshua Zirkzee after being substituted during the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

Then there is Dalot.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

This video can not be played

Liverpool and Man Utd fans give predictions ahead of Premier League match

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

This video can not be played

Why does Pochettino keep lemons in his office?

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

Further forward, with Benjamin Sesko out, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo have tended to be used in the number nine role. But Cunha likes to drop deep, while, after a bright start to the season, Mbeumo has scored twice in his past 12 appearances.

Neither Shea Lacey nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Both caught the eye on England Under-20 duty during the international break. Pochettino has history for giving young players a chance and the pair could benefit from that.

Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe have been the subject of numerous supporter protests and chants

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"We need to be united," said Pochettino.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:57:42 GMT

Pat Cummins spoke to the media on 12 November, calling Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense"

Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.

The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.

It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.

Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.

Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.

Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.

Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.

But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.

Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.

In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.

Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.

I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.

Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.

This video can not be played

Complete and utter nonsense - Cummins

Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.

The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.

Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.

After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.

He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.

Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.

The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.

If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.

Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.

And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.

Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.

Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.

His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.

Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.

Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.

Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.

Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.

What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.

Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.

What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.

Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:36:17 GMT

Former home secretary and foreign secretary Sir James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative candidate for mayor of London.

The MP for Braintree in Essex was chosen in a poll of party members in London, winning 86% of the vote.

Sir James saw off a challenge from Westminster City councillor Festus Akinbusoye and Richmond Park parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari.

He said London's "best days are ahead if we make a change at the forthcoming election". The next mayoral election will be in May 2028.

Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.

Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.

He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.

At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".

Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.

"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."

"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.

"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.

"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.

"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."

Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.

The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.

She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."

Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.

Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".

She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London.

"In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."

Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.

The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.

Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".

She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."

Furbank leads returning England trio for All Blacks visit

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:18:36 GMT

Furbank's play-making skills were key to Jack van Poortvliet's try in the win over Australia a fortnight ago

England have been boosted by the recovery and return of George Furbank, Seb Atkinson and Ollie Chessum to their starting line-up to face New Zealand on Saturday in the Nations Championship.

The trio, who all missed last weekend's win over Japan with knocks, are joined in the starting line-up by Will Joseph, who crossed for five tries against the Brave Blossoms.

Furbank held off the challenge of Freddie Steward, who impressed against Japan, to regain the full-back slot, while vice-captain Chessum brings ballast to a back row that is completed by Ben Curry and Ben Earl.

Fin Smith returns at fly-half to reprise a 10-12 combination with Atkinson that has started six of England's last seven Tests and dates back to their days as teenagers in Worcester Warriors academy.

Barring Joseph's inclusion for the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, England have named the same matchday 23 which combined excellently in the 45-12 victory over Australia a fortnight ago.

After last year's 33-19 success, England are aiming for successive wins over the All Blacks for the first time since beating them in November 2002 and June 2003 - five months before Rugby World Cup glory in Australia.

"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said head coach Steve Borthwick.

"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.

"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."

New Zealand, meanwhile, have also been bolstered by the return of big names.

England v New Zealand

Nations Championship

Saturday, 21 November at 14:10 GMT

Following their shock defeat by Wales in Cardiff last weekend, Jordie Barrett, Damian McKenzie and Cam Roigard are brought back in, while wing Will Jordan - his country's leading all-time try-scorer - has recovered from a hamstring issue to start.

Full-back Beauden Barrett, who skippered the side for the first time in Cardiff, will win his 150th Test cap, becoming only the fourth men's player - alongside Alun Wyn Jones, James Slipper and Sam Whitelock - to achieve the landmark.

Beauden and Jordie Barrett's brother Scott is in the second row, while Codie Taylor captains from hooker.

New Zealand lead the Nations Championship southern hemisphere standings by one point and any sort of victory over England is likely to be enough to book their place in the headline fixture of next weekend's play-off finals.

France, who lead the northern hemisphere table and play Argentina later on Saturday, would be their likeliest opponents.

A victory for England, however, could mean Borthwick's men forcing their way into the title play-off, while Ireland and South Africa, who meet in Dublin at 16:40 GMT, could also have a say in an intriguing finale to the group stage.
