Fiona Harvey to appear at Crown Court on harassment charge

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:39:56 GMT

A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.

Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.

During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.

Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.

The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.

She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.

Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.

She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.

Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:47:27 GMT

Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.

Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.

Here's what you need to know.

The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.

Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.

This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.

They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.

When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.

In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.

Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.

Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.

But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.

More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.

The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."

By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.

By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".

The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".

It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.

Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.

It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.

In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".

It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:26:39 GMT

After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews.

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".

It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.

"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.

Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.

Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".

About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".

Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.

"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.

"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.

"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.

Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".

The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.

On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

A group of Rockstar workers who were sacked by the company have also been protesting outside its offices, ahead of a tribunal which heard they were penalised for discussing working conditions in a private online forum while working on the game.

They claimed they were punished for being part of a workers' union, but Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, said employees made disparaging comments about the company on a semi-public Discord server and shared confidential information.

Players were able to download the 212GB game ahead of time, in order to be able to play it as soon as it was made available.

Some had even gone to the lengths of buying a whole new console dedicated to the game.

Broadband providers Virgin Media O2, as well as BT and EE, said internet traffic records had been broken in the days leading up to the UK release.

The BBC has heard from people planning to take time off work - as well as a company which has given its employees the day off - in order to dedicate time to the game.

Kieran Youens-Byrne, 34, from Manchester said he was "going on a pilgrimage to Wales" where he would be "completely off grid" for a week.

He added his partner Clare "has been incredibly understanding, although I suspect she's questioning why our romantic getaway revolves around a PlayStation".

Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:17:32 GMT

Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.

"I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.

The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance.

"I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said.

"But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance.

"I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.

"It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:01:35 GMT

US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.

The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.

"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."

Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."

Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.

She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.

Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.

Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.

"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.

"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."

Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.

Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.

Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.

The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.

Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.

Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.

Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.

The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.

Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next

BBC News Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:48:01 GMT

"Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.

It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.

Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.

"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.

A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.

Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.

The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday, saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.

He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.

That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.

They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.

The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.

But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.

After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.

Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.

Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.

What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.

The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.

And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.

Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.

Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.

Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.

It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.

But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.

"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.

There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.

Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".

Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.

Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.

"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.

"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.

"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.

And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?

Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.

A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.

But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.

Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.

One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."

That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.

Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.

But how much further could the reset go?

The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.

New Scientist is 70 years old – join us in celebrating

New Scientist November 18, 2026

Break open the bubbly, light the candles and get ready to party – New Scientist is 70 years old! Times have certainly changed since we published our first issue in 1956. Back then, some scientists had proposed that our carbon dioxide emissions were warming the planet, but the idea was controversial. Biologists were only beginning to unpick how DNA, whose structure had just been elucidated by Francis Crick, James Watson, Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, encoded the instructions for building organisms. The founders of this magazine couldn’t have envisaged the many ways that the web and smartphones would change daily life.

We are even old enough that what once seemed futuristic is now pleasantly quaint. Launching our first website, Planet Science, in 1995, we declared that, “As the technologies mature, quite soon and at a terminal near you, it may be possible to hear interviews with well-known scientists”. Our digital offering has expanded greatly since then, with these sorts of interviews now available across our podcast and video channels. That said, we also speculated that it might be possible to “manipulate three-dimensional models of molecules” on a future version of our website, which we still haven’t quite managed to deliver.

To mark our anniversary, we have put together a timeline of the biggest breakthroughs of the past 70 years. I enjoyed diving into our archives in search of how we reported era-defining moments. Our assessments haven’t always been on the money: after Yuri Gagarin’s space flight in 1961, for example, our correspondent declared “it is almost physically impossible for [the US] to beat the Russians to the moon”.

Advertisement

The secret to New Scientist‘s longevity is a devoted following of readers

A clear demonstration, if one were needed, that most predictions turn out to be wrong. But looking ahead is in New Scientist‘s DNA, so, bravely – or foolishly – we press on. The main feature in this special issue is a trip to the year 2096, seven decades from now, for an imagined article for our 140th anniversary. To make our predictions as informed as possible, Jacob Aron consulted a panoply of scientists for their views and wove it all together to create one plausible path for the future.

Sometimes, it turns out that fiction writers can see the future more accurately than scientists. Emily H. Wilson has trawled through 70 years of sci-fi in search of the most prescient predictions. Robert A. Heinlein, Ursula K. Le Guin, Octavia E. Butler and Cixin Liu are among those who have shown remarkable foresight.

Of course, the secret to New Scientist’s longevity is a devoted following who have been with us since the days of Daedalus, Enigma and Grimbledon Down. When we first started thinking about our anniversary, we wondered if there were readers who remembered our very first issue. We asked you for your stories about how you first encountered New Scientist and the role it has played in your life – and hundreds of you responded. It was a joy to read so many kind messages and wonderful stories. Most gratifyingly of all, we heard from a couple who met on our short-lived dating website in 2012 and are still happily married! You can read some of our favourite letters here.

Long-time readers may remember a couple of old faces who make an appearance in this issue. When I first joined New Scientist in 2015, I sat next to Andy Coghlan, a news reporter who had been on staff for almost as long as I had been sentient. Andy was hired in the days when job interviews took place in the pub and reporters away from the office had to file stories over the phone. He shares a few recollections about the huge stories he worked on, from Dolly the sheep to the world’s first face transplant. Meanwhile, in Almost the Last Word, former editors including Mick O’Hare reminisce about noble efforts to answer readers’ questions about noisy restaurants and champagne.

This article is part of a special series commemorating our 70th anniversary, featuring contributions from our most loyal readers and a few Nobel prize winners.

Finally, some fun and games. We thought you’d like a challenge, so we asked Nobel prizewinners to set some quiz questions. Barry Marshall, Jennifer Doudna and Saul Perlmutter gladly offered to test your knowledge of their specialist subjects: the bacteria that cause stomach ulcers, CRISPR gene editing and the expanding universe. We also have a special crossword that requires you to fill in the missing words from headlines that have appeared on our cover. Even Feedback is getting in on the action.

Despite all that has changed in the past 70 years, New Scientist remains one of a kind – a place where curious minds can feast on big ideas, baffling mysteries, hard-hitting journalism and the delightfully weird subjects of scientific inquiry. Thank you for being part of our story. It has been a great pleasure to put together this 70th anniversary issue – I hope you enjoy it too.

Sam Wong is New Scientist‘s anniversary editor

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

New Scientist November 18, 2026

In the past week, a Microsoft outage locked millions of people out of their email accounts, computer problems at a US bank stopped payments and a glitch in air traffic control systems grounded flights in the US. Even the US National Security Agency (NSA) reported that its secure intranet NSANet had fallen over, and Apple’s online services also went offline. The cluster of failures prompted rumours of a coordinated cyberattack by a foreign state or a hacking spree powered by AI.

Speculation about such ideas was so rife that the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was forced to reassure people that the government had “zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind”.

But why are we seeing so many outages all at once? There are certainly hackers, including state-backed ones who stage coordinated attacks. For instance, a boss at the UK’s intelligence, security and cyber agency – Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) – recently told New Scientist that Russia and China are staging “relentless” cyberattacks against the UK using AI. AI has also allowed even non-experts to uncover dramatic bugs in widely used software. But that isn’t what we have seen in recent days.

Advertisement

Rogue hacking AIs have changed the cybersecurity landscape

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) put its air traffic control outage down to “routine maintenance” in which copper communications lines were being upgraded to fibre-optic cable. The head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford, echoed Rubio in a press conference and said: “We see zero evidence of anything nefarious.”

Bank outages were put down to a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase. Microsoft blamed a trifecta of problems for its email issues: an old software bug, malfunctioning internal data connections and server capacity. As for the NSA glitch, the spy agency said only that problems arose “during scheduled routine maintenance”, and didn’t respond to a request for comment. Apple pinned its issues on an internal update.

The flurry of outages, then, is partly down to coincidence and partly explained by a chronic lack of investment in resilient infrastructure, says Daniel Dresner at the University of Manchester, UK. He says that not only is there no indication that these outages are linked, but there is no evidence that they are malicious hacks.

“Things are failing all the time,” says Dresner. “This stuff is really fragile.”

Free newsletter

Dresner says there has been an increasing trend – exacerbated by new AI models that can create computer code with unprecedented speed – to prioritise new features and updated interfaces over data validation and reliability.

“We all have what a colleague of mine called the ‘Big Mac mentality’: we want it with all the trimmings and we want it with speed. We’re happy because it’s working – until it fails,” says Dresner. “We wanted agility and we ended up with fragility.”

These sorts of failures aren’t rare, says Alon Hillel-Tuch at New York University. “The honest answer is that it isn’t really all happening now. Outages like these happen all the time. What’s unusual this week is that several big ones landed close together just as everyone started looking for a pattern. As for why it all seems to be happening at once, large outages are far more common than people realise,” he says.

Tim Stevens at King’s College London says that the technology sector has been developing profitable and desirable tools, but failing to build and maintain the infrastructure on which those tools rely. He says it is like a car firm selling sports cars when the roads are littered with potholes and dead ends. Spending money on fixing or improving infrastructure brings no immediate profit, so is overlooked.

Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet

“This is what we built and this is what we have predicted for years and years and years. It’s coming home to roost,” says Stevens. “If you’re going to build an entire global system on demonstrably insecure networks and systems, then this is what you’re going to get. I don’t think there’s anything more than coincidence in the current set of events, it’s just they seem to have come in a short period of time.”

George Loukas at the University of Greenwich, UK, says that US government cuts to cybersecurity efforts like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will certainly have worsened matters overall, but that the real reason for the enormous disruption we see when services go offline is that we all tend to use a very small number of digital tools.

“We are depending increasingly on digital environments which tend to be an oligopoly. Five years ago, that wouldn’t be the case. We would have exactly the same event, but not the same impact,” says Loukas.

The growth of domestic solar installations opens the possibility of hackers targeting their smart inverter devices as a way to cause widespread power-system failures

In many industries, says Loukas, governments have stepped in and broken up monopolies, but he has seen less progress in the digital world. Until there are many thriving, competing rivals in every sector of technology, we will be vulnerable to enormous outages that bring everything grinding to a halt until staff at one company can find a fix.

Stevens says that AI has led to the discovery of a great number of software bugs, which have required lots of patches. That low-hanging fruit has now been picked and we are seeing a slowdown, he says, but that burst of activity is likely to have been a good thing overall for security.

However, there are huge hurdles between us and a more resilient online world, due to the “perverse economics of cybersecurity”, says Stevens. “If you’re going to test something to oblivion [to make sure it’s secure and resilient], then your competitors have already stolen the market. It is what it is, and I’m quite pessimistic about how to address this. It’s an uphill battle, particularly when the economic incentives point in the opposite direction.”

Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers.

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

Advertisement

Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.

OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.

What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.

In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.

How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses

I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “AI as Normal Technology” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.

The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “impossible” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.

Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.

In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”

Huge extinct orca may have eaten other whales

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Orcas may have been top predators in the ocean for longer than we had thought.

Long ago in the North Sea, massive ancestors of modern orcas may have terrorised other whales. Though the fossil remains are too fragmented to conclusively categorise the orca as a new species, the findings are transforming researchers’ understanding of the animals’ evolution.

“At least 2.5 million years ago, orcas were already very large and capable of hunting large game,” says Hidde Bakker at the Natural History Museum Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

Advertisement

Orcas filmed making sunfish explode by ramming them at high speed

In 1994, fishing vessels trawling the bottom of the southern North Sea between the UK and the coast of the Netherlands pulled up truckloads of fossils and mammoth tusks. Dozens of these fossils, now housed at the museum in Rotterdam, appeared to belong to some large but unknown species of orca (Orcinus) that lived 2.1 million to 2.6 million years ago. But no one had systematically studied them.

Bakker and his colleagues took the five most information-rich specimens – two skull chunks, a jawbone and some vertebrae – and compared them with living and extinct members of the dolphin family, of which orcas are the largest living members.

The only other fossil orca species known, says Bakker, is a 3.5-metre-long species that swam in the Mediterranean Sea around Italy at around the same time as the North Sea orcas were around. Analysis of its fossils suggests that the Mediterranean orca probably predominantly ate fish. But based on certain skeletal and dental clues, the North Sea orca seemed equipped to hunt larger fare.

Free newsletter

For one thing, the orca was enormous. Bakker and his colleagues think it could have been 7.7 metres long, which puts it on par with some of the largest male orcas today. It also had features commonly seen in the modern orca populations – called “ecotypes” – that specialise in hunting marine mammals. In particular, its teeth were set in very deep sockets that were reinforced with bone.

“In most dolphins, that’s not the case,” Bakker says. “It’s just more like a groove with teeth placed in it.”

The orca – which still hasn’t been given a formal new species name – also had a relatively mobile head, which would have allowed it to grip and tear large prey. These traits all hint that this predator could attack other big, powerful animals such as other dolphins or baleen whales.

A group of orcas in Monterey Bay, California, use a submarine canyon to isolate whale calves, and launch coordinated attacks on prey in the open ocean

It is possible that these orcas evolved in the ecological vacuum left behind by the extinction of rapacious, whale-eating sperm whales.

“We have some evidence now that [dolphins] took over their top predator niche,” Bakker says.

Figuring out more precisely when those sperm whales went extinct could help researchers better test that hypothesis, says Olivier Lambert at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. He’s also curious to know whether chemical signatures in the North Sea orcas’ teeth and bones could further confirm their diet and their place in the marine food web.

“Did they already feed on large marine mammals, fish, or a combination?” Lambert says. “This [research] may provide some insights about the emergence of some social skills [in orcas], like the highly coordinated hunting of giant whales.”

Woman entered hibernation-like state during winter for more than 30 years

New Scientist November 19, 2026

A woman experienced episodes of a “hibernation-like” state – when her body temperature dropped as low as 31°C (88°F) – during the winter for more than three decades. A post-mortem analysis suggests this might have been caused by a reduced number of connections between neurons in a brain region called the hypothalamus.

Some warm-blooded animals – such as dormice and ground squirrels – can enter a state called torpor, in which they become less active, reduce their body temperature and slow their metabolism to save energy. Prolonged torpor, known as hibernation, usually occurs during the winter, when food is scarce and temperatures drop.

Low on energy? A new understanding of rest could help revitalise you

While humans don’t have this ability, some researchers think we may have the genetic hardware to enter a reduced energy state, and discovering how to trigger this could have health benefits.

Advertisement

Chiu-Xia Yi at the Amsterdam University Medical Centre and her colleagues were studying post-mortem brains, focusing on the hypothalamus – a brain region that controls body temperature, metabolism and the body clock. They came across the brain of a woman from the Netherlands whose medical records said she experienced a “hibernation-like syndrome”.

“When I learned about this particular brain donor, I discovered something quite extraordinary: she had experienced recurrent episodes of hypothermia and reduced activity during winter for more than 30 years, with a documented body temperature as low as 31°C,” says Yi. Most people would develop organ failure at such a low body temperature, but the woman recovered from torpor-like episodes for decades without organ damage, says Yi.

Free newsletter

The woman first developed the syndrome, which caused her to become sluggish, in her early 20s. Her medical records didn’t state how long each episode of torpor-like symptoms lasted, but they didn’t occur in the summer.

MRI scans taken when she was 55 revealed that her brain structure had no unusual features. She donated her brain to the Netherlands Brain Bank before she died at age 57 following unsuccessful surgical treatment for pneumonia, which was seemingly unrelated to her syndrome, says Yi.

There are seven known prior cases of humans seasonally entering a torpor-like state, says Matteo Cerri at the University of Bologna in Italy, who wasn’t involved in the study. But this woman seems to have experienced this for longer than others, and previous case reports didn’t examine people’s brains after they died for any changes that may underlie the torpor-like state, says Cerri.

To explore this, the researchers analysed slices of the woman’s hypothalamus. They found it contained about one-tenth of the amount of a protein called synaptophysin compared with three women of the same age who had no torpor-like symptoms.

Synaptophysin is found in synapses, the connections between neurons, so this suggests the woman’s brain contained fewer connections between neurons involved in regulating body temperature and the body clock. “Levels of synaptophysin in the hypothalamus decrease during hibernation in ground squirrels, suggesting a possible parallel between the woman’s condition and changes seen in hibernating mammals,” says Yi.

Radical new insights from the science of interoception – how the body senses its internal state – explain the real reasons we feel tired all the time, and how to re-energise

Further analysis revealed that neurons involved in controlling the body clock in the woman’s hypothalamus had almost completely lost a hormone called arginine vasopressin, while levels of another hormone called vasoactive intestinal peptide were also substantially reduced, compared with control brains.

All the neuronal changes may have enabled the woman to enter a torpor-like state in response to reduced exposure to sunlight or colder temperatures in the winter, without experiencing organ damage, says Yi. But it’s possible the brain changes resulted from, rather than caused, the woman’s syndrome, she says.

In ongoing work, the team is sequencing the woman’s genome, which could reveal any genetic mutations contributing to her syndrome. This could help pinpoint pathways that could be targeted with drugs to induce hibernation in people, for instance, to extend their survival while waiting for an organ transplant, or to reduce the need for food during space travel, says Cerri.

Neuropathology and Applied Neurobiology DOI: 10.1111/nan.70104

Cooking pollution dominates air quality at mealtimes in London

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Tougher pollution rules governing traffic, power generation and commerce in London mean an unexpected air-quality signal now dominates the city at certain points of the day: cooking emissions.

Pollution from commercial kitchens is now the dominant source of particulate matter pollution in London at midday and in the early evening, new analysis shows, outstripping emissions from traffic and other sources such as combustion.

The results are another sign that pollution levels in the city from traffic and power generation have fallen dramatically in recent years, says Ben Langford at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology. “It’s definitely a good news story,” he says, pointing out that particulate matter emissions for road transport have fallen by more than 90 per cent in the UK since 1996. “If you went back to 1996, the cooking signal would really be in the noise compared to the traffic.”

Advertisement

Cleaning up air pollution could weaken vital AMOC ocean current

Together with colleagues, Langford used a technique called aerosol mass spectrometry, which measures the chemical composition of air pollution particles in real time. This allowed the researchers to pinpoint the specific source of fine particulate matter – known as PM1 – and how this composition changes over the course of the day. The data was collected in London during summer and winter in 2021.

Fine particulate matter is generally measured as PM2.5, which describes particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or smaller. But a large proportion of PM2.5 is PM1 – particles with a diameter smaller than one micrometre. The smallest particles are often the most harmful, as they are able to stay airborne longer and pass into human bloodstreams.

While emissions from traffic still dominate ambient pollution levels, the team found that cooking emissions emerge as the dominant source of PM1 pollution during mealtimes in London, contributing up to 83 per cent of midday emissions and 87 per cent in the early evening.

This is likely dominated by emissions from shallow and deep-frying cooking oil in commercial kitchens, the researchers say. “In terms of what the city is directly emitting in primary aerosols, cooking is definitely becoming dominant, particularly at those peak mealtime periods,” says Langford.

The picture was similar in Beijing, where the team also collected data during winter 2016 and summer 2017. There, cooking emissions contributed up to 61 per cent of midday emissions and 76 per cent of early-evening emissions.

Free newsletter

Scientists are still working to understand whether the source of particulate emissions determines the potential harm to public health. It may be, for example, that PM1 caused by cooking emissions is less harmful to humans than PM1 caused by traffic or coal burning.

The study looks only at primary sources of emissions, which is the pollution being produced in the city itself. The air pollution residents are being exposed to could look quite different, including particulate pollution that has drifted in from the suburbs and beyond. “A lot of what you breathe in in London is not necessarily what’s emitted locally,” notes Langford.

The study also uses data collected from a very central location in London, close to lots of commercial restaurants but with few domestic residences, says Roy Harrison at the University of Birmingham, UK. “You’re not going to have the same level of wood burning, for example, as you have in the suburbs,” he points out. Research from Imperial College London suggests that 17 per cent of fine particle pollution in London comes from wood-burning stoves.

npj Climate and Atmospheric Science DOI: 10.1038/s41612-026-01583-6

Otherworldly image of a porcelain crab wins ocean photography contest

New Scientist November 19, 2026

This exquisite photo of a porcelain crab catching plankton while half-hidden in an anemone was named the overall winner of The Nature Conservancy’s Oceania Photo Contest. The blue of the shadows gives the image an otherworldly feel.

Despite the name and appearance, porcelain crabs aren’t crabs – the similarity is a result of convergent evolution. The photo of the small crustacean was taken on a coral reef off Gili Air Island in Indonesia by Tammy Nicholas.

A shot of a drifter or pelagic crab clinging to a piece of kelp, shown below, won second prize in the wildlife category of the awards. While it looks large, this crab is, in fact, just a centimetre across. The photo was taken near the Poor Knights Islands of New Zealand by Crispin Middleton.

Advertisement

A photograph of water lilies growing in the Cenote Carwash near Tulum, Mexico, shown below, took second place in the prize’s plants and fungi category. Cenotes are sinkholes linked to water-filled caves, and this one got its name because taxi drivers used to clean their cars there. Its Mayan name is Aktun Ha.

Vanessa Torres Macho took this image. The Oceania contest is open only to residents of Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, but the photographs can be taken anywhere.

A shot of sardines pursued by diving Cape gannets, shown below, took second place in the water category of the awards. This photo, by Justin Tan, was taken off Port St Johns in South Africa during the sardine run, when billions of sardines migrate north along the coast, for reasons that are still not understood.

Finally, the first prize in the people and nature category went to this image, below, of a researcher filming juvenile sperm whales and a calf off the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Photographer Vanessa Mignon says this filming was done under permit, but it is often done illegally.

The 28 best popular science books of 2026

New Scientist November 19, 2026

It’s the perfect time to dive into the year’s best non-fiction, whether you’re looking for gift-giving inspiration or a brilliant read for yourself. To help, here are the best popular science reads of 2026 according to New Scientist staff and writers. You’ll find the big names of science writing here, of course: Carlo Rovelli, Xand Van Tulleken, Maggie Aderin, Jim Al-Khalili. But there are also plenty of lesser-known gems, whether you’re interested in the power of heat to boost your health, a history of plants, why exactly humans sleep so little, or how to deal with the generally overwhelming nature of life. And if you think we’ve missed anything, do come and recommend your own favourite popular science reads here. Alison Flood

The nature of time is a subject that has perplexed us for centuries. What Jim Al-Khalili does so expertly here is to break down the topic into a series of separate mysteries, explain each one and then build back up again to show how they interrelate and inform each other. Why do we feel time flowing, why does that flow feel continuous like a river, and what exactly is the difference between the past and the future? Al-Khalili tackles all this and much more, and I finished the book feeling like I understood more or less everything about time I would ever need to. Admittedly, that probably isn’t the case, but the fact that Al-Khalili created that illusion is itself a testament to this brilliant book. Joshua Howgego

Hotwired: How the hidden power of heat makes us stronger explores how saunas and other forms of heat exposure can boost health and athletic performance, and possibly prepare us for a hotter world. Gifford once hated being hot, having grown up in “steamy, swampy” Washington DC, but his interest was piqued by studies from Finland showing that frequent sauna use reduces the risk of heart attacks, stroke and Alzheimer’s disease. Gifford brings us on his personal journey of learning to love heat. He doesn’t do anything in half measures, even signing himself up for one of the world’s most gruelling bike rides under the ferocious Texan sun. The rigorous science mixed with personal stories, humour and tales of tragedy and triumph make this a highly engaging read. Alice Klein

This is a stunningly rich and interdisciplinary book that invites the reader to understand our universe from the ground up, challenging us to think creatively and with urgency. Prescod-Weinstein doesn’t shy away from bringing anthropology, history and politics into the story of the cosmos, which enriches and expands it past more conventional approaches. And she has fun, too, as her book is replete with pop culture references, from Star Trek to Missy Elliot. Reading The Edge of Space-Time requires time and focus, and generously rewards both. Karmela Padavic-Callaghan

Our verdict on Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s The Edge of Space-Time: a wild ride

The world desperately needs us to change our attitudes to ecology, nature, food, energy, consumption and race. As Rebecca Solnit reminds us in this slender, hopeful and galvanising book, we’ve already come a long way. I was especially pleased to see the acknowledgement that symbiosis is a vital process in ecology, and a discussion of the growing understanding that we are part of, not separate from, nature. These are key points that Solnit and I chatted about when I interviewed her for the New Scientist podcast. “There is no going back,” Solnit writes, “though how we go forward is the work.” Rowan Hooper

The theoretical physicist sets out here to deliver a theory of everything, from space-time to ethics and consciousness. Based on a series of lectures, the book is rooted in quantum physics and divided into themed chapters that progressively expand Rovelli’s frame. He writes not just about the nitty-gritty of doing physics, but the character of science itself, what it can offer and how we should adjust our philosophical views of it – and the world. It’s an impassioned book well suited to readers who may know a little bit about physics, but crave answers to the biggest questions about physical existence. Karmela Padavic-Callaghan

Knowing how to care for ourselves feels harder than ever, thanks to the burgeoning wellness industry. Navigating the sea of supplements, wearable health monitors and at-home health tests is nearly impossible – even I don’t have the time to dig through every claim, and I am a full-time health journalist! The good news is that doctor, writer and TV presenter Xand Van Tulleken has. He takes on the wellness industry in his latest book Make Me Well: One doctor’s quest to understand the confusing world of wellness. It is a comprehensive, entertaining and informative read that will make you think twice before you buy into the latest wellness trend. Grace Wade

The wellness boom has brought a wide array of consumer products that promise to boost your health and happiness. Xand van Tulleken has delved into it all and explains how to think about the evidence behind the hype

Neil Price is unmatched at conveying the humanity, history and, frankly, weirdness of the Vikings. The Sea-King and the Sorceress almost doubles as a travelogue, taking us across – and, at times, well beyond – the medieval Norse world to visit the final resting places of an array of different people, not all of whom were professional raiders. Each person’s grave contains tantalising clues about the world in which they lived, including what they valued and who, in turn, cherished them, and why. Surprises and rich detail abound; it will make you think about the Viking Age in an entirely new way. Kelsey Hayes

We live in the moment, the “now”, yet according to physics, there is no such thing. Similarly, neuroscience tells us that “now” is just a construct, an illusion put together by the brain to help us get through the world. So why is now so central to our very existence? That is the subject of this enthralling and enlightening read by my colleague Jo Marchant. There are plenty of books on neuroscience, many on cosmology and even quite a few on quantum physics. But I don’t know of many that combine deep thinking from all these fields, or many writers who could manage it with such clarity. Yet that’s what Jo achieves in this fascinating book. Rowan Hooper

What is life, asks Melanie Challenger. She pushes an answer: life is matter that pursues goals, that has agency. A thunderstorm may be violently active, but it isn’t trying to achieve anything. In contrast, animals seek out comfort and pleasure, they try to mate, they avoid dangerous predators. Even a single-celled bacterium makes efforts to feed itself and to maintain its own internal chemistry. This may seem obvious, but different ideas – notably that living organisms are machines for propagating their genes – have seized many biologists’ minds. Challenger seeks to reclaim life’s active nature. Michael Marshall

What a treat it is to have two great books about plants to recommend at the end of 2026. Either of them is worthy of your time. How Flowers Made Our World by biologist David George Haskell is a lyrical contemplation of flowering plants, the angiosperms. The book’s central theme is their staggering importance to humanity and most other land-based life. But, as a whole, it is an assemblage of loosely linked essays, as reviewer Michael Marshall noted, each exploring different aspects of flowering plant biology. I found it beautifully written.

Green Kingdom, by gardener and historian Ben Dark, is more structured, exploring key evolutionary splits and groupings in the family tree of all land plants (not just angiosperms). At the same time, he deftly weaves in an extensive yet entertaining history of western botany, from Theophrastus to the molecular revolution. Almost inevitably, it skews rather white and male, but I found it very absorbing and interesting anyway.

Both books cover Carl Linnaeus and Charles Darwin, both books consider the profound significance of seagrasses and orchids, and both books do justice to the marvellous plant kingdom, but they do it in very different ways. Which one you pick is up to you. Penny Sarchet

Free newsletter

Our lives can often feel like a series of never-ending burdens. Rather than suggesting a one-size-fits-all approach to redressing that, broadcaster and author Claudia Hammond offers an evidence-based toolkit of psychological strategies for dealing with the diverse challenges we face – from the never-ending to-do list to imposter syndrome and perfectionism. Her suggestions are refreshingly realistic, and her writing is full of humour and humility. I thought I’d read everything there was to know about stress, but I was wrong. There is plenty of new and exciting material here for anyone who would like a little more resilience. David Robson

This year, my friend and New Scientist colleague Rowan Hooper delivered a true big-ideas book in the form of Togetherness, an exploration of symbiosis. I took from it that symbiosis isn’t a heart-warming and occasional freak occurrence of evolution, but instead a central organising principle of biology, one that occurs at every scale, from ecospheres to inside our cells, like zooming in on an infinitely repeating fractal. It’s an invigorating thesis that Rowan argues for and explores entertainingly, and one that has really stuck with me, not least in terms of how we account for symbiosis in our efforts to stop destroying the natural world so extensively. Penny Sarchet

Whether you like it or loathe it, it is hard not to have an opinion on artificial intelligence – but with discourse this heated, wouldn’t it be better to have an informed opinion? If you don’t know your transformers from your tokens (that’s the T in ChatGPT and the unit of data processing used by AI, respectively), then The AGI Chronicles by Kevin Roose is an excellent way to get caught up. Roose is a bit too much of an AI booster for my tastes, but he mostly moderates it well throughout this guide to the rapid progress in AI over the past 10 years or so. Jacob Aron

You are diverging. The cells in your body have been mutating ever since you were conceived, with different cell lines accumulating different mutations and becoming less alike. Sometimes, the result is cancer. But, as Roxanne Khamsi describes here, this divergence can lead to many other consequences, such as evolutionary battles between competing cell lines that cause many conditions, or affect how we respond to drugs. This could even be the root cause of ageing, meaning trying to slow it is a battle against an unstoppable force. Everyone with an interest in health should read this book – as Khamsi writes, medicine needs to take on board the fact that each of our cells is a bit different. Michael Le Page

For a non-physicist like me, this was a friendly and mind-expanding guide to the discoveries through history that led to a deeper understanding of the universe, and I thoroughly recommend it. Malik, a particle physicist, nods to the late Stephen Hawking’s take on the topic, A Brief History of Time, in her title. I found Hawking’s explanation a little harder to digest, but fans can check out Graham Farmelo’s look at the man behind the book, Hawking, also published this year. Alison Flood

We have been taught to avoid exposure to the sun for fear of skin cancer, but are we missing out on some surprising health benefits? In this enlightening book, Rowan Jacobsen examines the vital role that solar rays play in our biology, from lowering our blood pressure to soothing the immune system in conditions such as multiple sclerosis. It may even boost the activity of our mitochondria and enhance our metabolism. Perhaps most surprisingly, very few of these effects come from vitamin D. These are bold claims, but Jacobsen presents a compelling case and explores the complex scientific evidence with nuance. David Robson

As someone who has routinely described herself as “hormonal”, Signals: The inside story of our hormones was a breath of fresh air for me. Each chapter follows one of Hameed’s patients from her endocrinology clinic at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust in London, using their cases to anchor us while she takes us on a journey through different hormones and endocrine systems. While I did catch myself making various self-diagnoses based on the ailments encountered in each chapter, this book genuinely changed the way I see hormones. In fact, since finishing it back in July, I haven’t once declared that I was “feeling hormonal”. Sophie Berdugo

Why do we sleep so little? This is a question that many of us ask after a restless night, but it’s actually a crucial biological paradox. Humans sleep less than any other primate, so how did we evolve to need so little of it? In this fascinating book, evolutionary anthropologist David Samson delves into our deep past to unpick the conundrum of human sleep. In the process, he takes us on a journey that encompasses sleeping in chimpanzee nests and living with the Hadza, a hunter-gatherer society in Tanzania – and offers some intriguing tips for how to get a better night’s rest. Alison George

The James Webb Space Telescope launched on Christmas Day 2021, and has proved to be a tremendous Christmas gift for the picture desk here at New Scientist. We have eagerly awaited each and every new image beamed back to Earth. This stunning book brings together more than 200 of these otherworldly shots, cleverly curated not in chronological order of when they were captured, but according to how far back in time they allow us to look. Among them are some of the telescope’s most iconic photos, including shots of Earendel, the most distant star ever observed, and the resplendent Cosmic Cliffs in the Carina Nebula. Alongside these are lesser-seen delights, such as the sparkling galaxy NGC 1365, which almost looks like it’s winking back at you. Tim Boddy

Space scientist Maggie Aderin tells Karmela Padavic-Callaghan about these stunning photographs from the James Webb Space Telescope, which feature in her new book

I wasn’t especially looking forward to reading a book about consciousness, because what is there to say on a subject where we know so little? But Michael Pollan goes well beyond the “hard problem” (recognition of just how difficult it is to solve the mystery of consciousness) to write a beautiful book about the mind. Not only does he explore cutting-edge science, from fascinating evidence of plant consciousness to the few who study the unconscious, but he incorporates insights from fiction writers and older psychologists too. You may know less at the end than when you started, but the journey is thought-provoking and compelling. Olivia Goldhill

“End times fascism” is the term used by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor to describe the conglomeration of vested interests that are opposed to action on the crises of climate and nature that threaten to destabilise civilisation. Indeed, those vested interests – religious extremists, tech bro entrepreneurs and nationalist politicians – actively want to bring the crises on. Fascism, here, isn’t seen as the rise of nationalism that overwhelmed Europe in the 20th century, or isn’t just that anyway: it is the natural end point of capitalism. “Fascism is capitalism with bared teeth,” they write. Economists have failed because they don’t take ecology into account, and assume that we can just keep exploiting the planet. Klein and Taylor point to a way out – and remind us that people have always resisted and fought fascists. Rowan Hooper

Most of the dinosaurs have been extinct for millions of years, but one group has survived to the present day. We call them birds. Palaeontologist Steve Brusatte’s The Story of Birds does what it promises: it recounts how birds first evolved, how they took to the skies, how some of them survived the mass extinction 66 million years ago that took out all the other dinosaurs, and how modern birds came to be so widespread and diverse. Some of the story will be familiar to anyone with an interest in palaeontology, but Brusatte still manages to pack in a few surprises. Michael Marshall

This is a meticulously researched history book that pulls back the curtain on how ideas about biological sex and sexual reproduction arose through the work of Charles Darwin and his contemporaries. Brooks scours Darwin’s notebooks and letters to show that the great naturalist not only knew more about the queerness of the natural world than modern readers may assume, but also struggled to marry it with the mores of his time, cutting corners in his own writing in ways that still reverberate today. Karmela Padavic-Callaghan

Unless you are an extreme extrovert, conversation can often feel like a minefield of potential faux pas, from whether to tell someone they have something between their teeth to declaring our feelings for the loves of our lives. Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns examines various social dilemmas centred on the question of when it is and isn’t appropriate to share what we are thinking, and – if we do – how we can deliver those truth bombs without risking an explosion. I love Bohns’s writing: she comes across as the friend we’d always turn to when we need advice. David Robson

This is a book about evidence-based policy, which talks a lot about randomised trials and systematic reviews. It ought to be dry and hard-going, but in fact it’s one of the most absorbing and readable books I’ve tackled this year. Journalist Helen Pearson shows how evidence-based approaches have revolutionised medicine by giving us hard evidence about which treatments work and which don’t. Then she tackles a much gnarlier problem: can we use the same tools, like randomised controlled trials, to evaluate social policies, conservation programmes and parenting styles? This turns out to be truly difficult, because of pesky things called human beings. Michael Marshall

In the early days of 2026, I sat down with Jamie Bartlett’s latest book, How to Talk to AI, without having examined my instinctive distrust of chatbots and their kin terribly deeply. Now that I have read this handy primer to human-AI relations, that distrust has persisted, but it’s grounded in a deeper understanding of what makes this new suite of technologies so appealing – and so dangerous. In his book, Bartlett dispenses practical advice on communicating with AIs and reveals how and why things can go wrong. A lot has happened since I first picked up this book: titanic mathematical problems have been toppled, escaped agents have instigated hacks, voters have been bombarded with slop and fakery. The promise and the peril of the past few months means I was all the more grateful to have read How to Talk to AI. It is vital that we all know how best to interact with technologies that now play a huge role in our lives, whether we like it or not. Bethan Ackerley

I read this back in January with the New Scientist Book Club, but if the number of people I’ve told about it is anything to go by, it remains one of my top popular science reads of the year. Daisy Fancourt is a professor of psychobiology and epidemiology, and she’s here to tell us about “how the arts transform our health”, from helping with pain relief to improving our mental health. There is tons of science and plenty of case studies, and I found it all extraordinary, inspiring and convincing. Although I’m yet to join a choir (an activity Fancourt is very much in favour of), I’ve definitely experienced more live art this year as a result of reading it, and each time it has left me feeling better about the world. Bring on communal singing in 2027. Alison Flood
