How aquanauts could help save Florida’s reefs

New Scientist November 19, 2026

It sounds idyllic. Who wouldn’t want to occupy a newly built residence in the Florida Keys, complete with its own coral garden right outside the window? The only complication is that it is 17 metres below the surface of the Atlantic Ocean.

That is not putting off Jim Brittsan, though. “This is really exciting,” he says. Brittsan is the founder and executive director of coral restoration non-profit Sustainable Ocean and Reefs (SOAR). He is also the diver who arranged the temporary coral nursery beside the residence, having brought the corals from a site where, 10 metres closer to the surface, they faced increasing environmental stress. Now, in reduced temperatures, they are starting to flourish, hosting their own marine life – visible day and night, in all its busyness, from the underwater residence known as Vanguard just 15 metres away.

Vanguard is a long-stay underwater station for marine biologists. It was deployed in June 2026 at Tennessee Reef on the seafloor of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, around 8 kilometres south of Long Key. Its coral nursery looks like a strange marine shrubbery: the coral fragments are arranged on anchored ropes that stand upright in the water. Once Vanguard is operational, a more permanent nursery will be established and the corals will eventually be planted on the seabed as part of ongoing restoration efforts, with their long-term survival assessed through monitoring.

Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock

DEEP, the international design and engineering organisation that built Vanguard, aims to make humans aquatic by establishing more subsea habitats like it. These will allow people to live underwater for extended periods to engage in scientific research and conservation. This opens up unprecedented opportunities to do research because there is no need for divers to bounce up and down to a research vessel on the surface. Those round trips eat into valuable work hours, because divers can spend only limited time at depth and must ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness. “If we’re diving from a boat, we can do about 3 hours’ work a day at depth,” Brittsan says. “It’s much more efficient if we can just stay down there.”

There is plenty of work to do in the Florida Keys. Elkhorn (Acropora palmata) and staghorn (Acropora cervicornis) corals, which are vital reef-building species, are now considered functionally extinct in Florida. But it is not just in Florida waters that corals are struggling. Climate change, which brings elevated ocean temperatures, is a significant threat to corals around the world. In warmer waters, corals eject the algae that live in their tissues. This upends their mutually beneficial symbiosis in what is known as a bleaching event – without the algae and other symbionts, the corals are left a ghostly white. If temperatures do not fall and the algae do not return, the corals eventually die.

In September 2026, amid concerns about marine heat stress, SOAR received authorisation to relocate 11 different coral species to the new nursery next to Vanguard. The corals were transported using different methods depending on the species: acroporid corals were transferred submerged in bins of seawater, while other corals were moved encased in seawater-soaked bubble wrap and placed in temperature-controlled coolers. The corals were then placed in the temporary nursery in deeper water near Vanguard.

Vanguard should be fully commissioned early in 2027. After that, those transplanted corals, and their attending creatures, can be continuously monitored by aquanauts who will be living in the habitat for a week at a time.

Brittsan and his team have also observed juvenile long-spined sea urchins (Diadema antillarum) that naturally recruited to Vanguard. “A lot of Diadema have started settling all over the habitat,” he says. This species of sea urchin is considered a keystone because its grazing reduces algal cover on reefs, providing space for corals and other reef organisms to settle and grow. That is why DEEP is taking a holistic approach, also planning to build sponge nurseries outside the habitat, for instance. “You need corals, sponges, sea urchins and everything else,” says Thomas Potts, science program director at DEEP.

Diadema urchins are particularly active at night, which means short daytime dives would miss a lot of what needs monitoring. “That’s where Vanguard really comes into play,” Potts says. Resident scientists will be able to monitor marine life around the clock.

The lessons from Vanguard will inform marine research in the Florida Keys for years to come. Vanguard is also a proving ground for DEEP’s future habitats. “It’s a great place to train scientists that might be working in different habitats on the continental shelf,” says Potts. The longer-term vision is to build a fleet of undersea residences at other locations. “This could be replicated throughout the Florida Keys and even in other parts of the world,” Brittsan says. “It’ll be a game-changer.”

Follow @deepengineered on social media

Living among the species you are studying can provide deep insights, according to marine scientist Dr Steve Gittings. “We all know that if you really want to get to know a place, you should go and live there,” he says.

Gittings spent 27 years as chief scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office of National Marine Sanctuaries. In that time, he spent many weeks living on Aquarius Reef Base, an ocean-floor habitat used for vital marine surveys. One of the biggest advantages of living underwater, he says, is that it creates a deeper appreciation of the wide variety of phenomena that contribute to a healthy reef. “There’s millions of things going on that are super-critical.”

But it is not just a useful path to deeper insights: it is a transformative experience. An extended stay in the ocean changes people in the same way that astronauts are changed after living in space. “There’s an emotional connection to living underwater that keeps you dedicated and committed,” Gittings says. That is why he is so excited about the inspiration that Vanguard will give to the aquanauts who live there: they will gain an irrepressible, lasting desire to help nature heal itself by removing stressors where possible, he reckons. “Only nature can do the full restoration,” Gittings says. “Our role is to create the conditions that allow nature to do its thing.”

Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis

New Scientist November 19, 2026

Turmeric supplements seem to have little to no effect on pain and mobility problems caused by knee osteoarthritis. That’s according to one of the most rigorous assessments of the evidence yet, which focused on four randomised controlled trials comparing the supplements to placebo pills.

Osteoarthritis, which affects more than 500 million people worldwide, is caused by damage to cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, resulting in pain, stiffness and inflammation. Standard treatments include painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs that can ease symptoms. “But many people see little or no benefit,” says Philip Conaghan at the University of Leeds, UK, who wasn’t involved in the latest review.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Turmeric supplements are often touted as an alternative therapy. They contain curcumin, a compound that gives turmeric its yellow colour and is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties. Yet such beliefs are often based on prior flawed studies, says Ivan Shirinsky at the Research Institute of Internal and Preventive Medicine in Novosibirsk, Russia.

Advertisement

Shirinsky and his colleagues analysed results from four randomised controlled trials, collectively involving more than 370 participants with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were randomly assigned to take either a supplement containing turmeric extract or placebo pills two or three times per day, for between eight weeks and three months. Each trial used a slightly different supplement containing a different curcumin dose. “We looked at the most rigorous evidence available,” says Shirinsky.

Among those who took a placebo, knee pain decreased by 1.6 points, on average, on a scale from 0 to 10 by the end of the study. Those taking turmeric supplements experienced an average 2.3-point decrease in pain, meaning the difference between the turmeric and placebo groups was half that required to be meaningful to patients based on prior studies, says Shirinsky.

Free newsletter

In line with this, surveys revealed that turmeric supplements had no meaningful effect on participants’ quality of life or their ability to carry out everyday activities such as walking, getting up from a chair or climbing stairs.

“If somebody is taking one of these therapies and thinks it is helping their symptoms, I would never force them to stop,” says Conaghan, since it could be working for some people. “But the evidence suggests it’s not going to help you. I would save your money.”

However, the findings cannot provide a definitive answer, says Shirinsky. “All included studies used different formulations of turmeric, and this reduced the certainty of the evidence,” he says. What’s more, the evidence wasn’t strong enough to make conclusions around turmeric’s potential side effects; curcumin supplements have previously been found to cause liver problems in some people.

Further randomised controlled trials testing a standardised curcumin supplement could address such limitations, but Conaghan doesn’t think this is justified. “There are not enough clues in [existing research] to give me confidence that we should do more trials in this area,” he says. For instance, studies have shown that curcumin isn’t easily absorbed into the blood following ingestion, meaning it is unlikely to reach joints to have an effect, he says.

Cochrane Library DOI: 10.1002/14651858. CD014683

RNZ financial crisis: Fears that cuts to Pacific services could further China’s influence

New Zealand Herald November 19, 2026

China has boosted its presence in the Pacific in the last decade. Caretaker PM Christopher Luxon pictured at his matai ceremony in Samoa earlier this year. Composite Photo / NZME and Govt of Samoa

As Radio New Zealand grapples with its $11.8 million blowout, there are fears the broadcaster’s services to the Pacific could be impacted – enabling China to grow its influence in the region.

In an open letter sent to caretaker Prime Minister Christopher Luxon - who was bestowed a Samoan chief title earlier this year - and RNZ chairman Brent Impey, the Asia Pacific Media Network (APMN) called for RNZ’s dedicated Pacific services to be ring-fenced and protected from any budget cuts.

“The Pacific Service – started in 1990 and part of a Pacific broadcasting history dating back more than 75 years – is a vital communication link with Pacific nations,” the letter said.

“New Zealand is one of only two countries providing a shortwave service in the South Pacific. The other country is China.”

APMN is an independent network of journalists, academics and researchers from New Zealand and the Asia-Pacific region.

Its letter said Pacific countries rely heavily on RNZ Pacific’s radio news bulletins and “its Cyclone Watch Service is potentially lifesaving”.

The letter was signed by APMN chairwoman Dr Heather Devere, who wrote of concern for RNZ’s Pacific service amid efforts to rectify the broadcaster’s financial position.

RNZ staff took to the streets this week, protesting outside its offices in Auckland and Wellington, after news of the almost $12m blowout and plans to cut the equivalent of 58 fulltime roles by March next year.

Hours after those protests, interim chief executive Mark Stevens warned no part of the public broadcaster was safe. He said in an email that change proposals would be shared from this week and, if implemented, staff would progressively leave RNZ between next month and March 31.

Massey University Associate Professor Dr Anna Powles, who specialises in geopolitics and security in the Pacific, told the Herald any reduction in RNZ news services to the Pacific risked damaging New Zealand’s reputation.

“If you give up ground [like] surrendering shortwave radio access, then you are effectively giving another country the opportunity and ability to advance their own narratives.

“Those narratives may be counter to you and they may also be counter to the Pacific.”

Over the past decade, China has developed a sustained policing, diplomatic and economic presence in the Pacific, Powles said.

“New Zealand, Australia, the United States and so on were traditional partners in the Pacific – that landscape is changing now. We now live in a world where many more states are contesting for power.

“From a geopolitical perspective, the information environment is one of the key domains in which geopolitical contestation is taking place.”

In January 2017, Australia switched off its shortwave radio transmissions across the Pacific and China’s state-owned broadcaster took over some of those frequencies formerly used by Australia’s ABC news service.

“The way in which China does engage in the region has become much more targeted, much more strategic,” Powles said.

Asked about its response to the open letter, a Radio New Zealand spokeswoman told the Herald: “Any proposals will be guided by our charter, audience needs and strategy, with a focus on protecting audience services as far as possible.

“Our aim is to share information with affected teams as soon as possible and provide opportunities for feedback. We will follow a full and fair consultation process, meeting our obligations to staff and unions.”

RNZ Pacific, formerly known as Radio NZ International, started in 1990. However, shortwave broadcasting from New Zealand to the Pacific started in 1948.

RNZ’s Pacific service broadcasts 24 hours a day, in English and Pacific languages, in collaboration with 22 media partners, according to the letter.

“At the opening of its new shortwave transmitter in 2024, then Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters described the service as ‘seriously important’,” Devere wrote.

Shortwave transmission can travel long distances without needing cell towers or internet, so remote communities rely on shortwave radios to stay up to date with news and special bulletins during natural disasters.

“Our group regards it as an indispensable service that not only links New Zealand with its Pacific neighbours but also informs New Zealanders about affairs in those nations.”

About 20 local Pacific radio stations relay material from RNZ Pacific daily in countries and territories including Samoa, Fiji, Tonga, Cook Islands, Niue, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Nauru, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, French Polynesia, American Samoa and New Caledonia.

RNZ Pacific’s Cyclone Watch Service, in particular, is regarded as a crucial broadcast in island nations during cyclone season, from November to April each year.

Hourly bulletin updates are broadcast once a cyclone alert is issued. It can be a lifeline for villagers in remote areas who rely on shortwave radio – particularly when electricity is lost during a severe cyclone, hurricane, tsunami or other natural disaster.

Former RNZ Pacific editor Koroi Hawkins called RNZ’s Pacific service a “crucial pillar of the regional media landscape”.

He said its shortwave transmissions help keep communities informed even after storms have destroyed local broadcast and telecommunications infrastructure.

“I experienced this first-hand covering the devastation after the Category 5 Super Cyclone Pam in Vanuatu in 2015,” he said.

“A village chief in Erromango, Ben Lovo, who I was interviewing, thanked me profusely for the RNZ Pacific Shortwave service saying he had tuned into the warnings as the cyclone approached them and was able to warn people from his village and other villages of the exact moment the cyclone had hit, which saved many lives.”

Devere said RNZ’s Pacific service should be regarded as a specific contribution to New Zealand’s international relations, pointing out provision of a Pacific service was required under the RNZ charter.

“Importantly, those Pacific nations regard RNZ as a trusted source of reliable information.”

She said RNZ’s financial shortfalls and reports of cutbacks to redress them had prompted the group to write to Luxon.

“We note that the Pacific service is a separate line item in the Ministry for Culture and Heritage funding of RNZ which, we suggest, adds weight to the view that it should be treated as a discreet entity.

“Any reduction in funding or resources for the Pacific service would adversely impact not only New Zealand’s relationship with those countries, but also our own Pasifika peoples who rely on it for news about the countries with which they retain strong links.”

Luxon has been approached for comment.

Vaimoana Mase is the Pasifika editor for the Herald’s Talanoa section, sharing stories from the Pacific community. She won junior reporter of the year at the then Qantas Media Awards in 2010 and won the best opinion writing award at the 2023 Voyager Media Awards.

Weaving value into the clip: Fibre industries report warns of NZ’s skills, manufacturing gaps

New Zealand Herald November 19, 2026

Skeins of wool. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By Monique Steele of RNZ

A South Island company making medical bandages from merino wool has had to look abroad for manufacturing because of a lack of specialist wool processing in New Zealand.

It comes as a new industry report highlighted the challenges for natural fibre companies to expand in New Zealand, due to significant constraints in manufacturing capability and expertise.

Starting in 2019, WoolAid created what it claimed were the world’s first medical-grade bandages, nasal and mouth strips made from merino wool.

The clip was supplied from Zentera’s ZQ-certified farms in Mackenzie Country, Central Otago and Marlborough, and then manufactured offshore.

Founder and chief executive Lucas Smith interned at a wool weaving facility in Northern Italy, where the company’s main supply chain was now based.

“The Italians scour it, so they pull all the lanolin out of it, spin it and weave it to our standards,” he said.

“Then the fabric is exported to China to Shanghai, and then our crew at the bandage factory process it to our standards, and then we export it to market from there.”

Smith said it took a long time to develop a sterile system for working merino wool into strict United States Food and Drug Administration regulations.

“Because we’re a medical-grade product, we have to process wool to really high standards, FDA class one medical standards.

“So this had never been done before, and not a lot of mills were willing to work with me in the early years.”

He said the Italian facility was one of “just a handful of mills” that could do it, and New Zealand did not have the specialist equipment or expertise locally.

The patented products are available across Aotearoa, Canada and the United States.

Meanwhile, a new fibre industry report suggested the country’s fibre sectors needed to look at capturing value onshore by boosting manufacturing capability, workforce and marketing how local fibres could solve market problems.

The Future of Fibre Aotearoa report showed Aotearoa produced 171,530 tonnes of fibre each year, worth more than $926 million at the farmgate, led by strong wool into top markets China and India.

After wool, the next largest fibre markets were skins and hides, hemp, harakeke and mohair.

More than 180 people within the fibre industries contributed to the report, led by industry group Fashion and Textiles New Zealand and supported by funder Agricultural and Marketing Research and Development Trust (AGMARDT).

It highlighted structural barriers for the “fragmented” sectors, including limited processing and manufacturing capability, weak pathways to market, demand creation and skills losses across textile manufacturing, wool science and processing areas.

“Wool remains Aotearoa New Zealand’s largest fibre stream by volume and value, but it is on a structural decline path as sheep production becomes increasingly meat-led and wool export volumes continue to trend down,” it said.

“Our biggest fibre challenge is turning strengths into something markets can buy.”

Fashion and Textiles New Zealand’s chief executive Jacinta FitzGerald said New Zealand had incredible scourers and manufacturers of textiles, yarns and interiors, but the country needed to build up capability to harness greater value from fibres.

“We’ve got no shortage of really innovative ideas ... and where we’re finding gaps are coming up is taking those ideas and that good fibre to the market.

“In some situations we don’t have the testing facilities available in New Zealand to test performance.

“And other situations with different fibres, we may not have the manufacturing capability here, the infrastructure, to take things from pilot scale to commercial scale.”

FitzGerald said a lot of the downstream value through wool processing, manufacturing or product development was happening offshore.

“There are challenges that need to be addressed, not sort of a, ‘oh we just don’t have that machine’, it’s actually, ‘we have the machine, but it’s not accessible’, or ‘we have the machine, but the person who knows how to run it is no longer there’,” she said.

“And it’s really interesting once you start to drill down, how widespread that capability gap is.”

FitzGerald said New Zealand was well-positioned to take advantage of the global move towards natural and bio-materials, and saw other opportunities in building construction and interiors, health and wellbeing.

The report showcased companies like premium woollen accessories designer Honest Wolf of Rangitīkei, merino socks and accessories manufacturer Norsewood, and hemp-wool interiors manufacturer Rubisco as good examples of market-facing brands leaning on strong provenance.

Last year, more than 114,600 tonnes of wool was produced off 23.4 million animals in New Zealand from 11,046 farms, to the tune of $540m.

Police have apologised to an assault victim after mistakenly using a photo of him in a public appeal for information on his case.

About 3pm on Monday, the police media team emailed media a photo of two men with a statement titled, “Do you recognise these people”.

The men’s faces are turned towards the camera in the blurry image.

The statement said police were appealing for help from the public to identify the two males in relation to an investigation into a serious assault on Oceanbeach Rd in Mount Maunganui early on November 1.

“Police would like to speak with the males pictured, as we believe they may be able to assist in our enquiries,” the statement said.

The image was published online by the Bay of Plenty Times, NZ Herald and other media in stories about the plea for information. It also appeared on social media.

About 7am on Tuesday – 16 hours later – police emailed media asking them to urgently remove the photo and instead use two other photos.

These included a new photo of two males, and a version of the initial photo edited to obscure one person’s face with a black box.

Bay of Plenty Police criminal investigations manager, Detective Inspector Lew Warner, told the Bay of Plenty Times an internal communication error resulted in the victim being mistakenly included in a photo for an appeal for information.

“The image was amended on police channels as soon as the error was identified,” Warner said.

“We recognise that the use of this image was confronting for the victim and we have apologised to him for any distress this has caused.”

Police did not answer questions about when police identified the mistake, and what steps had been taken to ensure it would not happen again.

The victim declined to comment on the police error when contacted by the Bay of Plenty Times.

Police previously said he suffered “life-altering” injuries in the incident.

New Zealand triathlete Finnley Oliver, from Pāpāmoa, will be racing in Sunday’s World Triathlon Cup. Photo / Wayne Nevrillk

A rising Tauranga athlete gearing up for Sunday’s World Triathlon Cup says he’ll be hyping himself up with Katy Perry and Taylor Swift music before the big race.

Tauranga will host elite international and local triathletes at the World Triathlon Cup this Sunday, including Pāpāmoa-based athlete Finnley Oliver.

It is the first of three world-class triathlon events in Tauranga, followed by the World Triathlon Championship Series in 2027 and the World Triathlon Championship Grand Final in 2028.

This weekend’s event is held alongside the Mount’s annual Tinman Triathlon, now in its 38th year.

The Tinman Triathlon kicks off at 7.30am before the World Triathlon Cup begins, with the elite women racing at 2pm and elite men at 4pm.

Road closures will be in place across Mount Maunganui.

However, spectators can watch from The Mall, Marine Parade and the finish-line precinct near Salisbury Ave, where grandstands and a large screen will be installed.

The event will be broadcast on TVNZ+ and streamed internationally through World Triathlon channels.

Oliver, 20, said he felt “extremely excited” to race his first World Triathlon Cup on home soil.

He has been a triathlete for 10 years and previously competed at World Triathlon events, including the 2025 Junior World Championships in Wollongong, New South Wales, where he placed seventh.

This weekend will mark his first race in the elite category.

“I’d love to be right in contention to be the top Kiwi this weekend.”

He would be “over the moon” to finish in the top 10.

Strategy-wise, he said he needed to “put myself right in the mix before the run starts”.

He would love to make his World Series debut next year and make the World Series Grand Final in 2028.

His long-term goals include the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 and the Brisbane Olympics in 2032.

Before a race, he has two rituals: chicken fried rice the night before, and Katy Perry or Taylor Swift blasting in his headphones.

“Or maybe Rihanna.”

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale said triathlon was already part of Tauranga’s story with a proud history of events including the Eves Surfbreaker Triathlon, the Calley Homes Women’s Triathlon and the Marra Construction Tinman, all of which are hosted by Triathlon Tauranga.

He said hosting “world-class events” in Tauranga’s backyard benefited local athletes, clubs and the wider community.

The race helped put Tauranga on the map as a destination for major sporting events.

“We know many people come for an event, and then, while they’re here, discover everything else Tauranga has to offer. That’s good news for local businesses and helps encourage people to return in the future with friends and whānau.”

Triathlon NZ chief executive Pete de Wet said this weekend’s race, the first World Triathlon event in Tauranga, was a “long time coming”.

“It’s really great to be able to bring an international-level event to Tauranga to the community who generally are really strong behind the sport of triathlon.”

He said 49 females and 59 males would race, including seven female New Zealand triathletes and 11 males, one of whom was Taylor Reid, who represented New Zealand at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics.

But Whakatāne-born Hayden Wilde, who earned a silver medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics, would not be racing.

Double Olympian Nicole van der Kaay, from Taupō, will lead the Kiwi women, racing against Hungarian Márta Kropkó.

De Wet said races between May this year and May 2028 were inside the Olympic qualification window.

“All racing is really important for athletes to ensure they’re improving their world ranking, which is a key indicator in terms of their ability to qualify for the Olympic Games.

“For some of the younger ones, it’s the opportunity to race against quality fields, test themselves against some of the better athletes in the world, which they wouldn’t normally get to do if they were trying to race on the World Triathlon circuit.”

De Wet said New Zealand last hosted a World Triathlon Championship Grand Final in 2012 in Auckland.

“It’ll do a lot for New Zealand; it’ll do a lot for Tauranga.”

Rotorua business survey: Survival becomes top worry but more businesses optimistic about 2027

New Zealand Herald November 19, 2026

Rotorua Business Chamber chief executive Melanie Short speaking at the University of Waikato and Westpac Smarts Luncheon at the Novotel Hotel Rotorua. Photo / Stephen Parker

Business survival has become the top worry for industry leaders, according to the latest Rotorua Business Pulse Survey.

However, more businesses are optimistic the economic situation in Rotorua and nationwide will improve than in the previous survey in April.

One hundred Rotorua businesses were surveyed by RotoruaNZ and the Rotorua Business Chamber from October 13 to November 6 in the biannual survey.

The results were shared at the University of Waikato and Westpac Smarts Luncheon at Rotorua’s Novotel Hotel on Tuesday.

It found business survival had overtaken future work and sales as the top worry for businesses since the previous survey.

Just over half of businesses were very or extremely concerned about geopolitical volatility and inflation, while 44% felt this way about energy price increases.

It found 35% of respondents believed Rotorua’s economic situation would be better in a year, up 37 points on the last survey.

The proportion who believed the economy would improve for the country (35%) and their business (45%) were also up by 40 and 32 points, respectively.

Some 54% of businesses wanted the council to prioritise business growth and investment attraction, and 43% wanted the next Government to prioritise tourism and regional development.

Businesses using AI had more than doubled from 41% in April 2024 to 91% in October 2026.

Survey participant and Secret Spot Hot Tubs Rotorua co-owner Keith Kolver told the Rotorua Daily Post the business was “ticking away” and visitors were enjoying the hot tubs and saunas.

“We’re still ahead of our targets for the year, which is good, but we’re working hard to achieve it, let’s say.”

He said fuel prices were affecting visitors, noting “Auckland slows down” when they went up.

Visitation picked up again when prices decreased, he said.

“People are still moving around, but they might be buying a cheaper burger than the top-end burger or just having a burger and not chips now.”

Patchell Group chief executive Brent Whibley said the manufacturing business was starting to experience a “real positive lift” in orders after being “flat for two years”.

He was feeling “really optimistic about what 2027 looks like” but also uncertain.

“We don’t have the same sort of forward book like we have had historically.”

Whibley said it was struggling to recruit skilled tradespeople, which was a concern.

“From a Rotorua perspective we’re hoping that we can continue … to increase our profile nationally, so that we can encourage more people into the community.”

Red Stag Timber general manager Tim Rigter said business was “steady”.

“I’d say the market’s reasonable for this time of year … but not as strong as we would have expected going into summer."

The election and cost of living were contributing factors, he said.

“The outlook’s reasonable … we’re expecting summer to be okay after New Year.”

RotoruaNZ chief executive Andrew Wilson said in a statement the survey results were encouraging after a difficult first half of the year, when businesses were dealing with “significant uncertainty” around fuel and energy prices, rising operating costs and impacts on profitability.

Wilson said expectations for business activity, profitability and investment had “rebounded strongly”.

Operating costs continued to be a major concern, with about 85% of respondents expecting business costs to rise over the next 12 months. The net score for affordability of doing business was -85%.

Wilson said the contrast between improving confidence and persistent cost pressures reflected the balancing act facing local businesses.

“Businesses are seeing more opportunities ahead, but they’re still having to manage their margins carefully and make considered decisions about investment.

“There’s a sense of renewed momentum, but businesses will need to see that confidence translate into sustained activity and profitability.”

At the event, business chamber chief executive Melanie Short said the survey found the community wanted certainty and stability.

“I’m looking to move from cautious optimism back to relentless positivity in 2027.”

In a statement, she said businesses wanted to see Rotorua growing, with a vibrant inner city, a thriving economy and continued investment in infrastructure and services.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said it was fantastic to see confidence returning across the business community.

The council valued business feedback on priorities for the next Long-term Plan.

“While challenges remain, there’s a real sense of progress and I’m keen to take this feedback on board to help deliver better opportunities and outcomes for our community.”

Comments from survey respondents about businesses and the Rotorua economy included that it had been tough, but they felt “positive about what’s coming next”.

Another said the economy would continue to suffer “if we don’t tidy up the beggars and vagrants in the city centre”.

The survey again found persistent challenges around flight scheduling, cancellations and reliability had driven some business travellers to fly from Tauranga and Auckland Airports instead of Rotorua.

Rotorua Airport chief executive Nicole Brewer said it encouraged flying from Rotorua when possible.

“Strong local support is essential to sustaining existing services and building the case for improved frequency and connectivity in the future.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Ngunguru Ford Rd residents seek traffic calming after two horses are put down

New Zealand Herald November 19, 2026

Vikki and Brent Wells' granddaughter Sienna Austin with Pop (left) and Spice during their final goodbye about six months ago.

Warning: This story contains graphic details of injuries suffered by an animal.

Calls for action are growing in a rural Northland community after two horses were put down within six months following incidents their owners believe were triggered by deliberately noisy drivers.

Both horses belonged to Brent and Vikki Wells and their family, who say the animals suffered catastrophic injuries after being spooked by vehicles on Ngunguru Ford Rd, Whangārei.

The Wells have lived at the property since last November and quickly realised being on one of the only straight stretches of the road meant they copped the worst of passing traffic.

Their breeding mare Spice had to be put down about six months after they moved in. Spice bolted through a fence and fell on a metal driveway one night after a passing vehicle repeatedly backfired – an act the Wells believe was deliberate.

The mare tore away much of her lip, suffered a knee wound to the bone and lost a large section of skin from her lower leg, injuries so severe a veterinarian said euthanasia was the only humane option.

A second breeding mare and former racehorse, Pop, was euthanised over the weekend after a similar incident. The horse had to remain in the paddock overnight until a digger arrived the following morning to bury her.

The horses were related and had been part of the family for 23 years. Both daughters had grown up with them, and the Wells said their deaths had been particularly hard on the family’s grandchildren, one of whom was especially attached to the animals.

After Spice was injured, Brent spent the night beside the horse while a veterinarian administered large doses of morphine and the family faced the painful decision of whether there was any hope of recovery.

Vikki said the family were left facing veterinary bills, the cost of hiring diggers to bury the horses and the emotional toll of losing long-loved animals.

The Wells also saw insensitive comments on a community Facebook page where some people questioned why young people should not be allowed to “have some fun”.

“I’ve got no issue with young fellows wanting to have a bit of fun with cars, but not at the expense of others. They need to go and hoon around somewhere where it’s not going to affect anybody,” Vikki said.

Neighbour Sarsha Te Tai, who also owns horses, said the deaths reflected the community’s long-standing concerns about speeding vehicles, dirt bikes and drivers deliberately revving engines and backfiring along the rural road at all hours.

She recalled one occasion when a motorcyclist doing wheelies on the roadside berm caused a horse she was handling to panic, wrenching her arm before running off.

Pop’s death at the weekend prompted Te Tai to launch a petition calling for traffic-calming measures including speed humps, additional stock-warning signs and a lower posted speed limit on the affected stretch of Ngunguru Ford Rd.

She said residents wanted practical measures that would force drivers to slow down and better recognise the presence of livestock and children using the roadside.

Children from Glenbervie School, Kamo Intermediate and Tikipunga High School used the route daily to catch their school buses.

Te Tai said local children could no longer safely ride bicycles on the road.

“What has to happen? Does one of the kids actually have to get hit before something happens?”

Te Tai said residents were not asking for anything extraordinary.

“We deserve to live in peace.

“We shouldn’t have to put our horses down the back paddock and not be able to graze our front paddocks because we can’t trust the motorists around.”

Police confirmed receiving a report after the alleged May incident, including a vehicle travelling at speed and creating excessive engine/exhaust noise.

Senior Sergeant Ryan Gray, Whangārei/Kaipara road policing manager, said there was no evidence to establish the driving behaviour caused the horse’s death.

He said police had provided advice and proactive measures to monitor driving concerns on Ngunguru Ford Rd.

“We encourage anyone who witnesses unsafe or antisocial driving to report it to 111 if it’s happening now, or 105 after the fact.”

Sarah Curtis is a news reporter for the Northern Advocate. She has 20 years’ journalism experience, mostly covering East Coast courts for the Gisborne Herald.

After her daughter was stabbed to death, Tabitha Acret was faced with two options. She chose to take on the system

Sydney Morning Herald November 20, 2026

Four years ago, Acret’s daughter Mackenzie was killed in a horrific attack by her former partner. Now the grieving mother is striving to prevent other families from losing a loved one to domestic violence.

By the time Tabitha Acret sat down in her lounge room on a Sunday afternoon in spring, she’d done the grocery shopping and a few loads of washing, taken the dog for a walk on the beach, and hosted a playdate. She checked her work schedule for the week, then opened Instagram on her phone.

Someone had sent her a private message: “I called the police two hours ago, he’s breaching the AVO, no one’s come, what should I do?” As Acret’s two boys played with their black Labrador in their Newcastle backyard, she quickly punched in her reply: “Put the kids in the car. You need to drive to the police station.”

This is far from the first plea for help Acret has received. The 48-year-old dental hygienist and academic receives messages from women living in fear almost daily. And not just from her local area. Women reach out from all over the world. “Last week, I had someone from Italy, someone from America, and someone from Germany,” she says. “I say to them, ‘If you’ve got enough money, run. Not just leave the home. Leave the state. Start a whole new life. Get off social media. Run.’ I really hate that I give that advice but … that will be what saves your life.”

We’re sitting at Acret’s kitchen table the Monday morning after she received that message. It’s late September, and it’s been another horror weekend of domestic violence, with three women allegedly murdered in NSW alone in separate incidents, including a 23-year-old woman, a 90-year-old grandmother, and a 70-year-old woman. According to the nationwide register kept by Australian Femicide Watch, 61 women have been killed this year.

Acret didn’t need to read any of those statistics or headlines to know the deadly cost of domestic violence in this country. Her daughter, Mackenzie Anderson, was stabbed 78 times by her former partner, just 16 days after he was released on parole in 2022. Mackenzie, who loved to dance and was studying to become a yoga teacher, was just 21 years old.

A neighbour who heard her screams rescued Mackenzie’s 23-month-old son from what police later described as a “horrendous scene”. Three years later, a judge sentenced Tyrone Thompson to 22 years and six months in prison, with a non-parole period of 15 years and six months, meaning he could be free before he turns 40. When Acret heard the sentence, she ran from the packed courtroom and collapsed.

“I was shaking … They said, ‘We’re calling you an ambulance’ because I had lost feeling in my legs and hands and couldn’t get up … I was like, ‘I’m not leaving this place in an ambulance.’ And then they were like, ‘We’re going to police-escort you home.’ ”

Acret refused. Instead, she walked out onto the front steps of the courthouse and made a promise. “We’re in the midst of an epidemic of gender-based violence where women are being killed at an alarming rate and the only acceptable number is zero,” she told reporters, vowing to fight for change in honour of Mackenzie. “Her voice was taken from her, but mine will not be silenced. I will continue to speak, to push for change, and to stand up for every woman who has ever felt unsafe, unheard or unseen. Mackenzie’s legacy will be one of action, of justice and of hope.”

She has not stopped fighting since.

Now raising her grandson alongside Mackenzie’s 13-year-old brother, Acret has thrown herself into a relentless mission to protect women from dangerous perpetrators and give victims and their families a louder voice in the criminal justice system. Nominated for NSW Australian of the Year this month, she has convinced politicians to introduce tougher sentencing for domestic violence murderers, become a sought-after public speaker, and grown accustomed to fronting the television cameras.

But what you don’t see is the woman sitting up until the early hours of the morning, reviewing the files of violent offenders, then rising at dawn to drive two hours for a meeting to discuss whether they should be released from prison. You don’t see the woman ferrying her grandson, who turned two a fortnight after his mother was killed, between therapy appointments. And you don’t see the abuse she cops online for having the audacity to speak out when yet another woman is murdered.

The way Acret sees things, she’s got two choices. “I can be silent, or I can get up and I can turn it into purpose,” she says. “It’s about channelling that grief into something else.”

Four years after her daughter lost her life in the most horrific circumstances, Acret has lost none of her urgency, because, she says, “If we look at the numbers, we’re not getting any better.”

On the night of March 25, 2022, Tabitha Acret was in a Cairns hotel room with her then-eight-year-old son. It had been her birthday the previous day, and they’d been snorkelling on the Great Barrier Reef to celebrate. It was about 2am when her husband phoned. Police officers had come to their Newcastle home to deliver the shocking news that her daughter, Mackenzie, had been killed.

As her son slept, Acret booked a 6am flight, packed their bags, and made the decision to get him home before letting him know that his sister was gone. “I think you just go into survival mode,” she says. “It’s like, there’s other people that need me … so that’s what has to be the No.1 thing right now.”

Only later would she learn the details of what happened that night. How Tyrone Thompson had broken into her daughter’s home. How a neighbour had seen her terrified face pressed up against a window. How Thompson had stabbed Mackenzie with kitchen knives that Acret had given her daughter for Christmas.

Mackenzie had known she was in danger when her ex-boyfriend was released from prison after serving time for assaulting her. She contacted domestic violence organisations, asking for help to install security cameras and doors, and an apprehended domestic violence order was issued.

Acret had asked Mackenzie to move in with her and her husband, Mackenzie’s stepfather, but adds that she did not realise the full extent of the threat, and that Mackenzie had hidden much of the abuse from her. It was only after she died that Acret realised the danger she’d been in. “She reported eight times that he’d breached the AVO,” she says.

The first month after her daughter was killed passed in a blur. There were meetings with police, funeral arrangements to be made, and Acret and her husband were now caring for their grandson. She says he didn’t sleep for days after police brought him to their house.

After a few months, Acret began working from home but didn’t return to clinical dental work for more than a year because, she says, she didn’t have the strength to care for patients. She gained 30 kilograms as an eating disorder she had long struggled with flared.

Outraged by the sentence given to her daughter’s killer, she clung to the hope that his sentence would be increased on appeal. She felt the initial sentence just didn’t fit the grievous nature of the crime. “That just wasn’t what we were expecting,” she says.

When the appeal failed in August 2025, Acret went home devastated, and that night, began writing what would become a 200-page document that she would eventually deliver to NSW Premier Chris Minns, making the case for why tougher sentencing for domestic violence murders was urgently needed.

It worked. In October 2025, the NSW government introduced legislation to enshrine a standard non-parole period of 25 years in prison for anyone convicted of the murder of a current or former partner, giving the state the toughest sentencing laws in the country. “She spoke passionately and very sincerely about the very low sentence that her daughter’s killer got,” Minns tells Good Weekend. “It was incredibly convincing. It certainly convinced me that we needed change.”

In May, Minns went further, appointing Acret to the Serious Offenders Review Council, which advises authorities on whether prisoners should be released back into the community on parole or work release. Acret also serves on an advisory group where people with lived experience of domestic and sexual violence help inform government policies and services. “We need to get the perspective of victims’ families,” says Minns, describing Acret as a “fiercely intelligent” and inspiring advocate, whom he met in “terrible circumstances”, when she was dealing with both a crushing loss, and navigating the justice system. “I’d never met anybody like her. She is a remarkable person.”

All this advocacy work takes time, of course, and for Acret it’s squeezed in between running her own dental education business (she has spoken at seven overseas conferences this year), working in a Newcastle dental surgery, and her role as an academic at the University of Sydney, where she created a course teaching dental students how to spot signs of domestic violence, in the hope that they might be able to offer support to patients. “That’s the glamour of doing advocacy work,” she says. “Most victim advocates are working full-time jobs. Most of the stuff has to happen after the kids go to bed.”

I arrive at Acret’s Newcastle home not long after dawn on a recent Tuesday, and she slips out her front door in a grey pantsuit and black heels, leaving her husband and two boys sleeping inside. She checks that she’s got her Corrective Services NSW security ID card before we set off through the quiet suburbs. Winding around the cobalt-blue expanse of Lake Macquarie before joining the parade of commuters on the freeway to Sydney, Acret sips from a large travel cup that rattles when she picks it up. “It’s ice and Diet Coke,” she confesses. “Don’t tell my dental professional friends ... but Diet Coke is my vice in life.”

Two hours later, she walks into a Department of Communities and Justice office in Parramatta for a meeting to review the cases of 21 prisoners – all men bar one – who have been convicted of serious crimes. In the past six months, she’s reviewed the files of dozens of murderers, terrorists, rapists and child abusers. “Lots of DV murders,” she says. “It’s like, ‘There’s another one, there’s another one.’ It’s upsetting to know that there’s that many there.”

Most people would probably forgive Acret if she wanted to lock up perpetrators and throw away the key, but that’s not what she wants. “Putting them in jail, as much as I am for punishments, isn’t going to solve the problem. We need to rehabilitate them in some way. If we really want to prevent violence,” she says, “making them better people is actually the answer.”

Acret, who constantly reads the latest research on domestic violence from around the world, believes offenders should undergo intense counselling and be more closely monitored when released from prison. Prolific on social media, she posts almost daily about the issue, with the aim of raising awareness and driving change.

Back at her kitchen table, she shows me just how far we have to go. Scrolling through posts on her phone, she points to unsettling comments people have made about Mackenzie’s death, blaming her daughter for her own murder. One reads: “Should of done the dishes”. Another writes: “The government needs to run a education campaign for women. How not to antagonise a man until he has to send you back to the lord.”

Acret hasn’t been shocked by the misogynistic hate she encounters online. Comments like these only prove her point, she says, that dangerous attitudes towards women are more prevalent than we care to admit. She says she knows she shouldn’t engage, but sometimes can’t help herself.

“One, it upsets me, ‘Oh my god, like, she’s dead. Can you not leave her alone?’ And two, it upsets me that … it’s not just an attack on Mackenzie. It’s an attack on us as women. It’s a culture that’s so toxic towards us that people look for how to blame the victim more than they look to blame the perpetrator, and that makes me angry and upset,” she says. “I suppose when your mental health’s a little bit lower, those kinds of comments really can get to you. And then there’s other times where I’m like, ‘Thank you, that’s the fuel that I needed today.’ ”

Already a seasoned public speaker after years spent addressing conference halls full of dental professionals, Acret is inundated with requests to speak at charity and corporate events. Next Wednesday, she’ll deliver a keynote address in Newcastle to mark the start of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-based Violence global campaign.

I wonder what it’s like to retell the story of her daughter’s murder over and over again, but she says describing the trauma to countless strangers isn’t actually the most difficult part. “What I find more draining is afterwards. Everyone wants to come up and speak to you and often they cry and you’re consoling their grief,” she says. “It’s very emotionally draining … I never really know what I’m meant to say.”

Some people, mostly women, question her grief online, she says, and want to know, “Why aren’t you crying? If this was me, I couldn’t get out of bed and do this.”

“Well, what choice do I have?” she says, frustrated. “If I cried on national television non-stop and couldn’t get any words out … no one can hear my message. I don’t have the luxury. I totally understand that some people don’t have the capacity to do it and there’s no judgment for it, but I do have the capacity to do it, so you should just do it.”

3:24

After her daughter’s death, Tabitha Acret chose to take on the system

After Mackenzie was killed in a horrific attack by her former partner, her grieving mother is striving to prevent other families from losing a loved one to the scourge of domestic violence.

It’s clear that Acret doesn’t have much time to care what people think. Her focus is on looking after Mackenzie’s brother and son. The latter often pulls her childhood photo album out from under the television and asks whether he looks like his mum. Now six and just finishing kindergarten, he has also asked whether the man who killed his mother will come to their house when he is released from jail.

Most Tuesdays, Acret collects her grandson from school after lunch to take him to therapy. On a recent afternoon, he hopped in the car carrying a well-loved stuffed rabbit, telling Acret that he played in the sandpit at lunchtime. Acret is angry that this little boy, who has been diagnosed with complex PTSD, was never officially recognised as a victim.

Determined to ensure all children receive the support they need, in September she launched a petition calling on Australian federal and state governments to legally recognise children who witness domestic violence as victims, and provide them with full access to victim support, trauma-informed counselling and compensation schemes. More than 28,000 people have so far signed her petition, with some leaving comments describing how their children were present while they were assaulted. It shouldn’t be surprising. Research shows that four in 10 Australians have been exposed to domestic violence as children.

The man who killed Acret’s daughter had an abusive upbringing, she points out, and this was noted by the judge in sentencing. While emphasising that not all people who witness violence go on to commit offences, she says supporting child victims is vital if we are to break the cycle.

She also wants people to know how the devastating impact of her daughter’s murder extends far beyond her own family, to Mackenzie’s neighbours and friends – some of whom now struggle with their own mental health – and strangers who never knew her in life but have been exposed to the trauma of her death. She often thinks of the police officers and paramedics who responded after Mackenzie phoned triple-0 that night, and the court staff who had tears in their eyes listening to the graphic details of her murder.

“The butterfly effect from this stuff that hits the community, we’ve never really looked at what the cost of that is, but … if we looked at how many people were affected from one murder … I think we’d find that it’s massive.”

She also worries for the people working on the frontlines of this incessant crisis, such as those struggling to find beds for women in packed refuges. “Imagine working in that space and turning people away,” Acret says. “Imagine the toll that it puts on them.”

I ask about the toll it takes on her, receiving message after message from women desperate to ask how they can escape violence. The woman who contacted her on that September day told Acret she eventually went to the police station, but often Acret doesn’t find out what happens to those who message her.

Cheryl Dey, who has known Acret for almost 25 years, worries that her friend takes on too much. “I often say, ‘You can take a break,’ but I don’t think she can take a break,” says Dey. “I think that she needs to keep moving forward. I think having too much downtime is not a good thing for her and it’s one of her coping mechanisms, staying engaged and staying busy and keeping moving, keeping things happening.”

Dey describes her friend as a “ball of energy”. “She doesn’t sleep. That’s her secret weapon. She’s very goal-oriented and she sets those goals and does whatever it takes to make them happen.”

Conversation with Acret moves quickly, mirroring the hectic pace of her life. One moment we’re swapping notes on the interminable joys of making school lunches. The next, she’s critiquing the criminal justice system. She chats freely and she’s funny, often making jokes at her own expense. Laughter, warm and genuine, comes frequently.

But, her friend Dey notes, there are plenty of dark moments. “She has those moments, but then she knows that she needs to get up and keep moving and she doesn’t stay down for long, even though that darkness will never fully go away.”

Acret has undergone counselling, and says exercise helps. She’d never been a runner, but signed up for the 2024 New York marathon the day after listening to a podcast about how running can help with grief. After clocking up her first 42 kilometres through the streets of New York, she was hooked. She then set her sights on tackling the eight world marathon majors. She says she doesn’t train as much as she should, but she’s already ticked off Berlin, Sydney and Chicago. Next on her list is Tokyo in March. “I think it was important to show the kids that life has to go on,” she says. “We have to keep achieving things.”

One of Acret’s next goals is to convince authorities to hold a coronial inquest into Mackenzie’s murder to investigate whether systemic failings contributed to her death. “We can’t make a difference if we’re not looking at where we went wrong,” she says, and it’s not just the criminal justice system that she believes needs to change. She argues that perpetrators’ records should be more publicly available, and that women have a right to know exactly who they’re connecting with on dating apps.

The media, too, must lift its game, she argues. While Indigenous women are more likely to be victims of domestic violence, Acret points out that their deaths – along with those of women of different ethnic backgrounds and older women – typically receive much less attention than that given to victims who look like her blonde-haired, blue-eyed daughter. “If you’re young and … white, let’s be honest, then you get a lot of media coverage,” she says. “If you’re a woman of colour, we don’t see that much coverage.”

Tara Hunter, deputy CEO of Full Stop Australia, an organisation that supports people affected by sexual and domestic violence, met Acret about a year after her daughter was murdered.

“I think advocacy in this space is really challenging,” Hunter says, “and you do have to, at times … be courageous and actually say the things that people don’t always want to hear, and create a sense of discomfort because of your lived experience, and I have seen Tabitha do that in ways that are incredibly authentic, but also she’s very strategic.”

Victim-survivors and their families shouldn’t have to share their experiences to create change, says Hunter, but in doing so, Acret has put a “human face to this issue. She’s challenged that notion that people are just a number because, I think, she’s shared her story, but also kept the story of who Mackenzie was alive, rather than just making her a statistic.”

As Mackenzie’s son and brother grow older, Tabitha Acret is determined to make sure the boys remember her for more than just the brutal way in which she was stolen from them. Every July, they travel to Byron Bay to celebrate Mackenzie’s birthday. Acret says her daughter had wanted to move there and teach yoga. It’s where her ashes were scattered and where they had their last family holiday together.

Acret buys the boys a present she thinks Mackenzie would have bought them, and they share a cake. Mackenzie was big on birthdays, she says, showing me a photograph taken on her son’s second birthday. Acret took the photo, but it was Mackenzie who picked out the sky-blue cake, decorated with Toy Story characters. “That was the cake Kenzie ordered him,” says Acret, “before she died.”

The bakery delivered the cake to Acret’s house and refused to let her pay for it. Such kindnesses – from messages to birthday gifts – were common in the aftermath of her daughter’s death. “As much as you see this awful side of life, this other side of life comes in abundance,” she says. “There are really kind people out there that want to help for no reason.”

The day after his birthday, Acret dressed her grandson in clothes she thought Mackenzie would like, and they headed to a surf club for her funeral. After Acret spoke, she asked people to dance, because she wanted to celebrate the things her daughter loved. She is not consumed with vengefulness but driven by a desire to stop other women from suffering the way her daughter did, to prevent other families from the searing pain of losing a loved one to the scourge of domestic violence.

“You can sit around and say things have got to change, but if you really want things to change, you’ve got to get up and do it.” And now, she says, she knows that she has the ability to just keep getting up. “You don’t know what you can do until you have to.”

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

The smiling assassin: How Warren Pickering wants to soften One Nation and smash their rivals

Sydney Morning Herald November 20, 2026

Pauline Hanson’s man in Victoria thinks he can smooth One Nation’s hard edges, and do politics differently in the process.

Warren Pickering, 43, former brickie turned army engineer, One Nation Victorian president, candidate for Pakenham, want-to-be premier, and man whose past drug and alcohol misdeeds threatened to kill off but might have enhanced his political ambitions, approaches The Age and does something unexpected. He smiles.

We are in One Nation heartland – Pakenham, about 60 kilometres south-east of Melbourne, outside One Nation HQ, a storage unit staked with posters and corflutes in a warehouse estate off the Koo Wee Rup Service Road. The leader has just stepped out of an oversized Ford Ranger bearing the distinctive orange livery and logo of Pauline Hanson’s right-wing party.

One Nation is pilloried by some for its politics of racial division, lauded by others as salvation from self-serving governments blind to the pain of the people. Either way, it is one point ahead of the state Labor government in The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor poll.

The smile is unexpected because at one point, The Age and other media outlets were barred from One Nation’s events. But today there is friendliness, and no trace of shame about the embarrassing details of his private life, leaked to the media by his ex-wife, which prompted an extraordinary press conference where he defended himself, backed by his daughter and one of his stepsons.

There is also zero small talk. Pickering seems incapable of it, discussing in rapid succession how One Nation is bringing new people into politics, the Diary of a CEO podcast, the metal band Rage Against the Machine, the changing Overton window of acceptable political discourse, and his desire to form government. The party has distributed 5000 corflutes across the state ahead of next week’s election.

The core of his pitch is to do politics differently. “What is absolutely missing is that real-world, hands-on exposure to some of the systemic issues we face,” says Pickering, the favourite with the bookies to claim what would be an historic victory in Pakenham.

“Victoria is now officially the worst state in the country to do business, and that’s a crying shame, because we still produce 25 per cent of Australia’s GDP. Thirty per cent of Australia’s domestic produce still comes from Victoria.”

He laments that Victoria is per capita an economic powerhouse, but with new and increased taxes, 130 businesses closed and moved interstate in the 2023-24 financial year. “We need to make Victoria fertile ground for investment once more.”

To this end, Pickering’s agenda today consists of visits to the Pakenham cricket club, a business manufacturing glamping tents, two mental health initiatives, a truck business, the local branch of the State Emergency Service, and an evening campaign launch.

“If you are not burning the candle at both ends are you serious about saving the state?” he asks at one point on the road, after railing about how the government is stifling innovation, missing the turnoff for a mental health charity in the process.

Pickering, who is on his fourth campaign for the party, proudly points out that One Nation is not the official federal opposition, but “is steering the political agenda”.

But why should we vote for you?

“Because I’m prepared and I’ve got a proven track record, not only as state leader of this party in Victoria for five years, but through my defence career … I’ve got a proven ability to mediate and work with different groups, with different interests, to achieve better outcomes.”

“I’ve operated in high-threat, dangerous environments. Now, I understand the absolute need for a cool head and a calm hand.”

Well, it worked for World War II General Dwight D Eisenhower, whose first political office was as the 34th President of the United States.

Pickering contrasts himself with political leaders who are “largely insecure in their leadership, to the point where they need to be the face of everything”.

Like whom? “Well, like anybody that’s led this state in the last decade.”

Leaving it to the professionals, he says, means we are living under the most fiscally and morally bankrupt state government in Australian history.

“I was a part of the generation that Raged Against the Machine,” he says, referring to the 1990s metal band.

Pickering was born in Gippsland. His mum was a farmer and his dad a truckie. He left school to start his bricklaying apprenticeship at 17. His daughter Jhett was born when he was 21, according to a slick campaign video which shows them at his parents’ country property, playing guitars and tinkering with cars.

Pickering raised Jhett and her three stepbrothers with former partner Joanne Scott, who made shocking allegations against him of drug use, drink-driving and an open sexual relationship, but Pickering dealt with them in an emotional press conference in September, which some commentators thought enhanced his reputation.

He served in the Australian Army as a combat engineer and served as a trainer in Middle East combat zones as well as humanitarian and disaster relief missions in Australia. He moved to Army Reserve when he had sole custody of Jhett, then a teenager finishing school in Queensland while he worked for BHP and Coles. “She was my purpose.”

Politics was “almost entirely by accident”. He was frustrated as COVID-19 lockdowns kept him in Queensland away from his ageing parents in Melbourne.

“But then it became a point of frustration when my army unit asked me to come down and man a border point on the Victorian border, because Victoria’s in lockdown. Well, hang on, things started to not add up to me, to be honest.”

Pickering reached out to One Nation. “The biggest thing I noticed after moving back to Victoria after COVID was that my daughter didn’t have the same opportunities at 18 years old that I had in Victoria at 18 years old. Now, to me that said, well, you have failed as a society.”

Corey Christoph, 39, became friends with Pickering nearly 20 years ago, when both men were single parents raising young children.

“He has always been a very intelligent and articulate person, he’s always been a passionate friend who has your back no matter what,” says Christoph.

Christoph met Pickering when he was a bricklayer, and knows his brother and father. “(They are) tradies and truckies - the stuff that keeps the country moving. ”

The plumber says he was sceptical of Pickering’s move into politics, but that it has made him politically aware.

“I was always that guy that would go in and draw dicks on the ballot paper – (he) has given me a drive to research where my preferences go. I want to see Warren successful.”

1:24

A rapid-fire round with Warren Pickering

One Nation’s Victorian leader reveals his favourite author and his dream dinner guest.

Victoria now has One Nation’s largest membership of any state, but Pickering won’t give figures. He estimates 40 per cent of members are new to politics.

What about One Nation’s racist and anti-immigration baggage? Earlier in the month, police arrested a 64-year-old man in a One Nation cap who allegedly gave a Nazi salute.

“Give us a chance to prove those stereotypes and prejudices wrong, or at least try to understand our rationale for our positions on things. Because they’re not coming from a place of division or hate. They’re coming from a place of what’s best for protecting Australian culture and our economy,” Pickering says smoothly.

When the biggest press pack so far of the state election campaign gathered on a Monday earlier this month on the verandah of state parliament for One Nation’s live government spending tracker announcement, Pauline Hanson walked out in front of Pickering before standing to the side to let her state leader do the talking.

Previously banned outlets such as ABC, Guardian Australia and The Age were there. Pickering walked up to the array of microphones and – again – smiled.

(At another point, when asked about this habit, he responds: “I am guilty of having a sunny disposition, I must say.“)

The press conference was designed to draw attention to the state’s massive debt.

“Corruption only happens in the darkness, we are going to turn on the light,” Pickering said, adding that the aim once in government was to “open the books ourselves and revolutionise the way budgets are done in this state”.

Press gallery consensus is that Pickering performs better than expected. His riposte to sharp questions about One Nation’s vetting procedures after the disendorsement of a candidate was to point out that state Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s husband stood down as a candidate in 2014 due to social media posts.

Pickering doesn’t have to prove he is better than Premier Ben Carroll or Opposition Leader Wilson to collect votes – he just has to reinforce that he is not Premier Carroll or Opposition Leader Wilson and is outside their world.

Thus, when challenged over his refusal to get policies costed by the parliamentary budget office, he says government spending forecasts are always spectacularly wrong, and he wants to see the true state of the budget after the election before getting policies costed.

The bellwether mortgage belt seat of Pakenham has the highest rate of mortgage arrears in the country. It was historically Liberal until it was abolished in 2002, but when it was reconstituted in 2022, it was won by Labor’s Emma Vulin from the Liberal Party by a couple of hundred votes. Vulin is not recontesting after she was diagnosed with motor neurone disease.

Late last month, over lunch at the Cardinia Club in Pakenham (chosen so he can eat lunch without being interrupted by supporters), Pickering is calm when I turn up the heat, telling him point-blank that his schtick that One Nation’s political outsiders can run the state better than the professional incumbents is just naive.

“I don’t think I am,” he says mildly. “But I also believe I can’t exactly project what it’s going to be like, but I can say I’m prepared for anything.”

He credits this to the army, which is never far away, with 9am becoming “0900 hours” and his service tags hanging from the Ford Ranger’s rearview mirror. You suspect he starts the day with an exceedingly well-made bed.

Occasionally, he rolls up his sleeves to reveal the start of his arm tattoos, and, if you look closely, a touch of psoriasis on his knuckles.

He has not declared One Nation’s political donations but says billionaire Gina Rinehart is not helping to fund the campaign. “Absolutely not. Nothing. I wish it was. Donations will be declared when the Victorian Electoral Commission requires it, which will be after the election.”

One Nation had a disastrous history in Victoria. Attempts to get the party off the ground in the state in 1998 led to large protests outside party events in Hawthorn and Geelong and other places.

Their first concerted state campaign was in 2022, where One Nation polled about 3.5 per cent of the vote, and Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell was elected to the upper house as the party’s sole parliamentarian.

Their policy platform that election was a single-sheet pamphlet authorised from an address at Brisbane Airport. This year, One Nation’s plan is a 64-page A4-sized document titled “The Real Deal For Victoria” that includes policies on affordable energy, stronger police, faster justice, safer communities, and nuclear power.

Pickering also has a strategy to combat the penchant of neo-Nazis supporting the party.

“We need to break down the prejudice, prejudices, stereotypes, and some of the perceived hard edges of this party. To make it okay to support this party publicly, and I think the only way we can do that is to humanise our movement through visibility.”

During the course of the day, Pickering meets Bo Bo and Travis Davis, founders of the support charity Have Hope Inc, which they founded after losing their son Aaron to suicide in 2016 at age 23.

He also meets Paul Withall, who as part of the Zerosuicide Community Awareness Program, takes his white truck filled with about 2500 shoes – each representing a man or boy lost to suicide each year – and lays them in front of parliaments. Pickering draws a heart on the truck. The men embrace, and Pickering tells him: “We are all people, stop dividing us by race and gender.”

But how is it meeting people given the embarrassment over the revelations about his past drug use and relationship confessions?

“It’s not even something that crosses my mind, to be honest,” Pickering replies.

“I’ve reconciled myself with the light and the dark in my life. I did that a long time ago and all I’ve ever done since was try and be a better person.

“Some days you do better, some days you go backwards, but so long as you’re trying to be a better person, a better human every single day, I think you’re on the right trajectory.”

He points out young people now have their entire lives digitally recorded. Telling them that they cannot make a mistake in their 20s before living a life of redemption and public service “is not a sound message to a young generation”.

“I hope that this sets an example to the political sphere, that real people from the real world, with real, quote unquote, baggage, are going to enter the political sphere, and they’re not going to like it. Too bad. We’re coming.”

Commentators decided the One Nation leader acquitted himself well during this week’s debate against Carroll, Wilson and Greens leader Ellen Sandell.

“Pickering needed to show that One Nation will be able to mix it in the next parliament and did,” reported The Age’s Chip Le Grand, adding that “Pickering of all the leaders looked like he was enjoying the stoush”.

Prior to the debate, Pickering’s preferred premier rating was at 15 per cent, compared with 35 per cent for Wilson and 21 per cent for Carroll, according to Resolve. But Pickering is at his most emphatic on two occasions. Firstly, when stating his premiership ambitions: “We want to form government. Absolutely, we do.”

And then when talking about who in One Nation will run the show in Victoria after the election. Will it be Barnaby Joyce? Pauline Hanson?

“That will absolutely be me.”

UK ready to let in 100,000 from EU on youth scheme as reset talks go ‘to the wire’

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:52:05 GMT

Britain understood to have made concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on wider deal continue

British and EU negotiators have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 young EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme, as negotiations on the UK-EU reset talks go “down to the wire”.

Tensions in Brussels remained high on Thursday afternoon as ambassadors began crunch talks on the latest draft of the wider agreement, with sources confirming both sides were still battling over the exact nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules, in a second part of the deal.

It is understood the UK made concessions in meetings on Thursday to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, from 50,000-80,000 to a new cap of 100,000.

It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.

The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham is due in Brussels for a summit with EU leaders, the two sides still need to resolve some central sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.

France is perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said one EU diplomat.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, also including tuition fees for EU students in the UK, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.

Another EU diplomat said ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.

Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for EU students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.

“We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, including a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment and is expected to add 0.4% to British GDP.

The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”

According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.

But after a meeting of EU ambassadors that ended late on Wednesday, the issue remained unresolved. The EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”

Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.

A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
