In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.

“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.

The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international tuition fee rate.

The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was an UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.

“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.

“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”

Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:07:23 GMT

Hotly anticipated Bonnie and Clyde-inspired adventure GTA VI has gamers glued to their screens around the world

Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.

GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.

The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.

Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.

The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.

Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled ‌on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.

The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”

Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”

The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.

Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.

Among the game’s fans is Sean Little, a self-employed painter and decorator. He persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a “non-interference contract”, giving him a week off dad duties to play in peace in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland.

Myles_Away, a UK-based streamer on the Twitch platform, told the BBC he planned to play for “13 or 14 hours” on Thursday.

Rugby players face anxious wait as judges consider state of concussion case

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:57:19 GMT

Players claim brain injury caused by negligence

Defendants want cases to be struck out due to delays

Hundreds of former rugby players taking legal action against the game’s governing bodies face an anxious wait to learn whether their cases will be allowed to proceed towards trial. The players allege they are suffering from neurological damage caused by the professional negligence of the defendants, World Rugby, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) and the Rugby Football League.

After two days of hearings at the Royal Courts of Justice the presiding judges, Senior Master Cook and Mr Justice Cotter, retired to consider whether or not the case will be able to continue in anything like its current form.

The two-day hearing had been intended to deal with the selection of a shortlist of test cases from among the hundreds of claimants. Those cases would then go on to stand trial on behalf of the whole group. Instead it was entirely taken over by yet another protracted argument about whether or not the claimants should be granted relief from sanctions after their legal team, KP Law, missed a deadline set by the court for completing the disclosure of all the documents related to the testing process they underwent when they joined the action.

When KP Law joined the case in July, its lead counsel, Paul Downes KC, described the state of the disclosure process conducted by the previous firm Rylands Garth as “shambolic”. At that point all 378 of the claimants in the rugby union case, as well as the vast majority of the 173 in the rugby league case, had been struck out because of the failure of their previous law firm to disclose the relevant documents. Senior Master Cook extended the claimants relief from this sanction on the condition that KP Law was able to rectify the situation by 30 October. KP Law says it has provided 2,000 additional documents, but has now appealed for a further extension till January in order to provide the remainder.

“The litigation has been at the mercy of the complainants’ conduct for far too long,” said Nina Goolamali KC, lead counsel for World Rugby. She argued that the proposed trial date of October 2028 was not achievable or realistic given the delays in disclosure.

Neil Block KC, lead counsel for the RFU, said it would be “impossible” to hold a trial at that date, while Michael Kent KC, representing the WRU, said the case had become bogged down in “an endless debate about disclosure”. All three pushed for the cases to stand as struck out.

Downes was able to point to a list of 39 players, 22 in rugby union, 17 in rugby league, who he said were “substantially in compliance” with the court orders. “At its height I would say we have 39 compliant claimants, but the defence might dispute that and they might be right,” Downes said.

He warned that if the remainder of the cases stood as struck out, the next stage would be “a very substantial piece of satellite litigation” about which the hundreds of claimants were in breach of at the time of 30 October.

Thomas Frank admits he has a point to prove after taking reins at Crystal Palace

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:50:10 GMT

Dane was sacked by Tottenham in February

‘I know what I want and the direction we should go in’

Thomas Frank has admitted he has a point to prove on his return to management as he aims to steer Crystal Palace away from relegation trouble after taking over as manager.

The Dane was confirmed as Pierre Sage’s successor on Monday with Palace at the bottom of the table after 10 matches having conceded 24 goals – the most in the Premier League. They face a crucial trip to Coventry on Saturday and Frank admitted he had been “surprised about how good it feels” after returning to work for the first time since being sacked by Tottenham in February.

The 53-year-old spent most of the intervening period travelling, working as a pundit at the World Cup and taking in trips to Japan, Australia and his native Denmark, where he was visiting friends and family when he received the SOS call from Palace last week. Frank previously spent seven years in charge of Brentford but left Spurs after just eight months with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history. He believes he has learned from that experience.

“I think you’ve all got an ego,” he said. “Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it’s not the critics. It’s more what I can bring myself, what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better. I think that’s the big thing.

“In this world there’s a lot of clever people out there. But they only know a 10th of the truth. And that’s a 10th of the truth at Brentford and a 10th of the truth at Tottenham. That’s just the way it is – if you can’t handle that as a coach or a player or whatever, then you shouldn’t be in this business. I’m just very happy to be back in the game, very happy to be in a fantastic club, at Palace, where you walk in the door and you just feel the energy. You feel the people. It just feels good.”

Frank said he is planning to pick Roy Hodgson’s brains in the coming days after recalling a conversation they had when the former England and Palace manager was still at Selhurst Park.

“I was thinking, does it ever go away? The worry, do you get more relaxed about everything?” he asked Hodgson. “‘No chance, it’s impossible.’ I thought it would have been a little bit easier with age and experience. But in a way can’t help ourselves. I know what I want and the direction we should go in.”

Justin Cochrane – one of Thomas Tuchel’s assistants for England – has joined as first-team coach and took his first session with Palace on Monday less than 24 hours after the Nations League victory over Spain in Madrid. He is expected to be joined on Palace’s backroom staff by Bernardo Cueva, with Frank confirming that a deal with Chelsea is “very close” for the Mexican. Both worked with Frank at Brentford, where he spent almost nine years as an assistant and then manager. He is also hoping to add Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, who has been credited for his prowess on set-pieces: an area that Palace have struggled with for some time.

Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand harassed victims with YouTube message

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:30:14 GMT

Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’

The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.

After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.

A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed.

Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.

“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.

It is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.

Recent reports have claimed that Brand, who is jailed in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, is likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead after protesting his innocence.

It is understood that there has been no such proposal, and he is likely to remain in Littlehey, a specialist prison for sex offenders.

The government has no power to compel YouTube’s direct owner, Google, to remove the video, but has been in “dialogue” with the tech firm over it.

“We trust that they will do the right thing,” a Downing Street spokesperson said when asked about the standoff. They said: “The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.

“We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.”

No 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: “Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.”

A spokesperson for Google said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”

Kemi Badenoch said if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.

The Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.

“I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.”

While Surrey are running a formal recruitment process that remains open, it is understood the former captain is viewed internally as the favourite to replace Gareth Batty, who left after four years last month for an assistant coach’s job at the Chennai Super Kings.

Surrey’s recruitment is being run by the director of cricket, Alec Stewart, who played with Hollioake and previously brought him back to the club after 20 years away for one season as assistant coach under Batty in 2024, when they won the County Championship.

The former England all-rounder went on to join Kent as head coach at the end of that year, leading them to promotion back to Division One last summer in his second season at the club.

Hollioake spent almost 20 years away from cricket during which he lived in his native Australia, taking up cage fighting as well as doing charity work and travelling as he attempted to process the tragic death of his brother, Ben, in a car accident in 2002 at the age of 24.

Hollioake captained Surrey for six years towards the end of a playing career in which he played four Test matches for England and 35 one-day internationals, 14 as captain. As Surrey captain he led the side to three championship titles before retiring relatively early at the age of 33.

On returning to Surrey as a member of Batty’s backroom staff Hollioake told the Guardian that he was “coming home” and, despite his success at Kent, the 55-year-old would find the head coach’s job at the Oval difficult to turn down.

Surrey have signalled their intention to bounce back strongly after a disappointing seventh-place finish in the championship last season, signing Jimmy Anderson on a one-year deal to complement an experienced squad that contains nine players on England and Wales Cricket Board central contracts.

While Surrey’s recruitment has some way to run, Finch is understood to have agreed to join MI London to replace Kieron Pollard, who has in effect been promoted by the part-owners Reliance Industries to become Mumbai Indians’ head coach.

The former Australian one-day captain will be taking on his first head coaching job, and may also join Pollard’s backroom team in Mumbai.

England braced for All Black-lash in the ultimate test of their mini-upturn

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:15:05 GMT

New Zealand should provide a huge reaction to their shock defeat in Wales with enticing clash even more instructive

From the Bay of Islands on the northern tip of New Zealand to Invercargill in the deep south, there is rare unanimity this week. Back in the day there would be parochial arguments about, say, the ratio of Aucklanders to Cantabrians in the starting XV. This time there is nationwide recognition that absolutely nothing matters beyond a bounce-back win for the boys in black on Saturday.

It is the inevitable upshot of last weekend’s seismic defeat by Wales, a result that prompted Dave Rennie, the head coach, to admit his reshuffled team had “let ourselves and our country down”. The former All Black scrum-half Justin Marshall went a step further. “We were arrogant enough to think that we could make those changes and still protect our history, and now look what’s happened,” a wounded Marshall told the GBRNRZ podcast.

And even in this noisiest of rugby weeks, the New Zealand teamsheet speaks loudest. Injuries aside this is the strongest selection these touring All Blacks could have fielded and the Kiwi desire for atonement is almost tangible. “They’ve got 500 more caps this week,” said Steve Borthwick, primed for a significant Black-lash. “It’s a very different proposition of a team.”

But hang on. England’s lineup for this ultimate test of their latest mini-upturn is also pretty much their best current squad, give or take the injured Manny Feyi-Waboso and Alex Mitchell and which of the Curry twins is available. The message it sends is also straightforward amid the mind games and ref baiting elsewhere, albeit with a subtle reference here and there. “I think the last time we had this depth was about a year ago,” suggested Borthwick, quietly referring his audience to his side’s 33-19 win against New Zealand last November.

This time around, by and large, he simply wants the team to go out and show the intent and accuracy they displayed from the start of their 45-22 win against Australia: “Two weeks ago I was saying the players were bringing the fire in their club shirts and I want them to bring that in an England shirt.” Don’t over-clutter their minds and identify a specific target and, as a general rule, England tend to respond well to the big occasion, particularly at home.

It is easy to forget, though, just how many selectorial roundabouts England have circumnavigated to reach this point. Of the starting XV who beat Scott “Razor” Robertson’s leaden-footed visitors last year there are no survivors behind the scrum and only one – Ben Earl – in the back row. Where, previously, Freddie Steward, Tom Roebuck, Ollie Lawrence, Fraser Dingwall and George Ford were the backline men in possession, the baton has now passed to George Furbank, Will Joseph, Henry Slade, Seb Atkinson and Fin Smith.

Which makes Saturday’s enticing fixture even more instructive. Not since the 2002-03 season – and that was a first – have England beaten the All Blacks twice in a row. And everyone knows what Clive Woodward’s squad subsequently went on to do at an upcoming World Cup in Australia. Then, too, everyone knew where they stood in the selectorial pecking order when everyone was fit.

Borthwick, accordingly, does not want to dwell on the ramped-up threat the All Blacks may or may not offer aerially or at the breakdown at the expense of diluting his own team’s self-belief. “We’re well aware of the history and how many times results have gone against England,” he said. “We’re well aware they’re an older team with 350 more caps than us.

“[But] at the same time we recognise we’re playing at our own stadium, in front of the players’ families and fans. These last couple of weekends the players have produced performances that have made their families and the England fans proud. We want to make sure we put out that level of performance this weekend.”

Borthwick also reckons one of the key springboards to victory will be a fast start, all the more so given the momentum that Wales established straight out of the blocks in Cardiff. “I want the players to jump into this game,” said the head coach. “Too many times I’ve watched the players watch, metaphorically, the start of the game. One of the most pleasing things this month is the way the team has started. I want that this weekend.”

If England can also match Wales’s defensive hunger, so much the better from their perspective. As New Zealand showed in the Greatest Rivalry series against South Africa, they can strike from anywhere and the restoration of, among others, the quicksilver Damian McKenzie, the talismanic Jordie Barrett and the prolific Will Jordan should reinstate the cutting edge so visibly lacking in the final quarter at the Principality Stadium.

There is also a 150th cap for Beauden Barrett, a remarkable achievement worthy of global recognition. Barrett is only the fourth player and the first back to reach the milestone in top-level men’s rugby history while his teammate Anton Lienert-Brown is set to win his 100th cap as well. Twickenham in November can be a tough place to go but in Test rugby, as both centurions will tell you, plenty can change from one week to the next.

Woman raped by strangers after being drugged by husband calls for consent law changes

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:54:01 GMT

Four men convicted of sexual assault and rape of Joanne Young, whose husband advertised her on UK swinging websites

Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years

A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday.

Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

On Thursday, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.

The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries.

The Crown Prosecution Service said it was the first time a jury had convicted multiple defendants relating to organised drug-facilitated sexual assault in England.

After the verdicts, Wiltshire police said that although rare, the true scale of drug-facilitated sexual offences in the UK could be significantly underreported.

In a statement outside court, Joanne Young – whose bravery was praised by the judge – said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.

Saying that she now lives “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, she added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed.

“At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.

A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, had admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

A spokesperson for Wiltshire police, which investigated Young’s offending, said other victims in similar cases may not know they had been targeted.

He added: “While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly underreported crime type.

“Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging.”

Joanne said the abuse had had a devastating impact on her life and the lives of her children but that she hoped the verdict would give other victims of abuse the confidence to come forward.

“The court has today shown that there will be consequences for those who make the choice to abuse,” she said. “I’m determined that their choices will not define me, and I will now use my experience to try to help others. I also owe it to myself to live the best life I can with my children and loved ones as we move forward.”

Mr Justice Saini refused bail applications for the four men convicted on Thursday, telling them they all faced “significant custodial sentences”.

All of the men, including Young and Hamilton, will be sentenced on 21 and 22 December at Winchester crown court.

Young, a father of three, pleaded guilty in January to a total of 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife. He also admitted three charges of making indecent images of children, one of possessing prohibited images of children in July 2024 and four counts of possessing an extreme pornographic image between January 2019 and January 2024.

Over more than a decade, Young – who served as a Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 – drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

Prosecutors told the court the case was about whether it was ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first.

Sanderson-Doyle responded to an online advert in 2015 and visited the couple’s home in June 2016. Young filmed him sexually assaulting Joanne as she was drugged, blindfolded and restrained, and heard saying “No”.

Wilkins went to the home in July 2016. Young filmed Wilkins abusing Joanne who again was blindfolded, restrained and seemingly asleep, without obtaining her consent. Police footage of his arrest shows the officers identifying him through distinctive tattoos.

Macksoni visited and raped Joanne in February 2017, while Hassan sexually assaulted her in February 2023. Messages and digital evidence showed Young arranged for Hassan to visit and Hassan had sexual contact with her while she believed he was her husband.

Speaking after the verdicts, James Foster, a specialist prosecutor at the CPS, said: “These men chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.

“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse.

“During the trial, Macksoni, Wilkins, Sanderson-Doyle and Hassan hid behind the claim that they believed she was freely entering into a sexual relationship with them, despite never seeking reassurances that this was in fact the case.”

It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:36:23 GMT

From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

More likely this new class consciousness springs from their sharpened experience of life chances among their own generation. They are more likely to think class has become increasingly significant over the past two decades and they’re right: within their own generation, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has found inequality in the UK is growing more than within other cohorts.

The class antennae of young people have been honed by the obstacles they face that older generations felt less, when class was better disguised by generally rising living standards. What they see around them is the growing inheritocracy – the widening chasm between those who get substantial help from parents at crucial points in their lives and those with no backup.

The IFS has been sending warnings for years: choosing your parents well matters more than your own talents and hard work. Rewards for merit and effort are declining – and young people see it everywhere. Political platitudes about working hard and playing by the rules ignore the evidence they see with their own eyes. For those receiving inheritances in the UK, the gap between expectations at the top and bottom is greatly widening: the bottom fifth are projected to get 5% of their lifetime income from inheritance, while the top fifth, already better paid, could get 29%. The better off are likely to receive it earlier, making it easier to buy a house, take time to choose their job carefully, save less and retire earlier.

As so many young people – many more than the million Neets – struggle to make their way into a career they are qualified for, they can see how class matters far more than money and inheritance. Getting a leg-up from your family background and connections, or just worldly advice from those in the know, is worth everything. The under-35s consider nepotism a serious issue: nearly twice as many are concerned about it as among the apparently socially contented over-55s. This week’s LSE research on cross-class friendships in the US and UK was heartening: they make jokes to get over the awkwardness of revelations of privilege, described by Sam Friedman and Rose Butler as the “omnipresent threat” between them.

How well I recognise that. Admitting to being middle class can be embarrassing. That’s why I have tried in my memoir, An Uneasy Inheritance: My Family and Other Radicals, to be honest about how powerfully privilege is passed down the generations, bequeathing self-confidence and security with second and third chances if you mess up. My family of successful leftwing professionals were all confounded by how to square their advantages with their beliefs – sometimes comically, never denying that privilege, just blushing.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

It’s hardly surprising that 40% of those under 35 in Britain think they would benefit from being part of another class. How strange is the social obtuseness or denial of the over-55s, of whom only 14% believe they would have done better if they came from another class. They may be victims of the classlessness myth spread with skill by the right to hide how their wealth soared in the 1980s. Some may be relics of my own youth in the 1960s, a decade rife with the popular social fantasy that we were all classless now, with the same clothes, hair and music, sitting on and smoking the same grass at the Isle of Wight festival, on the same anti-Vietnam demos. The 1960s and 70s did see inequality reducing, yet when I went to university in 1966, only 6% of my cohort did the same.

This class awakening among young people ripples around the world. In Britain, as the wealth divide within the young generation widens, Labour seems to be catching the moment. Andy Burnham and Alan Milburn this week pledged a seismic shift in priorities towards young people, with the recent announcement of the breaking of the triple lock on pensions by 2030 also signalling the way to a generational redistribution.

Most shocking, but barely remarked on in the media coverage of Milburn’s tome of a report, was the massive decline in public spending on young people compared with steep rises for the old. In figures taken from the Intergenerational Foundation, he reports that between 2004 and 2024, pensioners in Britain got 55% more, while the sum per child only rose by 20%. As Milburn writes, this is “neither sustainable nor is it fair”.

To push for redistribution of opportunity, private wealth and public money, this awakening of youth class consciousness needs to organise into active politics.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:30:09 GMT

A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

The bar is high; in 2007, the ICJ found Serbia responsible for failing to prevent genocide in Srebrenica in 1995, but not for directly committing it. Genocidal intent must be the “only reasonable inference” from a pattern of conduct. Legal scholars have pointed out that that need not preclude its coexistence with other aims. The court has not changed the standard, but shown how it can be applied.

Yet even before the ruling, the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, had accused Navi Pillay, this year’s Nobel peace laureate, of intending to lower the legal threshold so that it could be “weaponised against American and allied soldiers”. There is grave concern that the US will impose sanctions on Ms Pillay and fellow judges, as it has on the international criminal court, which holds individuals rather than states accountable. Israel is currently before the ICJ on genocide charges, and the relevance of Thursday’s finding to Gaza is obvious.

But this case is first and foremost important as an attempt to bring some measure of justice for the Rohingya, whose suffering began decades ago and continues. Survivors in refugee camps greeted the findings with applause as they watched the session on Thursday. The UN warned in August that human rights in Myanmar had hit a new low, citing the “ever-worsening brutal abuse” of members of the minority. The military has forcibly conscripted those it despises in the civil war – fuelling atrocities against them by one of the junta’s adversaries, the Arakan army. Those who have found safety abroad also face returning to danger. India has repatriated Rohingya refugees, and there are growing concerns that Malaysia may send back many more, following a visit by Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s junta.

Myanmar now has two years to set out plans for full restitution, including the safe and voluntary return home that survivors still seek. If and when it fails, the court will take up the issue. But governments must play their part. The UK’s expulsion of Myanmar’s military attache was a small but welcome step. It must do much more to step up the pressure on the junta and other parties in Myanmar to ensure the safety of the Rohingya, and urge other governments to do likewise. States that believe in international law must do all they can to back this ruling and ensure that it has real consequences, both to protect the Rohingya and to show support for the court itself.

The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:25:09 GMT

For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem

The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months.

The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes, is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester, rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed, wrote, coded and soundtracked its virtual world.

The video game portrays a country awash with vice and hypocrisy, where the American dream is alive and well – provided you trample on someone else to achieve it. There is no way to win if you play by the rules. In the game’s main hub, Vice City, lawyers and police are scarcely more honest than drug dealers and thieves, while conspiracy theorists, crypto scammers and narcissistic influencers abound. But it would be wrong to think that the game simply revels in corruption. By giving its two main characters, Jason and Lucia, histories and vulnerabilities, the game asks players to sympathise with people who are both society’s victims and its perpetrators.

The GTA series has long faced criticism for its violence and casual misogyny, treating women as sex objects or punchlines. GTA VI marks a shift. Lucia, its first female lead, confronts the sexism around her, while other women emerge as characters in their own right. Even the violence, reviews suggest, feels less gratuitous. The game portrays a Trumpian America where wealth, spectacle and criminality blend together. But its satire no longer relies quite so heavily on making women its targets.

Why is one of the most culturally important depictions of the US a fantasy in which the American dream can be pursued most freely by breaking the law? This is a question that hangs over GTA VI. It was created by a team of 5,000 people, many of whom are based outside the US (Rockstar, the company behind the game, is headquartered in Scotland). This is an America created largely by outsiders. But then, as one of Rockstar’s lead developers Rob Nelson said: “We’re all outsiders to this version of America.”

Mr Nelson thinks that the game’s real innovation may not be the scale of the world that Rockstar has built, but the morally complex relationship that its developers have created between the player and this imagined world. Reviewers remark on behaving more considerately while playing the game, and how it rewards attentiveness in some of its fictional relationships and encourages players to talk their way out of trouble rather than immediately reaching for a gun. After decades of allowing players to behave badly online with impunity, GTA VI doesn’t necessarily want them to be good, but it asks them to think twice about being bad.

Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:15:48 GMT

Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

Business live – latest updates

Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company.

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees.

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia. More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn.

The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing.

But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year).

Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years.

Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical.

What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate.

Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

“Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”.

Here’s how we can give Neets a fighting chance

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:07:42 GMT

Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle the youth jobs crisis

Why is Labour reinventing the wheel (Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people, 16 November)? There is an easier and less discriminatory way – and that is through the mainstream education system. This would not dump these young people into a post-16 Neet silo.

Further education (FE) colleges have been working in the area of young people’s training and further education for decades. Yet the sector has been continually undermined by successive governments allowing terrible salary discrimination against the FE sector and by the need to chase numbers (and cash) for A-level-type students. And why has the FE sector has not spoken up effectively for itself?

At the start of my career in an FE college, I taught apprentices – 16-year-olds plus full-time and day-release students – in plumbing, childcare, pre-nursing, catering etc, and advanced apprentices on residential bloc courses. These combined basic education and general studies – learning through training and specific skills training – all working with local and national companies and skilled careers advisers. This all took place in one local college, alongside full- and part-time GCSE and A-level courses for all ages. No discrimination.

Call FE colleges community colleges, and this will start to make sense. Call it Labour investing in the educational sector, not reducing welfare through the back door. The dispossessed young deserve a fresh start at 16 if they want – nurturing, educating and training with respect and parity in the community, and with proper funding, full- or part-time. This is what properly funded FE colleges could be best positioned to provide. Prof Anne Deighton Wolfson College, University of Oxford

Amid all the pitch-rolling and fanfare accompanying Alan Milburn’s report, what stands out in sharp relief is his ignorance of the challenges that disabled people like me experience in the workplace. With about 50% of disabled people and 73% of visually impaired people unemployed, there is little evidence that employers are onboard with his proposals.

For Milburn’s plan to stand a chance of succeeding, the government needs to take two steps. First, to take disability discrimination as seriously as other forms of discrimination. Currently, the Equality Act is so porous that employers can discriminate against disabled people with impunity.

Second, they urgently need to overhaul the Access to Work scheme to ensure that disabled people who are fortunate enough to be offered a job receive the additional support they need in a timely manner. I know disabled people who have had offers of employment withdrawn because Access to Work has taken too long.

Without making these changes, Milburn’s proposals will not get the support they need from the people who matter most – young disabled people. Tom Walker Liverpool

It is interesting that in all the discussions I’ve heard about ways to help young people into work, only the private sector has been mentioned in relation to apprenticeships and work experience. No mention has been made of the vast state employers such as the NHS.

As the biggest UK employer, does this government not see itself as having a significant direct role to play? Similarly, local government hasn’t entered the frame. Without the active involvement of these institutions, Milburn’s objectives of making a significant dent in the existence of nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training will never be met. There are just not enough hotels, restaurants or shops. Adrin Neatrour Newcastle upon Tyne

Amid debate over the billions needed to tackle youth joblessness let us not overlook a step that costs nothing. Employers replying kindly to every young applicant, including unsolicited ones, would stop young people feeling unworthy of even basic human courtesy. Small things matter. Alan C Coppin Former chair, Include charity

Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:07:23 GMT

Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework

Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them (Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November)? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt?

We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it?

Of course, academic integrity matters. There is an important distinction between using AI as a cognitive resource and passing off the result as entirely one’s own work. But placing the ethical burden of navigating this technological tsunami on young people while the adult world struggles to catch up is an extraordinary dereliction of pedagogical responsibility and care. Our job is to provide future-proof guidance and teach the young how to engage with and live and work alongside technologies that our generation continues to welcome so naively and unquestioningly into the world. Berthold Schoene Professor emeritus, Manchester Metropolitan University

As a person of Indian origin and a staunch supporter of Amnesty International and a person’s right to freedom of speech and thought, I am conflicted about my view on whether people like Nathan Cofnas should be allowed a platform or not (Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students, 15 November).

A huge part of me wants the likes of Cofnas to be allowed to speak provided there is a fair challenge and a decent debate where their ideas are debunked smartly, articulately and intelligently based on science and facts.

At the same time, I don’t want to hear their vile views, and more importantly I don’t want their ideas influencing young minds. I understand and share Ebony Riddell Bamber’s feelings of being insulted and in some way diminished by these people.

Net net, I come out on the side of freedom of speech and thought, which must at all times have a balancing debater to challenge their views. I think a solo platform is dangerous and wrong, and threatens the very values that freedom of speech and thought tries to protect. Let there be challenge and debate, and let’s show people with these views how flawed their arguments are. So Cofnas can have his platform, but let there also be a contrary speaker who can debate and balance the discussion. Raxa Mehta High Barnet, London

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:00:08 GMT

David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever

We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature.

Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. But there is nonetheless such a huge amount of energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste and film-making style to be had here.

Like Tarantino’s Kill Bill: Volume 2, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth repeats the ideas and characters of the first film a little pedantically, certainly, and the ending is rather truncated – again, I think, a function of the story being spread across film and book. But it maintains a headlong craziness with a flair so few can come anywhere near. It is a movie that once again gives us the brutality and scuzz of Ed Bunker, the urban crime-pastoral of Elmore Leonard, and naturally the classic Tarantino trope of two tough guys rolling up in a car, a little before the appointed hour, but in time for some backtalk and bickering. (Here, some loathsome hitmen argue about the illogical house-numbering sequence on LA’s Mulholland Drive.) Fincher’s direction perhaps speeds things up in the scene transitions, quicker than the chapter-by-chapter prolixity that Tarantino would have favoured. Female characters also tend to keep their shoes and socks on.

The setting is now almost 10 years on from the first film, the Los Angeles of 1977, the time and place of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Boogie Nights, in fact, and also the presidency of Jimmy Carter, though it is only Nixon who gets a namecheck. Sharon Tate is on TV advertising cigarettes. Cliff has grown a moustache and quit the stunt business, having sustained an injury that gives him a slight limp; his old pal Rick Dalton is apparently making a TV show in Australia.

These days, Cliff has moved out of his trailer and lives with his cantankerous old pawnshop-proprietor dad Gus (Peter Weller) and presides over a portfolio of side-hustles. He’s a movie theatre projectionist (like Pitt’s character in Fight Club) at LA’s historic New Beverly Cinema, a coyly proprietorial touch from the screenwriter and the venue’s present-day owner. Cliff tends bar at various joints on various nights of the week, has a gig at a demolition derby, and maintains unofficial connections with the screen acting world, which causes people to recognise him all over the city.

Most importantly, he is a discreet fixer and intermediary for influential people who are being extorted. Cliff is bemused to be contacted out of the blue by smart, willowy talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), a former movie critic once mentored by Pauline Kael, and this would appear to be how Tarantino has taken his idea for a movie critic character that was going to be the subject of his “final” movie. (Personally I was disappointed that the LA Times’s Kevin Thomas isn’t the one to have taken Karen under his wing.)

Karen, with whom Cliff falls passionately in love, introduces him to her client Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), who is currently acting in a TV show with blaxploitation star “Hot” Rod Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). We get a very amusing pastiche-montage of Charlie’s B-picture and TV credits, like the ones for Rick Dalton in the first picture. Charlie is fascinated by Cliff’s military record in the second world war, and Cliff agrees to take on a difficult job for him, his heart softened by the fact that he once had a tendresse for Charlie’s worldly wife Toni (Carla Cugino). So Cliff enters, or re-enters, or maybe just gets further into, a world of violent crime.

The film can only work with the drawlingly imperturbable good humour of Brad Pitt as Cliff. His performance is endlessly watchable and entertaining, but also enigmatic, in that Cliff’s battle-hardened experience of the world has left him with an easygoing carapace of calm. Cliff is essentially surprised by nothing, affected by nothing; this is a function of Cliff’s character and Pitt’s own almost sphinx-like address to the camera. It is Cliff’s inability to be seriously rattled by anything which provides the ironic torsion and charge to the movie. It is Pitt’s great comic creation.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is in UK and US cinemas from 25 November, and Australian cinemas from 26 November; it is on Netflix from 23 December.

Cop31 told it risks being ‘ghost’ summit as all mentions of ‘fossil fuels’ removed from draft text

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:58:21 GMT

Draft agreement also fails to show how developing countries will receive financial help to deal with climate crisis

Cop31 live – latest updates

Every mention of “fossil fuels” has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”.

The second draft of the key text, released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis.

Panama made the unusual move of writing to the Turkish and Australian presidents of the talks announcing that unless all its demands were met, it would block any outcome.

“We have listened carefully to the speeches of these days,” read the letter signed by Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro. “They are beautiful speeches. But while we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed … Outside this room and this conference, the world needs and expects radical change from us, and we are not delivering it.”

Cop negotiations require consensus, meaning that Panama’s stance, especially if supported by others, has the potential to upend the talks in their final hours.

The “cover decision” text is likely to be the main outcome of Cop31, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris agreement in limiting temperature rises and staving off the worst ravages of global heating.

But in slimming down by half an unwieldy 18-page first draft issued on Monday, the joint presidencies of Australia and Turkey cut many of the commitments – including a phaseout of fossil fuels, and stronger support for developing countries to adapt to extreme weather – that vulnerable countries were relying on.

Countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels at Cop28 in 2023, but negotiations since have failed to flesh out the ambition.

“Frontline communities will look on with despair,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank. “If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost Cop. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”

His verdict – that the talks had been “muzzled” by the refusal of some fossil fuel producing countries to allow a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” to stand – was echoed by campaigners around the world.

Rachitaa Gupta, global coordinator of the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice, said: “The cause of the climate crisis is clear, as well as who should pay for it. What’s remaining is the global north’s political resolve to provide this finance. The moral bankruptcy of the global north is very visible to all of us in the global south.”

Campaigners urged developing countries to reject the new drafts and keep fighting for a better outcome. “We are on the brink of an outrageous and utterly embarrassing lack of leadership by the Cop31 presidencies,” said Andreas Sieber, of the campaign group 350. org. “They have reduced one of the defining challenges of our time to an inconvenient paragraph they would rather delete.

“Rich countries’ failure on finance [for poorer nations] is a historic disgrace. They expect developing countries to shoulder the cost of a global transition while refusing to provide the means to deliver it. This is not a failure of technical negotiations. It is a shameless abdication of political responsibility.”

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of the negotiations, laid the blame for the weak text firmly at the door of the countries present. “We have put forward what we think, based on all our consultations, gives us the best chance of the most ambitious results that consensus will allow,” he said.

His Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum, the president of the conference, said there was “great enthusiasm” among the countries negotiating, and that the latest text showed a “strong commitment to the Paris agreement”.

He defended the exclusion of the words “fossil fuels” by saying it had been agreed at previous Cops. “I don’t think there’s any backsliding,” he said.

The commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” was exchanged in the text for the much weaker pledge to an “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience”, though there was reaffirmation that the goal of holding global temperature rises to 1.5C above preindustrial levels would remain central – even though it is now certain to be breached.

The pledge that 35% of global final energy demand should be met by electricity from 2035 was downgraded to a voluntary option among a suite of measures.

In a packed afternoon on the penultimate official day of the fortnight-long talks, a separate negotiating strand on climate finance produced a largely empty document, showing nations had failed to make progress on delivering the $300bn a year developed countries have pledged to the developing world by 2035.

Separately, at a historic leaders’ summit in Shenzhen between China, the US and Russia, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin vowed to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. Tlou Ramaru of the African Group of Negotiators described this as “hypocrisy”.

As countries digested the contents of the draft texts, the dual Cop presidencies of Australia and Turkey began to hold meetings with the main negotiating groups and individual countries, which were scheduled to go on through the night on Thursday, and probably into Friday morning. Although the talks are scheduled to end on Friday at 6pm in Turkey, Cops have a habit of over-running.

Jimmy Dimly is back and we should treasure him while we can

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:54:48 GMT

Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit

Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor

Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”.

As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024. A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip.

This time, the Tories are determined to take themselves a little more seriously. With the emphasis on a little. Enter James Cleverly. One of this column’s favourite sons. It’s only with his reappearance that you realise quite how much you’ve missed him. James has the CV of a political heavyweight. But at heart he still is, and always will be, Jimmy Dimly. The foreign secretary who rubbished Rishi Sunak’s Rwanda plan as “bat-shit crazy” only to find himself moved sideways to home secretary where he was forced to defend and implement it.

Things like this keep happening to Jimmy D. Disaster follows him around like an ultra-needy cockapoo. Yet you can’t help loving him for it. Because there’s something rather sweet about a man who takes himself quite so seriously. Never realising that the joke’s on him. People are laughing at him, not with him. A man who always seems to be living his life several sentences behind every conversation. Stuck in second gear. Someone who means well, but can’t quite keep up. We don’t know yet if Sadiq is planning to stand for a fourth term in 2028, but he may be looking at Dimly and thinking things could have been a lot worse.

Inside a central London office suite on Thursday morning, Jimmy D and the two other Tory mayoral candidates, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari, gathered to hear the results of the first round of voting. Or only round. The returning officer announced that Dimly had received 86% of the vote and was duly elected. Interestingly, we weren’t told how many people had voted. I guess it’s less embarrassing than saying Jimmy had received 43 votes. Fair to say that this is not an election that has gripped the Tory party. Nor London. No one is much interested in who is going to be runner-up again to Labour.

Jimmy D gave a big smile. This was his moment and he was going to milk it. He strode to the lectern to address a largely uninterested audience. First, he wanted to thank Festus and Sara for the brilliant campaigns they had run and for the lively conversations they had sparked. “You are an asset to London and the whole country,” he said. Er … hang on a mo. What campaigns and what conversations? This was the first time most of London had heard of Festus and Sara, so it was tragic that the acclaim was for their imminent return to obscurity.

“Nobody loves London more than me,” Dimly continued. So he wasn’t planning to stand again as an MP. He was all in for London. This sounded more like a man clinging to a life raft than an endorsement of the capital. In truth, he has always looked out of sorts in Kemi Badenoch’s Reform-lite Conservative party. He had been more of an old-school Tory who was never comfortable just trashing foreigners and people on benefits. So this was more a last chance of extending his political career while maintaining some self-respect rather than a statement of commitment. He might be a bit crap, but he was a bit crap with a heart.

We then got five minutes of a love letter to London. “The answer to ‘why London’ is because London is London,” he said gnomically. At times like these, Dimly excels himself. We should treasure him while we still have him. London was the best city in the world. Then, as if realising he had just given a party broadcast on behalf of Sadiq, he gave us five minutes on why London was the most rubbish city in the world.

Basically everything that was wrong with London was the fault of “Khan”. Jimmy couldn’t bring himself to use his first name. Everywhere you went there were people being murdered in front of your eyes and motorists had been deprived of the opportunity of driving at high speed and killing cyclists and pedestrians. Only Dimly could make London a fun place again. To all those people who had been up all night playing Grand Theft Auto VI, he was going to turn the capital into a video game. London was going to be bigger than big. So big no one would ever miss it again. Or something.

There was just time for a few questions. How did he feel about having supported Truss’s mini-budget and being pro-Brexit? On the whole, Londoners weren’t that keen on either of these. Two-thirds of Londoners reckoned Brexit had been a disaster. How was he going to reconcile that one? Now Jimmy D struggled with his hearing. Turned out he couldn’t make out the Brexit word.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

He didn’t want to talk about the past, he was the future. Except when he was talking about the Wrath of Khan. “Khan hates London,” he insisted. “What’s more Andy Burnham hates London too.” In the DimlyVerse, neither Sadiq nor Andy would be happy until the capital had been razed to the ground.

What about the commitment to abandoning net zero and membership of the ECHR? Those were Kemi’s red lines. Were they his? Jimmy shuffled awkwardly and mumbled “Yes”. A lie. Dimly believes in both. As do most Londoners. There has almost certainly been a pact that Kemi will look the other way so long as Jimmy doesn’t make a big deal about the differences in their politics.

Dimly just wanted to re-emphasise his commitment to London. He was all for the things that Londoners wanted. And if he wasn’t, he would do his best to pretend that he was. He couldn’t say fairer than that. “I am only going to comment on my comments,” he said in conclusion. Sometimes, it’s hard not to love him. At the very least, the next two years will be a golden time for sketch writers.
