How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:20:32 GMT

Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind

At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases.

According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK, fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard.

“Adopting a whole new lifestyle can feel daunting, especially when you’ve been eating a certain way your entire life,” says Alyssa Fontaine, a registered dietitian and nutritionist, a vegan, and founder of Plant-Based Dietitians USA & Canada.

In her experience, people worry switching to a plant-based diet means missing out on essential nutrients and giving up on dishes and traditions they enjoy. None of this has to be the case, she says.

So how does one start eating a plant-based diet? We asked experts.

A plant-based diet is one that consists primarily of – you guessed it – plants. This includes fruits and vegetables as well as nuts, legumes, whole grains and seeds. Typically, a plant-based diet excludes any foods derived from animals, like meat and dairy.

Not necessarily.

Per the Vegan Society, the oldest vegan charity in the world, which coined the term in 1944: “Veganism is a philosophy and a way of living which seeks to exclude – as far as is possible and practicable – all forms of exploitation of, and cruelty to, animals for food, clothing, or any other purpose; and by extension, promotes the development and use of animal-free alternatives for the benefit of animals, humans and the environment.”

In other words: “Veganism is not simply a diet devoid of animal foods, but a social justice movement, value and belief system that includes animals when considering how others ought to be treated,” says Taylor Wolfram, a registered dietitian and longtime vegan.

A person eating a plant-based diet may not consider themselves vegan, and could still buy animal products such as wool clothes or leather accessories.

Fontaine says she believes the three biggest benefits are health, environmental sustainability and animal welfare.

Health benefits: From a health perspective, plant-based diets are associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular disease, a lower risk of type 2 diabetes, and a decreased likelihood of various types of cancer including prostate, breast and colorectal.

Plant-based diets also tend to be lower in saturated fats and cholesterol, and higher in fiber, antioxidants and phytochemicals.

In her work with clients transitioning from an omnivorous diet to a plant-based one, Fontaine says, the biggest difference she sees is in fiber intake.

“When we replace meat with plant-based protein sources, such as legumes, nuts and seeds, we’re also adding fiber to our diet,” she explains.

“Eating a fiber-rich diet can make a huge difference in improving digestion and bowel regularity,” she says, a significant benefit given that 40% to 50% of Americans struggle with digestive issues, according to a survey by the American Gastroenterological Association.

Environmental sustainability: It’s hard to overstate the environmental impacts. Damien Watson, spokesperson for the Vegan Society, points to a 2023 study that found that, compared with high-meat diets, vegan diets have been associated with 75% lower greenhouse gas emissions, 66% lower biodiversity loss and 54% lower water use.

Animal welfare: Besides their devastating environmental impact, industrial farms have been criticized for keeping animals in inhumane conditions.

“The biggest benefit of a vegan lifestyle is living in alignment with your values and treating animals with respect,” says Wolfram.

“For me, personally, being vegan means that I live my life, as much as I can, doing no harm,” agrees Watson. “That’s good for my emotional wellbeing, as well as good for my physical health, and that of other living creatures and the world we inhabit.”

One of the biggest misconceptions about eating a plant-based diet is that you won’t get enough protein, says Fontaine.

“‘Where do you get your protein?’ If I had a pound for every time someone asked me that question …” says Watson. His protein comes primarily from beans (including soy and tofu), pulses, peas, nuts, broccoli and “loads of other healthy plants”.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“Inadequate protein intake is not a concern on a vegan or plant-based diet when the diet is properly planned,” says Sue-Ellen Anderson-Hayes, spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, adding that nutrition deficiencies occur “in all dietary patterns” without proper planning.

For further proof, Wolfram points to the numerous high-performing athletes who have adopted plant-based diets, like soccer star Alex Morgan, Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton and NBA player Chris Paul.

Start small: You don’t need to change everything all at once.

“I recommend substituting some animal foods with plant foods,” says Wolfram. For example, try black bean tacos instead of beef, soy milk in your cereal instead of dairy, or tofu stir-fries. “It doesn’t have to be complicated,” she says.

“Baby steps,” agrees Anderson-Hayes: put progress over perfection, and remember that not every day will look the same.

Identify your go-to meals: One of the greatest challenges in transitioning to a plant-based lifestyle is not knowing what to cook, says Fontaine. “Most of us have our established meals,” she says.

Changing your diet requires finding new recipes, seeking out new ingredients at the store and learning how to prepare them. But, Fontaine says, “spending a little extra time on meal prepping and developing new cooking skills in the beginning can make a big difference”.

One thing she often suggests to vegan clients is the “vegan go-to 10 method”: finding 10 vegan meals you love and making them on repeat until preparing them becomes second nature. Once these are in place, planning meals, shopping and cooking becomes much easier.

More from How to start:

How to start meditating

How to start weightlifting

How to start budgeting

How to start running

Research supplements and/or fortified foods: The one vitamin that vegans need to be particularly conscientious about consuming is B12, which helps support the nervous system and is not made by plants, says Watson.

Anderson-Hayes also suggests regularly consuming sea vegetables or seaweed for iodine, and fortified foods like nutritional yeast and soy milk for vitamin D and calcium.

Learn how to order at restaurants: It is easier than ever to eat a plant-based diet, says Watson. “It is rare now to find a restaurant that doesn’t offer a vegan option, and most supermarkets have whole sections devoted to plant-based food,” he says.

This can require some forethought. Anderson-Hayes recommends checking out restaurant menus beforehand to see what your options will be. Look for items like “black bean burgers, black bean and corn salad, hummus, falafels or falafel burgers”, she says.

Consult an expert: A plant-based diet can be “healthy, nutritious and sustainable”, but it isn’t “one-size-fits-all”, says Fontaine.

“Everyone is at a different stage of life and has different nutritional needs,” she says.

Because of this, it can be helpful to work with a registered dietitian, says Wolfram. If this is not in your budget, she also recommends reputable free online resources, like VeganHealth. org. “It’s written by vegan, registered dietitians,” she explains.

Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:14:55 GMT

Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:13:23 GMT

Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:27:08 GMT

Milburn’s review doesn’t ask what kind of work young people will be going into: zero hours, minimum wage, mind-numbing. Do we have the guts to solve that?

One big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government.

Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself. These figures have not appeared in any of this week’s coverage, but to understand the review’s context and its chances of success they are vital.

Let’s start with 1,500%. That is how much more the press talks about “economic inactivity” now, compared with 2017. Back then, a newspaper reader would barely see the phrase; by 2024, it was appearing literally thousands of times, often on front pages. There was a similar huge rise in the use of the term “sicknote”. From near-silence a few years ago, these phrases have become a daily drumbeat, sounded across print and broadcast. And their major motif is young people.

Yet it is not news, not even close. As Milburn says, the Neet rate has been roughly the same for a quarter of a century. This is a serious and long-lasting problem, rooted in economic and social failure, rather than a shock event. But Britain’s rightwing media is unrivalled at manufacturing an urgent crisis. A decade ago, they helped turn Brexit from a fringe obsession of men with red faces and pink trousers into a national referendum and then a racist reality. In the 2020s, they have done a number both on people seeking asylum here and youngsters out of work.

The 1,500% figure comes from James Morrison, who in his new book The Workless: Stigma, Unpaid Labour and the Myth of Economic Inactivity, charts a “moral panic”. Take the first lady of Reform UK, Isabel Oakeshott, laying into the “parasites” who “prefer to just sit on the sofa and order their Deliveroo and drive their Motability free vehicle and take everything that the state can offer”. Oakeshott delivered this reportage on a TV channel owned by the Australia-born American billionaire Rupert Murdoch, before herself leaving the UK tax system to live in Dubai. Parasites come in many shapes and sizes.

This rightwing moral panic over kids off work and playing Grand Theft Auto forms the backdrop against which Keir Starmer last year turned to Milburn. As Westminster reporters often remind us, Milburn is a grandee from the Blair years. As they are too discreet to mention, he also left his post as health secretary and went on to make millions from private equity healthcare. His review is that familiar Blairite tug of war between two opposing forces: an acceptance that poverty and inequality are “at the core” of the problem, and policies that strip many young disabled people of benefits and make them still poorer.

Our next number is 0, which stands for zero employees. Because the overwhelming majority of companies in this country have no staff. Think: Uber drivers, gas fitters, pilates instructors. These are sole traders. And here lies the problem for Milburn, who plans to pay employers to hire Neets. Of the £3.6bn of benefits taken off young people, £1.1bn will be handed to businesses that recruit them. But hardly any of those ideal companies exist.

Politicians still imagine the UK as a land of toolmakers and assembly lines. Burnham promises to “reindustrialise Britain”, while George Osborne pledged a “march of the makers”. In reality, our largest private employers include Tesco and Asda, and Amazon warehouses. There is a land dominated by Volkswagen and Siemens – it’s called Germany.

You can’t push people into jobs that aren’t there, offered by employers that don’t exist, in an economy that you’ve dreamed up. One of Milburn’s own surveys shows that only 17% of businesses think a Whitehall bung will prompt them to hire more young people than they otherwise would. Far more likely is that companies pocket the three grand for making the same hires they were going to make all along.

Our last number is 1 in 4. A quarter of all British jobs are “bad jobs”, calculates Kirsten Sehnbruch at the London School of Economics, marked by precarious contracts or crap pay and conditions. In London, the proportion of bad jobs rises to 1 in 3. That lump of bad jobs remains huge despite low unemployment, so market forces clearly aren’t working. However warm his words, Milburn expects Neets to take this kind of work: zero-hours contracts (which the new workers’ rights law will limit, not scrap), minimum wage, jobs that treat you like an automaton.

So what?, you may say: at least it’s a start. But after 20 years advising governments on labour markets, Sehnbruch has a rule: land in the “bad job” economy and you’re unlikely to get out. Universal credit forces you from one bad job into another, while there isn’t good state-subsidised training that would enable you really to get a leg up. Career ladder? Forget it.

On rare occasions, the government does accept this. When in 2017 the headlines were about Deliveroo drivers and Sports Direct warehouses, Theresa May asked another Blairite grandee, Matthew Taylor, to report on modern workplaces. Among his key findings was that British jobs were characterised by “one-sided flexibility”, where only the employers benefited from flexibility. Perhaps Taylor’s review offered too much realism for Westminster, because hardly any of its recommendations were made law.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The Milburn report and the moral panic out of which it emerged obsesses over how to get young people into work; it doesn’t ask what kind of jobs market they’re going into. Yet these last two figures show that Britain’s labour market is the opposite of that confected by Westminster and the press. Twenty-five per cent of workers are in bad jobs, largely subsidised by the taxpayer, with poverty pay topped up by the state; and about 20% of the working-age population are in no jobs, subsidised by the taxpayer. Milburn’s proposed mix of “work coaches” and three-grand bungs won’t do much to change that.

What would? Part of the answer lies in the two major goals Burnham has set himself: a council housebuilding boom and a national care service. Rather than hope in vain that Britain’s private sector will deliver these huge public goods, he should drive the public sector to deliver both directly – as they did before the “40 years of neoliberalism” that the prime minister rightly criticises. He should direct them to take on and train up a proportion of young people who want to join the workforce.

As the labour market researcher Thanos Angelopoulos points out, that would redirect taxpayer money away from landlords and private care agencies, lift millions of families out of bad accommodation and worries about care for their elderly and sick relatives, and provide significant public assets. It would also give good jobs to our next generation. Why not? It’s got to be better than a little tinkering before ordering up another review.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

Sonia Exelby’s disappearance sparked an international search. The accused man, Dwain Hall, denies murdering her

Prosecutors in Ocala, Florida, have been laying out an extraordinary criminal case against Dwain C Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver accused of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, of Portsmouth, England.

Prosecutors allege that Hall lured Exelby to the US before killing her in October last year and burying her body in a shallow grave in Marion Oaks. Hall has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. After Hall’s arrest in November 2025, investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.

The authorities have said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from Gainesville airport in central Florida. He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

In a text message from Exelby’s phone to a friend, she said she felt scared and trapped, according to the arrest affidavit. “I’m sorry, he keeps taking my phone, he doesn’t trust me with it,” she wrote. “He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him.”

In opening statements this week, assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said Exelby’s parents struggled with mental illness and addiction and that their daughter had also struggled with mental illness and twice attempted suicide.

She had visited a website depicting graphic sexual abuse of women, where Hall was among several men who contacted her.

Berndt said in court that Exelby “was trying to find some substitute” to the self-harm. “Unfortunately, she found another outlet.” Berndt said Exelby was “trying to find someone who would kill her”.

“Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible,” Berndt added.

After she disappeared from her home, a former boyfriend, Stevie Hunt, contacted the authorities, the court heard.

In court, Hunt described Exelby as a kind, beautiful and loving woman, while her sister talked about their difficult childhood. Hunt told the court that Exelby experienced mood swings that sometimes lasted for days and had been in therapy for more than a decade.

Hall has denied killing Exelby but acknowledged in a police interview that he had been in contact with her and that the two had been intimate. Evidence linking Hall to Exelby’s death includes a shovel with Exelby’s blood on it, cellphone data, and a knife recovered from a friend of the defendant.

Prosecutors have said jurors will be shown photographs and surveillance video of Hall making purchases including rope, a shovel, deodorant and other items at a local Walmart store.

Hall’s defense attorney Junior Barrett said in opening statements that his client was not a murderer and asked jurors to carefully consider the facts, witness testimony and circumstances of the case.

“We believe that when you listen to all the facts and evidence in this case, you will arrive at the decision that Dwain Hall did not murder,” Barrett said.

The case continues.

Fifa sparks tension with demand for tax-free status in UK for Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:00:06 GMT

It also wants exchange-rate fees exemption for 2035

Fifa at loggerheads with UK’s four FAs and government

Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four football associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.

The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress in Zurich on Monday and the Guardian has learned there is tension behind the scenes over many of Fifa’s requirements, which multiple sources involved in the discussions have indicated will not be met.

Fifa is understood to have requested blanket exemptions on tax for all football-related activities for it and its broadcast and commercial partners, as well as its suppliers and staff. It also wants ticket sales – projected to reach 4.5m for the 48-team competition – to be VAT-free and for currency exchange fees to be waived.

Government sources have told the Guardian such blanket exemptions will not be granted for financial reasons and the optics of giving tax breaks to Fifa, which has cash reserves of more than $4bn (£3bn).

Fifa’s governance crisis has also complicated matters, with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, having called on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to resign on multiple occasions, and the FA preparing to endorse France’s Philippe Diallo at March’s presidential election.

Negotiations involving Fifa, the Treasury and the domestic FAs will continue after the UK bid has been ratified. Some carve-outs may be granted but the government is adamant the World Cup will not receive the wholesale tax-free status Fifa is seeking.

An FA spokesperson said: “We provided every guarantee that we can provide under the laws of the country and flagged any deviations transparently. Our approach is also consistent with every major event the UK has hosted or is due to host, including London 2012 and Euro 2028.”

Fifa identified in its evaluation report of the bid the UK’s tax and legal framework as a “medium risk” for the tournament, which would need to be addressed.

Fifa’s tax requirements have proved challenging for many tournament hosts in recent years, including last summer’s men’s World Cup. After months of negotiations with the US Treasury, Fifa succeeded in securing a late exemption from federal taxes for the 48 competing teams, although many were forced to pay state and city tax on their World Cup earnings depending on the location of their matches.

The tax adviser Oriana Morrison, who has worked for many national associations, said: “Fifa will ask for the world but ultimately accept the minimum that enables the tournament to be commercially viable. There are likely to be some difficult conversations ahead as the tournament will not generate anywhere near as much money as the men’s World Cup, so the margins are far tighter.”

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:00:06 GMT

Joanne Young, who has waived anonymity, was subjected to years of drugging and rape by former Swindon councillor, who invited other men to assault her

When Philip Young served as a Conservative party councillor for Swindon council, his contemporaries viewed him as a perfectly normal family man with “no edge to him”.

But behind closed doors he orchestrated a systematic campaign of abuse against his then wife, Joanne Young, secretly administering sedatives to render her unconscious, disoriented and amnesiac. Over a period of at least 15 years, he and other men raped and sexually assaulted her in her own bed at their home in Swindon.

The father of three pleaded guilty to more than 50 offences, including drugging, raping and sexually assaulting Joanne, who has been praised for her bravery in waiving her anonymity. His co-accused Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni and Mohammed Hassan were convicted on Thursday by a jury of their involvement. Another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty in February to rape.

The high-profile case has drawn comparisons to the Gisèle Pelicot trial in France, and it can now be revealed that the Crown Prosecution Service and Wiltshire police met the French team of investigators and prosecutors for advice.

Testimony and police interviews paint a picture of a carefully maintained domestic facade masking a predatory reality. Joanne, who was married to Young for 20 years and had been with him since 2002, described their relationship as traditionally monogamous and her own preferences as strictly “vanilla”.

Because of his heavy snoring, they slept in separate rooms, with Joanne eventually occupying a spacious second-floor loft conversion featuring a large black headboard and purple bedding.

Unknown to her, Young was exploiting this arrangement, and taking advantage of a common evening routine – sharing a nightcap of vodka after returning from social occasions – to spike her drinks with sedatives including zolpidem and ketamine that he is now believed to have bought online from countries including India.

The nightmare began to unravel on the night of 18 February 2023 after an evening out at the Blunsdon Arms. Joanne half-woke to find herself wearing a soft blindfold and wrist restraints, with a stranger’s hand on her wrist. She realised an unknown man was in her bedroom. When she attempted to move, Young whispered “get down”, causing the intruder to duck. Severely shortsighted and without her glasses, Joanne fled to the en suite bathroom and locked herself inside.

The following morning, Young apologised, claiming he had invited a man over from an online forum just to watch. The confession left Joanne deeply traumatised and questioning her marriage. She struggled to access counselling, while also managing impending redundancies at their shared business, a consulting firm.

The full scale of Young’s twisted operation was exposed after the National Crime Agency flagged illegal activity linked to him – the uploading of a bestiality image – on the messaging and livestreaming app Kik. Wiltshire police raided his home in July 2024.

Officers discovered digital caches of videos showing his then wife incapacitated, restrained and being sexually assaulted by a range of strangers, who it later emerged had been recruited via Craigslist, Grindr, Reddit and swinging websites. Young used multiple online aliases – such as “londonmonkey” – and posted advertisements across major cities such as London, Bristol and Bath, often messaging under the guise of Joanne.

He used at least 20 unique advertisement IDs and the titles included “Fuck my tied and blindfolded wife – mw4m – 35 (North Swindon)” and “Fuck my wife – 18th September – Central Bath hotel – mw4m”. The abbreviation “mw4m” was used in the posts to denote a man and woman looking for a man.

He told officers that in intimate moments his wife would sometimes tell him to “do what you want” and he would use Grindr to find men nearby to quickly arrive and “strip and join in”. But Joanne later told detectives and the court she did not consent to other men having sex with her, adding the relationship “was monogamous, always monogamous”.

The following day, 5 July 2024, Young answered “no comment” to all questions put to him by officers. Hair sample analysis conducted by a forensic toxicologist who also worked on the Pelicot trial revealed traces of ketamine and zolpidem in Joanne’s hair. Residues of zolpidem were also detected inside a plastic bag found in Young’s old bedside table.

In January, Young pleaded guilty at Winchester crown court to 11 counts of rape and 11 counts of administering a substance with intent to stupefy Joanne. He also admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, including a single count that covered at least 200 acts of voyeurism; seven counts of assault by penetration; four counts of sexual assault and one count of publishing obscene articles on at least 500 occasions. He later admitted to charges of making indecent images of children, one count of possessing a prohibited image of a child, and four charges of possessing an extreme pornographic image.

But four of his co-accused denied charges of rape and sexual assault, which meant Joanne was subjected to the brutal process of a trial, in which she was again praised for giving evidence to the court. The jury rejected the defendants’ claims that they believed the acts were consensual, securing guilty verdicts across all counts for the co-accused.

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor recruited via Craigslist in 2016 and captured on video assaulting the victim while wearing a balaclava, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration.

Wilkins, a 62-year-old taxi driver who participated in July 2016, recorded performing a sex act on the sleeping and snoring victim, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape.

Macksoni, a waste management worker who communicated with Young using the codename “Blunsdon” and was filmed abusing Joanne in February 2017, was convicted of rape.

Hassan, who was involved in the February 2023 incident in which Joanne woke up and discovered a stranger in her room, was found guilty of sexual assault.

Friends who socialised with the couple – sharing meals at the Blunsdon Arms and Greek restaurants, and playing Trivial Pursuit – recalled an outwardly normal family life with three children.

However, friends such as Andrew and Emma Brown and Rachel Williams said they had frequently noticed Young glued to his mobile phone during gatherings, an obsession now recognised as coordinating with strangers online.

It emerged in the trial that a potential opportunity to catch Young 10 years earlier may have been missed. In 2015, officers investigated an impounded package from India addressed to Young containing 120 zolpidem tablets – a class C drug known as a potential “date rape” substance. Young claimed ignorance, suggesting someone had misused his business details. An intelligence report was filed but no further action was taken.

A spokesperson for Wiltshire police said it was “understandable that questions may be asked” with the benefit of hindsight. “However, based on the information available at the time, the attending officer’s actions were both appropriate and proportionate,” they added.

“At that point, Young was a person of previously good character, with no criminal convictions, and there was no intelligence, information or evidence to suggest he posed a risk of committing the serious offences that have since come to light. The interaction was dealt with reasonably and in line with the information known at the time.”

Young later obtained multiple legitimate prescriptions for zolpidem and zopiclone from his GP between 2018 and 2022.

The revelations have sent shock waves through political circles in Swindon. A senior non-elected official close to Swindon borough council when Young served expressed profound shock at the former councillor’s conviction, telling the Guardian the revelations were “horrific” and “hideous”.

Young, who served as a cabinet member for regeneration and economic development between 2007 and 2010, was remembered as a progressive and engaging colleague. He held the political lead for Forward Swindon, an urban regeneration company responsible for revamping the town’s railway station forecourt among other projects, and liaised with the local business improvement district.

According to the source, the council was a difficult authority with challenging members at the time, but Young stood out as a clear exception. “He was one of the much more easy-to-get-along-with members [and] seemed to be considerate of staff,” the official noted, describing his approach as representing the “more modern thinking of councillors”.

The official said Young had shown no warning signs of his future criminal behaviour, in either his language or demeanour. “There was absolutely … no reason given to think that there was something unusual about this fellow,” the official said, adding that colleagues had generally considered Young to be “one of the good guys”.

A Conservative party source, who was close to the council at the time Young served, told the Guardian of the anger and betrayal they had felt upon learning of the former councillor’s crimes, saying the revelations had come as a “complete shock”.

Young was viewed as a highly capable and “brilliant councillor” who played a hands-on role in trying to revive Swindon’s town centre after the financial crash, they said. They revealed that Young had been so highly regarded for his public speaking and specialised skills that he was actively encouraged to run for council leader before he stepped down to become a director at the New Swindon Company.

Publicly, Young presented as a “perfectly normal family man” and successful business owner with “no edge to him”. “He wasn’t creepy in any way … I would never, ever have suspected anything untoward,” the source said.

Learning of the offences from a national newspaper reporter last Christmas had left former colleagues “beyond shocked” and “speechless”, they said. Expressing sympathy for the victims and for Young’s children, regarding the legacy he had left them, the source said the scale of his deception made them wonder “if you ever know anybody”.

After the convictions, questions still remain about the extent of Young’s offending. Police later discovered a receipt for a camcorder dating back to 2011, raising investigators’ suspicions that the covert recording and abuse may have started earlier than the window covered by the charges.

Meanwhile, authorities continue efforts to identify an elusive offender captured in the digital evidence who has yet to be identified despite several police appeals. Young has been questioned via his lawyers about the identity of the individual but has not assisted with inquiries.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

‘We don’t produce Neets’: the London school recognised at World’s Best School awards

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:46:13 GMT

Swiss Cottage school for children with complex needs is place where ‘every child feels they belong’, education secretary says

For Maria, the hardest part of having a child with complex needs has been the grief: mourning the life she had imagined for her son, for her family – and coming to terms with how lonely the reality of parenting him can be.

“There are wonderful days but there are very hard ones too,” she added, tears coursing down her face.

Thanks to a school dedicated to children and young people with multiple, severe and complex special needs, however, Maria is not alone any more.

Already the recipient of seven consecutive “outstanding” Ofsted ratings, the Swiss Cottage School, Development and Research Centre, operated by the local authority in Camden, has now received worldwide recognition as winner of the World’s Best School prize for community collaboration. It is the first time a school in England has won the prize.

The school has attracted the attention of those in government: the education secretary, Lucy Powell, said it was “a case in point of what we want to replicate through our Send reforms: a system where every child feels they belong and can access the support they need, close to home, without a fight”.

On paper, the Swiss Cottage school is just one of more than 1,000 state-funded special schools in England, catering for the country’s 10,000-plus children with profound developmental and learning difficulties.

But in reality, “Swiss”, as its families fondly call it, is run very differently. “Swiss has become our second family,” said Maria. “Support for children with complex needs is split across education, healthcare and social services. But Swiss does it all for us.”

“You have no idea,” she added, breathing out a great sigh of relief, “how much stress and weight that removes from parents’ shoulders.”

Instead of focusing solely on teaching their own pupils, Swiss is also different in that it operates an integrated research and training hub, leads teacher training programmes and conducts educational research.

It shares its best practices with hundreds of mainstream and special schools across the UK and internationally: over the last year alone, it has had delegations from South America, Uzbekistan, Saudi Arabia and Sweden.

Syra Sowe, head of the school, is reluctant to name names, but several UK schools have changed their teacher training, curriculums and planning, she said, after Swiss’s input. “Just to be clear, we don’t just use these partnerships to disseminate best practice,” she added. “We also learn from others.”

Until Maria found Swiss, her family were stuck in a nightmare. Her 18-year-old son, Alex, has Sotos syndrome, a rare genetic condition that has left him struggling with epilepsy, scoliosis, autism and severe developmental delays.

“Before Alex came here, no one understood him and he was raging. He hit, kicked and bit everyone; he was beyond therapy,” she said.

No nursery would keep Alex for more than an hour before calling his mother to collect him. By contrast, he has never had to leave Swiss early.

“This school has given him back his childhood. They immediately saw behind his disabilities to a child who needed an education – and had the right to an education,” Maria said. “He’s now a sociable young man who’s curious about everything, and who loves learning.”

Alex will leave Swiss this September and Maria is determined that his education will continue. Her son, she is resolved, will not become one of the approximately 38% of Neets (not in education, employment or training) who have multiple or complex needs – roughly translating to about 380,000 young people.

With the help of Swiss, Maria is confident this will not happen to Alex. It is a matter of intense pride to Sowe that her students all, without exception, go on to further education, training or specialist support. “We don’t produce Neets,” she said. “Any limits we think these children have are actually limits on our own imaginations and ambitions for them.”

The potential can be unclear to the untrained eye but teachers at the school see it clearly. On a tour of the school, one pupil grabbed the camera of the Guardian photographer and smelled it. Then he took Sowe’s lanyard and sniffed it too.

Grinning, he leapt back to the plateglass window of the school’s roof garden, happily slapping it, rocking and making a series of vocalisations.

Sowe’s reaction was one of pride. “That child has the most incredible olfactory sensitivity and olfactory memory,” she said. “He virtually navigates the world through smell; he’s amazing.”

Key to drawing out each child’s individual potential is the bespoke curriculum the school provides for each child, adjusted every week around the child’s evolving individual communication, cognitive and physical needs, at meetings between teaching staff, therapists, specialists, nurses, physiotherapists and the NHS Camhs professionals embedded in the school.

The school pushes the conventional boundaries of a special school in other interesting ways: rather than preparing pupils for a world they may struggle to access, its Employ ME programme not only gives its young people experience of working in the outside world – but aims to give the outside world experience of their unique skills and strengths.

“A key part of what we do is teach the universe how incredible our young people are,” said Sowe. “And what they have to offer, so the universe has more to offer to them when they leave us.”

Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:52:10 GMT

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.

Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.

“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.

It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:24:54 GMT

Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case

Lucy Letby’s lawyer has said the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns.

The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin.

The jury in the case were never told of the restriction placed on Hindmarsh, who was described by the prosecution in court as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Letby’s lawyer Mark McDonald, who has applied to the miscarriages of justice watchdog, the Criminal Cases Review Commission, for Letby’s convictions to be referred back to the court of appeal, said: “These revelations about Prof Hindmarsh, and the failure to disclose material information about him to the defence at trial, raise fundamental questions, and it is more urgent than ever that the court of appeal re-examines the safety of all Lucy Letby’s convictions.

“She is an innocent woman in prison, serving whole-life sentences, yet material information that could have been of critical importance to her defence was not disclosed. Did the police know? How did this information remain undisclosed?

“We need answers. Lucy deserves answers. She should not have to spend another day behind bars while these fundamental questions remain unanswered.”

Two senior lawyers said serious concerns about an expert’s professional abilities, and non-disclosure to the defence, could be grounds for an appeal against convictions.

Letby’s defence lawyers were never told that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice, nor of an April 2023 tribunal ruling imposing a restriction. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has also said it was not informed.

Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Hindmarsh’s opinion that two babies were poisoned with insulin, for which Letby was found guilty of attempted murder, was considered crucial to Letby being convicted. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical and scientific experts have contributed to reports submitted with her CCRC application, arguing that the prosecution’s medical case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong.

This week a Guardian investigation revealed that while the trial was going on, Hindmarsh’s employer barred him from clinical practice, and reported to the General Medical Council (GMC), which was already investigating him, that it believed he posed a risk to the safety of child patients.

Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin – at University College London hospitals trust (UCLH) when the trial began. He had also been an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital.

In March 2023, while the trial was continuing at Manchester crown court, Dr Tim Hodgson, a medical director at UCLH, wrote to the GMC: “On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Prof [Hindmarsh] to practise clinically even under supervision … I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Prof Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

Hodgson set out safety concerns, including two cases in which he said Hindmarsh had advised child patients to stop taking insulin. The GMC then applied for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended, which Hindmarsh opposed. His barrister argued it would be disproportionate, and would impede his ability to work as an expert witness in legal cases.

On 21 April 2023, a medical practitioners tribunal declined to suspend Hindmarsh but ordered that he must be directly supervised in his clinical work. That appears to have had no practical effect because UCLH had barred him from treating patients at all.

Hindmarsh did tell Cheshire constabulary, which instructed him in the case, about the GMC investigation in December 2022, and the CPS informed Letby’s defence team, but said it would oppose the jury being told. The jury was never informed that the GMC had launched an investigation into concerns about Hindmarsh, referred by UCLH and Great Ormond Street. His contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated in July 2022, and the jury was not told about that either.

Nick Johnson KC, the lead prosecution barrister, described Hindmarsh to the jury on 23 February 2023 as “the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field” of insulin.

Letby’s defence team was not informed about the further developments of March and April 2023, including that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice; and the jury was never told.

McDonald said: “It is staggering that Hindmarsh was presented as the pre-eminent expert on insulin at the trial, gave crucial evidence alleging babies were poisoned with insulin – which many eminent experts say was wrong – and it was never disclosed that he was considered by his own hospital [to be] unsafe to treat children with insulin, and barred from clinical practice.”

A representative of Hindmarsh declined to answer questions from the Guardian, including whether he had failed to disclose the March and April developments to Cheshire constabulary. The police force declined to comment. The CPS confirmed it was never given the information.

The criminal procedure rules require expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them anything, including disciplinary proceedings, “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. The rules were introduced in 2014 after recommendations by the Law Commission to improve expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice.

The commission was set up after a series of notorious miscarriages of justice based partly on flawed evidence from medical expert witnesses. The cases included Sally Clark, a solicitor who was wrongly convicted in 1999 of killing her two infant sons.

Clark’s convictions were overturned in 2003 after a CCRC referral to the court of appeal, principally because key medical evidence had not been disclosed to the defence. A striking statistical opinion presented by an expert witness for the prosecution, about the likelihood of both sons dying, was also shown to be catastrophically wrong. Clark had spent more than three years in prison condemned as a child killer and never recovered from her ordeal; she died in 2007 of acute alcohol poisoning.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, said of the rules: “If there was a failure to make relevant disclosure of material undermining an expert’s opinion evidence, and where that opinion evidence was relevant to the central issues before the jury, then that failure could form part of the grounds of appeal. It all depends upon the facts of a particular case and potential weight of the non-disclosure upon the jury’s verdict.”

Pete Weatherby KC, a barrister with extensive experience of criminal trials, said: “The expert witness disclosure rules are there to protect the integrity of the trial process and avoid miscarriages of justice. Expert evidence was pivotal in the Lucy Letby prosecution because there was no direct or forensic evidence that she committed any of the criminal acts of which she was accused.

“Serious concerns about an expert’s conduct or judgment may be highly relevant to assessing their expertise, credibility, and the reliability of their evidence. If those concerns were not before the jury, that could be very significant for an appeal. If the full details were not obtained by the prosecution, and disclosed to the defence at the time, that would be even more significant.”

In an authoritarian economy, Jensen Huang may be too big to fail

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:00:49 GMT

A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable

Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.

Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.

We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.

An economy can also be described along the same continuum.

Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. Through labor unions, workers also had some say.

But the US economy has become far more authoritarian.

In recent decades, it’s become concentrated in the hands of a few giant corporations. Economies of scale have enabled those corporations to spread their fixed costs over many goods and services, and the US government has nearly abandoned antitrust (anti-monopoly) enforcement.

Labor unions have shrunk from representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today.

More recently – over the last five years – something else has occurred, especially in big tech, that’s pushed the economy much further toward authoritarianism.

A handful of men – among them, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang – have not only become the richest people in the world, with significant political clout. They also control the direction and pace of technologies on which the US and the world depend.

These men are, in fact, the authoritarians of the new economy. They have unparalleled power over every aspect of the lives of Americans and millions of others around the world. And they have leveraged themselves to be, or seem, too big to fail.

The leverage works like this.

Nvidia’s value depends on Jensen Huang.

Hours after Huang’s resignation last Thursday, Nvidia stock dropped 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing approximately $490bn of Nvidia’s value by the time the market opened.

Since the start of the leadership controversy at Nvidia on 8 November, the company has lost about $800bn in market value.

The AI industry, in turn, depends on Nvidia. Nvidia controls about 90% of the global market share of advanced AI chips. It has also become the major financier for the entire AI industry. Some call Nvidia the “central bank of AI”.

Nvidia’s $5tn market value (before 8 November) equaled about 8% of the total value of the S&P 500.

The US economy, in turn, depends on the AI industry. In the first quarter of 2025, the buildouts of datacenters using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of US economic growth. Over the past two years, AI has been responsible for roughly half of America’s overall growth.

This huge leverage also works in reverse. Analysts fear that Nvidia’s collapse could cause the AI bubble to burst, triggering a failure that could threaten the entire US, if not also the world, economy.

Most Americans’ 401(k)s are invested in giant index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The Nasdaq and S&P 500, in turn, are based largely on 10 huge corporations. These 10 corporations are all connected to Nvidia. Together, they comprise about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market.

What all this means is Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.

More than 177,000 people have so far signed a “Stand with Jensen” open letter demanding that Nvidia’s board of directors “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Signers include Elon Musk; the Y Combinator president, Garry Tan; the Epic Games CEO, Tim Sweeney; and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees.

Huang is discussing a possible return to the company, though the chair of the company’s board has said it’s not considering the move. One Huang ally talks of a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return, ‌and garner support from ‌Trump. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person told the Financial Times, adding that the efforts have Huang’s support.

Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as Nvidia CEO, adding that he thought Huang had “learned a big lesson”.

Exactly what “big lesson” did Trump have in mind? That it’s not a good look for the CEO of the US’s most valuable corporation to have a romantic relationship out of wedlock?

Or that such a CEO shouldn’t break the law by supplying America’s most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy?

On Tuesday, it was announced that Huang has agreed to appear on 1 December before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.

Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he? We may soon find out.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich. substack. com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK
