Nothing compares to her: Sinéad O’Connor’s 20 best songs – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:00:48 GMT

The Irish singer-songwriter would have turned 60 in early December. To mark the occasion, we revisit the best of a catalogue that’s far more than a certain Prince cover

This suitably uncompromising opener to the lengthy Faith and Courage offers a collage of radio static, Indian-inspired beats, dub bassline and whispered vocals. More importantly, it’s fantastic: you might call it trip-hop were Sinéad O’Connor’s vocal not so intense as to negate any potential for relaxation on the part of the listener.

From O’Connor’s final album, I’m Not Bossy, I’m the Boss – she abandoned an almost-complete follow-up with producer David Holmes after the death of her son – The Voice of My Doctor is grinding, distorted blues rock. Its lyric, a saga of infidelity delivered with real fury, references Nothing Compares 2 U.

Am I Not Your Girl? now seems wildly ahead of its time; a collection of covers of American Broadway, jazz and film standards (before such things became reliable pop staples), all fabulously orchestrated. Here, the blasting John Barry-style brass presages the 90s easy-listening revival, but the real drama lies in O’Connor’s astonishing vocal.

An explosion of life-affirming joy in a catalogue not much given to that kind of thing, the ramshackle but wildly catchy 4th and Vine is an untrammelled delight. Extra points for the simple-but-great video, featuring a beaming O’Connor and band belting it out in a packed Irish pub.

O’Connor was a friend of Kurt Cobain: after his death, she stripped back Nirvana’s All Apologies to almost nothing beyond an acoustic guitar and a vocal that replaces the original’s pained yowl with a kind of fierce, pure whisper. It is utterly haunting.

As close to a straightforward pop track as O’Connor ever recorded, the lissom funk of I Want Your (Hands on Me) bears the faint influence of Jam and Lewis in its production, and of their former employee Prince in its forthright lyrical approach to seduction. It’s sonically of its time, but a total banger nonetheless.

A stark, potent depiction of institutionalised racism and poverty in Thatcher-era Britain (“not the mythical land of Madame George and roses”) that still hits hard nearly 40 years on. “These are dangerous days – to say what you feel is to dig your own grave,” she notes, two years before her infamous SNL appearance.

The soaring melody and warm arrangement (it was co-produced by Brian Eno) can’t quite mask the sense of unease engendered by the lyrics. A saga of birth, love, hatred and regret, they’re oblique enough to be open to interpretation – is it about mother-daughter relations? – but powerful enough to knock you sideways.

An Irish folk standard with roots in a 17th-century poem, O’Connor’s take on I Am Stretched on Your Grave welds a stark, largely a cappella reading of the song to a baggy-era breakbeat. It’s an improbable idea that somehow succeeds in amping up its stark grief: you couldn’t imagine anyone dancing to it.

An entirely original break-up song, apparently inspired by O’Connor’s relationship with Peter Gabriel, the gently trip-hop influenced Thank You for Hearing Me occupies a complex but believable emotional space. It’s all gratitude and fond recollection until the final verse, when a note of darkness, a faint hint of screw-you, clouds the picture.

O’Connor’s debut single arrived in the autumn of 1987 – not, by any metric, a vintage year for pop music. But Troy would have attracted attention at any point in history: a lyric in which WB Yeats gets bound up with the singer’s childhood trauma, a vocal so powerful it’s almost alarming, a high-drama string arrangement.

There are fine moments on O’Connor’s 00s albums Sean-Nós Nua, Throw Down Your Arms and Theology, but 2012’s How About I Be Me (and You Be You)? still felt like an all-guns-blazing return to form. The Wolf Is Getting Married packs a mighty chorus, its lyrics brimming with fresh optimism, and her voice sounds magnificent.

This is O’Connor at her don’t-mess fiercest, dismissing “all this man-trolling” – no to another husband, or indeed another boyfriend – over a churning alt-rock backing. There’s a faint hint of the Beatles about the tune; the hook is absolutely immense. How on earth was this not a huge hit?

Co-producer John Reynolds said O’Connor’s vocal on Fire on Babylon “possessed an energy that was almost impossible to contain”. Certainly, there’s a harrowing, red-raw quality to her singing on a track that revisits her abusive childhood and unflinchingly excoriates her mother. The reggae-infused backing sweetens the pill a little.

From the largely acoustic EP Gospel Oak – a very different beast indeed to its fraught predecessor, 1994’s Universal Mother – This Is to Mother You is just an extraordinarily beautiful, tender song. Subsequently covered by Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, and reworked in 2009 as a charity duet with Mary J Blige, the original is still the keeper.

A one-off single that stalled just outside the UK Top 40, My Special Child was, perhaps, just too raw and personal in its treatment of the collapse of O’Connor’s marriage – and her decision to have an abortion – for mass consumption. There’s certainly nothing wrong with its stunning melody, nor its majestic and folky arrangement, though.

Co-written by Bono and produced by Bomb the Bass’s Tim Simenon, O’Connor’s contribution to the soundtrack for In the Name of the Father sets a folky melody and murder ballad-inspired lyric to a backdrop of pounding drums, ambient synths and distorted fiddle. Her voice sounds alternately flinty and agonised; the overall effect is stunning.

Despite its none-more-80s drums, O’Connor’s first hit sounded like nothing else in the charts on arrival. There’s a swaggering confidence about its faintly Clash-like guitar riff, its astonishing swooping vocal and its strange but intriguing words, complete with early statement of her unbiddable approach: “I have refused to take part.”

At first, it’s an exercise in restraint: nothing but an acoustic strum and O’Connor pouring out her heart about her divorce (the way she sings “I’ll talk but you won’t listen to me” is shattering). Then, a minute before the end, the strumming gets more frantic and a sense of catharsis kicks in. An awesome song.

In a sense, it feels unfair putting Nothing Compares 2 U at the top of this list. It’s a cover, lording it over umpteen examples of O’Connor’s songwriting skill; moreover, it enjoyed the kind of vast, unrepeatable success that overshadows the rest of her oeuvre in the eyes of casual listeners. But then again … just listen to it. More than 35 years of familiarity haven’t done anything to dull its emotional impact: her voice whispers and soars, shifting from sorrow to anger to despair, completely inhabiting a lyric in which every suggestion to forget heartbreak and move forward falls on deaf ears. “It’s my song now,” she once remarked – tough talk when the author was Prince, but absolutely correct.

Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:00:48 GMT

Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids

I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.

Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple, Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating.

Everyone knows that Grand Theft Auto is a violent game. It’s about crime and criminals, and VI’s story is about two fugitives in Vice City and the absolute dirtbags they meet along the way. You steal cars, run drugs, shoot cops and rival criminals and hold up gas stations; you kill hundreds of people over the course of the game. There are executions, brutal police raids and depictions of torture. None of that is particularly new, but it’s still pretty hardcore for, say, a nine-year-old. Plenty of millennials played Grand Theft Auto when we were underage, but video games are an awful lot more realistic now than they were 20 years ago; graphic violence on a PlayStation 2 from the 00s looks very different from graphic violence on a PlayStation 5 in 2026.

Let’s leave the violence aside for a minute, though: there is also a lot more explicit sexual content in GTA VI than any previous GTA game, or any other video game period. 2004’s Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas was briefly pulled from sale because it contained a sex minigame that you couldn’t even access without hacking the game’s code. GTA VI, meanwhile, contains a LOT of sex that is in no way hidden, including between the two main characters. On another character’s laptop, there in a browsable in-game version of OnlyFans that pulls exactly no punches. There is full-frontal nudity, male and female. One mission takes place during a porn shoot, several others in strip clubs and bars, one in a hotel where you can burst into the wrong room to find an ongoing orgy or a bunch of people eating sushi off a naked body. I don’t personally fancy explaining any of this to my kids!

Then there’s the drugs. You run drugs, you steal drugs, you sell drugs and you take drugs. Pretty much everyone in Vice City really enjoys their coke; there are copious party scenes where powder is everywhere, and the player characters can partake if you want. Chapter 3 of the game is literally titled “Tits Ass Drug Money”. You might read all of this and think, my teenager has seen worse. That’s perfectly fair – but this is not stuff a 10- or 12-year-old can really contextualise, in my opinion (and the opinion of the ratings boards). If you think your child is too young to watch Breaking Bad, they are definitely too young for Grand Theft Auto VI.

Sign up to Pushing Buttons

after newsletter promotion

Even the in-game TV and radio is full of vulgar humour. On a phone-in show, I heard a caller and the host vamp extensively about her boyfriend’s penis’s resemblance, in size and smell, to a chicken nugget. A psychic medium considers whether people can still indulge their foot fetishes in the afterlife, in incorporeal form. One of the in-game podcasts stars two female hosts talking in explicit detail about how attracted they are to various famous murderers. Walking past random pedestrians on the street you will frequently hear people talking at length about their dicks and what they have recently done with them. This is not what you might call mature humour, but it is adult.

To be clear: I am not here to start a moral panic about adult video game content. All of the above is fair game in media for adults and, truthfully, I found a lot of it extremely funny. But believe me, as both a parent and a person who has spent over 70 hours playing this game, GTA VI is not for kids. For some reason there remains an immense knowledge gap between children and parents when it comes to the content of video games, and I think it’s in everyone’s interests for parents to make informed decisions.

Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:38:05 GMT

New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday

‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’

Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.

United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.

“We are going to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”

Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after an overnight flight, having taken charge of his final USA match against Haiti. He toured the training ground and held meetings with senior staff and players not on international duty.

Members of Pochettino’s staff were in place earlier in the week as they seek to revitalise a team with one league win. Pochettino is waiting for United to ratify the appointment of Sílvia Tuyà, a strength and conditioning coach who worked with him with the USA. She travelled with him by private jet to Manchester but was not named among the staff later in the day.

“We need to go little by little, step by step,” Pochettino said. “We cannot go too fast but also we need to, at the same time, attack the priorities to build something.”

He said it was important he and his staff adapt to the culture of the club. “And then, with this sense of knowing the history of the club, try to create all together, because we are all different, a culture, a philosophy that can respect that identity, the history of the club. But at the same time, performing. If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”

Pochettino has coveted the United job and is a keen admirer of Sir Alex Ferguson, whom he describes as “the best coach in history”. Since the Scot’s retirement in 2013, United have failed to match his success but Pochettino said he was looking at “the potential of the club”. The weight of past achievements has hindered individuals over the past 13 years.

“The players need to express their talent,” Pochettino said. “We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now: it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.

“Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it’s too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back. When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.”

Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:03:24 GMT

The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Measles has come raging back in the US. Robert F Kennedy Jr should be impeached

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:00:25 GMT

He is responsible for the health of the American people. On his watch, thousands have become seriously ill

At least 11 Americans have died of measles since January 2025 – the month before Robert F Kennedy Jr became secretary of Health and Human Services.

One of Friday’s victims was a child, in Wisconsin, where a baby died of measles the week before. Pennsylvania has not disclosed the age of the other person.

Measles is a highly contagious but vaccine-preventable disease. It can kill you with pneumonia, leave you deaf, or permanently damage your immune system.

The disease was wiped out in the US a quarter-century ago. Yet in less than two years, outbreaks in 47 states have pushed the numbers of illnesses and deaths to levels unseen since 1991. The country has tallied more than 7,700 cases since January 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The majority of those sickened, hospitalized and killed by measles are under 20 years old; an alarming percentage are not yet five. In the past two years, 112 pregnant women have been hospitalized with complications of measles, until now extraordinarily rare. Two lost their pregnancies. A dozen babies have been born infected.

On 17 November, the Pan American Health Organization (Paho) revoked the US’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

Even before that, since the mid-1990s, only a few dozen to a few hundred cases were reported annually, and any small outbreaks were contained within the year, the standard for gaining and keeping the status. Now, says KFF Health News, “measles has re-established regular transmission in the country”.

The reason for this scourge is plain: a sliding vaccination rate. The reason for the slide is a growing suspicion of vaccines. That suspicion has been floating around for decades, but for its renewal and spread – as virulent as measles itself – we can thank the misinformation crusade led by the secretary of health and joined by the president.

Kennedy is a prolific conspiracy monger: wifi causes “leaky brain”; chemicals in the water turn children transgender. But his premier contribution to American stupidity has been to amplify the fiction that vaccinations cause autism.

Reuters called RFK Jr “the nation’s leading anti-vaccine activist”.

As the person responsible for safeguarding the health of the American people, Robert F Kennedy Jr is to blame for thousands of preventable cases of severe illness and at least 11 deaths. Almost to a person, these latter-day measles victims were unvaccinated.

Kennedy should be impeached.

Measles’ revival did not happen because the secretary of health was otherwise engaged, like so many of Trump’s incompetents. Rather, Kennedy seems almost deliberately to have invited fatal childhood diseases back into the US and nursed them to vitality.

The virus started spreading in Texas in January 2025, but the secretary has not mobilized the agency’s rumor-quelling mechanisms, or enlisted the help of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), ordinarily the government’s partner in guiding frightened families through outbreaks.

If Kennedy has transmitted any messages, they’re mixed. He disputed being labeled as “anti-vaccine”, and endorsed the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination as “effective”. Then he claimed it was “not safety tested”. (It is proven safe and effective.)

But in June 2025, in what he called “a bold step in restoring public trust” – and a long list of medical associations called the opposite – Kennedy fired all 17 members of the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunizations and packed the vaccine committee with vaccine skeptics. In January, following a presidential executive order full of pseudoscientific poppycock, the CDC released a plan to revise childhood immunization guidelines, both complicating and loosening them.

“At a time when parents, pediatricians and the public are looking for clear guidance and accurate information, this ill-considered decision will sow further chaos and confusion and erode confidence in immunizations,” the AAP president, Dr Andrew D Racine, said.

The AAP sued, and in March 2026 a federal judge annulled all votes taken by the reconstituted ACIP and ordered a restoration of the pre-Kennedy guidelines.

Nevertheless, Trump released another executive order this summer, debuting the anti-immunization committee’s “gold standard” recommendations. The president was keenest on breaking the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vax into separate shots. The three-in-one was “quite lethal”, he claimed, falsely. Experts say spacing out the immunizations would endanger children. Drugmakers suggest that the product can’t be sliced up anyway.

Kennedy has sown distrust in state health departments, long the source of data for the federal agencies. After Pennsylvania reported the deaths of two babies too young to be vaccinated, for instance, he posted without evidence that one of them “may … have been altogether fabricated”.

In September, the secretary ordered the CDC director, Erica Schwartz, to remove the two deaths from its publicly accessible data. In late October, Schwartz declined to sign off on an urgent health alert to clinicians encountering measles-related symptoms in pregnant patients that they have not seen in decades, or ever.

CDC higher-ups have inexplicably postponed other vaccine-related reports cleared for publication by expert readers. One was a study of infant mortality from whooping cough, or pertussis, which found that the mothers of most of the babies who died did not get a vaccine while pregnant that protects infants, who are most susceptible to severe pertussis.

Doctors were miffed. “We don’t have data on this part. The experience is limited,” a Canadian obstetrician told the Washington Post. “When I’m dealing with this situation, I’m dealing with not just Jane who’s pregnant, but the baby or babies inside her womb.”

The only conclusion to draw is that HHS doesn’t want us to know that vaccines save lives, and refusing them imperils lives, especially those of the most vulnerable.

After Paho withdrew the country’s measles elimination status this week, the CDC announced it would invest $100m to get it back: “We will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection. We will equip state, local, tribal, and territorial health departments with tools and technical support to identify communities at increased risk, engage trusted partners, detect cases quickly, and respond effectively to outbreaks,” reads its statement.

It’s hard to imagine this plan represents an epiphany for the man who squandered a half-century of public health progress in the first place.

This week, the chair of an independent US advisory committee to the Paho betrayed his disgust. “We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it,” he said.

No, “we” have not. The Trump administration has. It is a cult high on “lethality” and blasé about death, whether in Pennsylvania or Ukraine, Wisconsin or Iran.

Kennedy is the cult’s guru. In Indianapolis in April 2025, when more than 800 Americans had already contracted measles and three had died, he praised his staff –and, by implication, his own leadership. The CDC, he said, had “done a very good job containing the measles outbreak”.

Trump is the cult’s No 1 apostle. But this is not the first time he has shrugged off the demise of the people he was elected to serve. During the Covid-19 epidemic, Axios asked the president to comment on the 1,000 people who were dying every day from suffocation and organ failure caused by the virus.

Replied Trump: “It is what it is.”

Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 10:00:25 GMT

Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller

This review contains spoilers

Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger.

Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here.

Fielder was invited by Holmes to spend intimate time with her in 2023 in the weeks before prison, in the rented San Diego beachfront home she shared with her protective new partner Billy Evans, an alpha-dog blowhard, wannabe tech entrepreneur and Charlie Kirk enthusiast, with whom she has two small children. Holmes still claims to be innocent, a position she maintains here with the wide-eyed gaze and vacuous smile of a beauty pageant victor. (When she switches from contact lenses to glasses for the final car ride to prison it is a poignant moment of vulnerability.) It is Fielder’s mission to find out if she knows she is lying and to make her admit the truth, a job that will need considerable indirection and sympathetic subtlety, rather like Gitta Sereny’s conversations with Albert Speer. At any rate, he might discover how and why she has bought into her own delusional mythology.

What we get is an Olympic stare-out contest between two gladiators of the polite straight face. Fielder’s conversations with the equally pop-eyed Evans have the same tension. Who is going to lose their cool first? Holmes repeatedly insists that the technology works, by which she appears to mean that the technology has caused her to be certain in the present that it could and will work in the future; the theory is impeccable and all that remains is the small matter of getting whatever tech stuff they need to go in the little box.

You could call this approach fake-it-till-you-make-it, but Holmes clearly believes that faking it and making it are the same thing. Fielder is fascinated and suspicious at her evasive, ersatz-childlike failure to grasp what he is asking her, yet she appears also genuinely to lack a sense of truth and falsehood. She also seems to lack a sense of humour, revealed when Fielder shows her a clip of Abbott and Costello performing the legendary “Who’s on first” bit – a gloriously funny, insightful sequence. But Holmes flinches and sobs when Fielder shows her clips of Amanda Seyfried playing her in the dramatised miniseries The Dropout.

Is Holmes exactly the villain of this film? What sort of a dysfunctional, co-dependent relationship did she once have with Balwani? Is her gift for disingenuous idealism, ersatz innocence and a demure need to be insulated from the consequences of her actions something that always attracts a Rasputin, an abusive puppetmaster? Why did Evans and Holmes agree to Fielder as their interrogator anyway? It was supposedly because they liked the way he “thought outside the box”. But perhaps they appreciated the humour behind Fielder’s superb HBO TV show The Rehearsal, which recreates with elaborate sets real situations in ordinary people’s lives, a show that famously involved him getting a pilot’s licence to fly a 737. Maybe Holmes and Evans liked the way reality and fiction were merged or superimposed, and that this relativist approach to the facts would be congenial.

But what can Fielder and Oppenheim do, what should they do, once Holmes has been packed off to prison with questions still unanswered? The answer is purely outrageous: they call up Seyfried and get her to re-enact for the camera conversations with Holmes and Evans which they haven’t been able to film. Seyfried is explosively incredulous and overexcited about the whole business, in contrast to Fielder’s cool priestly reserve. Unlike everyone else, you can see everything of Seyfried’s emotions. But is she being directed in such a way as to be an unknowable enigma as well?

This is a film which, like the production history behind Andrew Jarecki’s Capturing the Friedmans from 2003, executes a whiplash change-of-mind about what the story actually is. The appearance of Seyfried, the one person who is allowed to be open about how uproarious this all is, creates a vivid kind of hyperreal version of Holmes, a shimmering uncanny-valley mirage, which refocuses the mind on how Holmes could be playing a role anyway – a suggestion first made by the New York Times, which she rejects. As for Evans himself, he has his own ideas about how he is going to keep Holmes present in his life and on his computer screen.

Of course, much of the narrative mystery has been created in the edit and by the musical score. Who knows how much has been withheld from us? But what an amazing high-wire act of audacity this is.

You Can See Everything is in UK and Irish cinemas from 20 November.

This year, the Greens have reshaped British politics. Now we need party systems to match that influence

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 10:00:24 GMT

Without Zack Polanski and Hannah Spencer, we might still be stuck with Keir Starmer. But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaul

Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP

In the aftermath of some difficult weeks for the Greens, one encouraging response has particularly stood out for me: the widespread agreement across progressive politics that the UK is better for having a strong Green party. One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t.

From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. As we increasingly win more council seats, assembly members, mayors and MPs, we are able, at all levels of government, to help restore the natural world, tackle climate breakdown and challenge the economic framework of neoliberalism that has governed us for too long.

As the pollster Luke Tryl from More in Common has observed, Green influence on the political landscape, including Andy Burnham’s conference speech, “has been outsized”. That influence includes creating the conditions for Burnham to become prime minister. To put it bluntly, if there had been no Zack Polanski leadership, and no Hannah Spencer win in the Gorton and Denton byelection, we would probably still be stuck with Keir Starmer. It was the Greens as much as anyone who forced Labour MPs to conclude they needed a more radical offer.

Burnham’s talk of reversing 40 years of neoliberalism and his pledge to establish a national commission on electoral reform are to be welcomed. But we need more radical action and more urgent delivery. Take last month’s budget of incrementalism and resounding failure to tax the super-rich – it’s now 41 years of neoliberalism we need to reverse. Moreover, Burnham’s greenlighting of fossil-fuel drilling at Jackdaw, his slashing of the warm homes plan to fund defence and likely watering down of targets for electric vehicles show that the Green party is needed more than ever – and that we have our work cut out for us.

And that’s what has made the fallout from the Greens’ “Zionism is racism” conference motion all the more damaging. I have made my personal view clear: it was never going to be possible to define such a contested term with such variable meanings, that itself historically arose from widespread racism in Russia and eastern Europe, in just a few words in a conference motion. The attempt has been dangerous and divisive, and takes the focus away from the appalling genocide in Gaza, rather than bringing opportunities to do what’s needed to isolate and constrain the Israeli government. But the prime minister’s call for a different kind of politics, “problem-solving, not point-scoring”, has not got off to a good start after his top-down edict to Labour councillors to end joint working with local Greens unless they renounced the motion.

This has led to the ending of many of our power-sharing agreements around the country, a move opposed by most Labour and Green councillors alike. It is also a move that will only hurt local residents, particularly if it paves the way for Reform UK or Conservative councillors to take over. This hardly fits with Burnham’s support for devolution and local autonomy.

Within all progressive parties and across them, we need to be modelling better ways of doing politics, particularly since the political system is likely to remain fragmented. The most recent YouGov poll puts five parties in double digits with Labour ahead, but only on 27% of the vote. As we anticipate a world of proportional representation and multiparty government, we’re going to have to learn how to deal with differences in a less binary and confrontational way. It cannot be right that progressive parties would rather risk Reform gaining power than find ways to work effectively together.

For we Greens, the challenge is also to make our internal structures fit for purpose, and in line with the scale of our new membership and the importance of the role the party now plays on the national stage. I welcome the fact that the leadership has established a working group to look at examples from across the world of how progressive parties with mass memberships develop effective policy, and to put forward proposals for models that could work well for our party.

The truth is that systems that might have served the party well when it had a membership of just a few tens of thousands and a handful of elected representatives simply aren’t up to the job for a party of several hundred thousand members. With over a thousand Greens now holding office, decisions need to be made more efficiently and policy developed more effectively. This was a foreseeable challenge. Indeed in the period when I was co-leader, some eight years ago, I was one of the instigators of the last review that sought – with only partial success – to make positive democratic changes. But it is now a more urgent one.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

So let’s try to model disagreement well. If means shape ends then both Labour and the Greens need to show how to do politics differently, not least to fend off the threat of a united right. The motion and the debate around it won’t just go away and nor should it. It needs to be resolved, but in ways that grow trust, respect and mutual understanding.

Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP

The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:01:21 GMT

Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his conviction.

The Altruists opens in 2016 with an untraditional meet-cute between SBF (as Bankman-Fried was known) and Ellison when she joins the trading firm he works at. They bond over mathematical strategies, their Ivy League professor parentage, veganism and their commitment to effective altruism. The last was a movement that invited people to apply utilitarian principles – where could your money do most practical good – and divorce charitable donation decisions from emotion and irrationality. Thus it followed that the best thing you could do was make as much money as possible and then give it all away. Many in the tech industry approved this message, whether through genuine belief or as a sop to conscience. It is surely a phenomenon that deserves a thorough examination of its own – the mix of good intentions, self-righteousness, skewed entitlement, scope for monstrous egos, misuse and hypocrisy it combines is an almost overwhelmingly delicious prospect and I hope someone has it in their sights.

Our so far relatively endearing pair of number monkeys begin a relationship – almost entirely on Caroline’s polyamorous terms – while SBF co-founds his first company, Alameda, in 2017, from which he then forces out his business partner. Caroline comes on board instead and together they start making profits.

The timeline then starts to split between the rise (2016 in New York), the precarious peaking (2018, Hong Kong) and the fall (the Bahamas, 2022). Not for the first time I find myself thanking the Mike Judge sitcom Silicon Valley for giving me at least a small purchase on what the hell is happening, and wishing that a drama could follow its lead in integrating explanations for the minimally computer- and fiscally literate lay audience seamlessly into the action so we can properly appreciate what is going on.

Because – it’s a lot. At the heart of the downfall is an $8bn (£6bn) hole in the Alameda/FTX finances, whose funds should never have been mixed, where customer deposits should be. Before then, there are technical challenges, clever plays by more experienced (and more corrupt) players, risk-averse investors and regulatory issues to deal with. This could be simplified without too much loss to the drama, because the meat of that is really to do with the messy humanity that SBF and Ellison – and, by inference, the rest of the tech titans – are trying to banish from the trades and the models they think could be perfect.

At its best, The Altruists is about the ineffable; it’s about trust, about understanding yourself and others, about being able to gauge moods as well as markets and how inextricably and infuriatingly they can be linked. Above all, it is about how important self-image and a belief in that self-image can be, and how much people can lie to themselves and others to protect it. SBF recruits his friends and betrays them. The pair donate huge amounts to charity but live bounteously in the Bahamas and are planning to build the $200m (£151m) complex FTX “needs” as bankruptcy looms.

Anchored by brilliant performances from Boyle and Garner, two of the best young screen actors working today, and supported by fine turns elsewhere (especially from Karan Soni as the most emotionally brutalised of SBF’s victims), The Altruists stays just the right side of coherent. In the end, it manages to evoke the chaos, the insubstantiality of the algorithmic economy we all depend on now, and the insanity of the idea that any handful of people in whom such vast amounts of wealth and power are concentrated could ever be up to the task, without quite itself collapsing. But it’s a high-wire act and you mustn’t lose focus for a moment. And I recommend a Silicon Valley rewatch to prep before you begin.

The Altruists is on Netflix

IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 07:16:45 GMT

Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk

Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.

Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”

The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.

This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.

The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise, a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.

But some countries – chiefly Russia, India and the Arab group of countries including Saudi Arabia – want to delay publication of AR7 until 2029, after the global stocktake is completed. They argue, with the backing of some climate campaigners, that developing countries are disadvantaged in trying to submit science to the IPCC. As a result, some claim, the work is permeated by racist assumptions that guarantee the privilege of developed countries.

Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, told the Guardian the IPCC’s scenarios for cutting greenhouse gas emissions – known as “mitigation” in UN jargon – were “biased against the interests of the global south”.

For instance, she said, one assumption was that cutting emissions should be done where it was most cost-efficient. “And where is it cheap to do mitigation? In the global south.” Changing the assumptions would produce different scenarios, Nacpil said.

Nacpil said singling out Saudi Arabia, “whose behaviour we’re not always sympathetic with”, was “also very racist”. She asked: “Who started the fossil fuel industries in this region? Who enjoyed it for now dozens of decades? Whose multinational companies really grew from the extraction of oil and gas in the Middle East? This is not us taking sides. This is us saying: ‘But the pot is calling the kettle black.’ And they’re using their economic, political, and racial power to do this.”

Rockström rejected this. “The pathways to the future represent different socioeconomic realities around the world,” he told the Guardian, in an interview at Cop31. “This is based on the best evidence we have, and this evidence has no north or south bias. It represents the best peer-reviewed science of our understanding of how to close income gaps in poor countries versus rich countries, demographic changes, health projections, and of course also therefore forecasting socioeconomic development. It’s an objective, evidence-based analysis of the reality.”

He added: “We have to defend that objective science. We should not use science as the arena to fight for justice or human rights or even democracy. That’s not the role of science.”

Many other developing countries, including small islands and the least developed countries, have called for the IPCC report to be completed without delay.

Raju Pandit Chhetri, a negotiator from Nepal, said calling the IPCC racist was “a political line”. “What we need to do in this process is really respect the science,” he said. “Coming from Nepal, I can tell you the impacts in just a few hours’ time: losing thousands of lives, let alone billions of pounds worth of property. There are countries who think that making stronger science will put pressure on them to [cut emissions].”

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

The core committees of the IPCC are run by pairs of scientists, one each from developed and developing countries. China, India and Saudi Arabia all supply leading scientists to the organisation, but insiders acknowledge that parts of the process are dominated by European researchers.

The IPCC said that out of 664 appointed authors working on the drafts of its three working group reports, 51% came from developing countries and economies in transition – an increase of almost half, compared with the last report in 2021. Each chapter across the three reports includes at least one developing-country chapter scientist.

A spokesperson for the IPCC said: “IPCC is absolutely committed to promoting diversity and inclusion and has taken multiple steps to do so during its seventh cycle. As the UN body assessing the science related to climate change, we uphold and stand by the core values of integrity, professionalism and respect for diversity and gender. In the current cycle, the IPCC introduced institutional measures that implement equity and inclusivity.”

Rockström said even if AR7 was delayed, the science in AR6 would be enough to show that current pledges, made last year before Cop30, must be vastly improved. “We have all the evidence we need. Even if you based your updates [on emissions pledges] only on AR6, we would still be making enormous progress,” he said.

Others fear a delay could be used by countries to derail the global stocktake, for instance by arguing it too must be delayed or modified. “It’s throwing more sand in the gears,” one expert involved in the process said.

The row has been going on all year, but is coming to a head because the body meets soon to decide its budget. Although it has reserves of cash to draw on, if a budget cannot be agreed there will be little chance of the IPCC being able to produce its reports before the stocktake.

Technically, the IPCC issues cannot be solved at Cop because they can only be agreed within the body itself, but as governments are meeting in Turkey, some form of compromise may be possible. The chair of the IPCC, the British scientist Jim Skea, extended his attendance at Cop31 for further talks on the issue.

The first draft of the “cover decision” from Cop31, released on Monday, contains references to the need for IPCC science. Though it is likely to be revised several times yet, the draft “recognises the central role of the best available science and of the IPCC” and “recognises the value of a full range of knowledge and participation in the IPCC, including contributions from Indigenous peoples, people of African descent, local communities, non-English speaking regions, and developing countries, and allow sufficient time to prepare comprehensive and credible scientific assessments”.

Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:00:19 GMT

Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

The two had become fast friends since they met at Power Slap 17, which took place last October in Saudi Arabia. They host a podcast together, called The Slappy Hour (sample chat: “I had questions for his chin … but the chin question’s gone”). “As the sport’s so new, it’s great to have someone to bounce ideas off,” said Robinson. It’s not uncommon for competitors to destroy each other on stage, then later compare notes. When I spoke to Damien “the Bell” Dibbell, an affable 24-year-old American heavyweight whom many consider the greatest slap-fighter alive, he mentioned that he met his best friend, Duane “the Iron Giant” Crespo, after knocking him unconscious in the second round.

In the Crowne Plaza, conversation veered from recent rule changes – beards were now limited to a few millimetres, much glorious facial hair had been lost – to a controversial incident in Power Slap 21 when Anthony “Kiing” DeFrank had refused to alter his stance after being accused of “turtling”, breaking the rules by tucking his chin flush into his neck to receive the slap. Despite his protests, he was disqualified. Word was he’d never slap again.

Seen from a certain perspective, Power Slap is less a sport in its own right than one whittled down from other sports: think football reduced to penalties or rugby with just conversions. Like boxing, it is a combat sport, separated by gender and weight divisions (from flyweight to super-heavyweight). Unlike boxing, competitors are forbidden from dodging or blocking the blows. Like darts, Power Slap is turn-based. Unlike darts, contestants effectively take turns at being the board.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.

This is a sport precision-made for our moment. It is designed to be viewed on TikTok and YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, one thumb-swipe at a time. Power Slap’s CEO, Frank Lamicella, a former corporate lawyer from New York, will happily admit it was created with short attention spans in mind. The only real buildup comes in the contestants’ walk to the stage and the brief seconds they spend rehearsing their slap before striking, like snooker players feathering a cue. A round lasts a couple of minutes; titles can be decided in seconds. As every action is a potential knockout, the highlights come pre-packaged. It is nothing but highlights.

Since its launch in November 2022, Power Slap has gained 4 million YouTube subscribers. On TikTok it has more than 9 million. Perhaps even more importantly – though admittedly unverifiably – Power Slap claims that clips of the sport have racked up 25bn total views across all online platforms. Its live events are now held almost every month, in locations from Las Vegas to Abu Dhabi.

The founder of Power Slap is Dana White, the man behind the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), whose accomplishments include organising a cage fight on the White House lawn to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Donald Trump is such a fan of White that he recently asked him to be his press secretary. (He later claimed he was just kidding.)

White expects Power Slap to be the biggest sport in the world soon. In explaining its appeal, he likes to invoke the school playground: no matter what kids are up to, when a fight breaks out, everyone watches. Violence is a universal language. Or, as he told a podcast last year, “everyone understands a slap”. He sells “holy shit moments”, he said, and Power Slap has more than most.

According to White, Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade. The companies lining up to plaster their name over Power Slap include energy drink suppliers such as Monster Energy and cryptocurrency platforms such as VeChain. Erectile dysfunction drug company Rugiet recently sponsored Power Slap’s action replay.

Power Slap is not without its detractors, many of whom deem it less a sport than violence for the hell of it. The Brain Injury Association of America has demanded its immediate end. Chris Nowinski, CEO of the Concussion Legacy Foundation, has wondered: “What’s next, ‘who can survive a stabbing?’” Even podcaster Joe Rogan, a noted proponent of UFC – itself criticised for brutality – has called Power Slap “free brain damage”.

In Belgrade, Robinson was confident but apprehensive. Power Slap 22 marked the first time the competition had been held in Europe. It was only his second Power Slap, having risen through the less glamorous UK scene where they slap over a barrel. He wanted to do his local scene proud. His opponent the following day was Pavol “Glitch” Horelican, an undefeated Slovakian. Yet his long-term goal was taking down Dibbell, the Apollo Creed to his Rocky. “He’s an ungodly genetic freak,” Robinson told me. “He’s probably the perfect slap-fighter.” In Serbia, the two went out for dinner, though they were careful not to talk tactics.

Both Robinson and Kenny had been at the hotel for the best part of a week, fulfilling various media duties. One of the challenges, it turns out, for a sport that is both ultra-collegial and ultra-violent, is ramping up aggression when required. For his pre-fight face-off with Horelican earlier that day, Robinson did his best with the required pantomime smack-talk, but his heart wasn’t in it. He’d taken him out to dinner, too, and even taught him how he tenses his muscles to prepare for a slap. (Kenny was aghast: “What the fuck you doing?”)

In the hours before the fight, Robinson told me, he planned to work himself into a state of frenzy by imagining Horelican responsible for the death of his entire family, a sort of John Wick-plus. Kenny, the Canadian, said he would be aiming for a Zen state, through meditation.

Roughly speaking, the history of sport is a story of compression and contraction, or at least the growing understanding that we all have homes to go to. Many events began as endurance contests: boxing matches went on until one person could no longer stand; Test cricket could span weeks. (One match, between England and South Africa, lasted 12 days and was eventually abandoned as England had a ship to catch.) Before the modern marathon, the Victorians followed “pedestrianism”, six-day walking races during which competitors steadily consumed beef tea. By the dawn of the TV age, most competitive sports required only small tweaks, rather than total reinventions, to accommodate themselves to the new medium. Football kick-off times changed, table-tennis balls were very slightly enlarged. Now that we have arrived at the viral clip stage of human culture, we have new requirements. Hence Power Slap.

The first professional slap, as far as anyone can tell, took place a little over a decade ago. A Californian man called Raymond Hernandez ran a touring expo called The Ink Masters Tattoo Show and wanted some non-tattoo-based entertainment. He had recently toured Japan, and remembered a segment from a gameshow that made him laugh: five men in a circle, each taking turns to slap the man to his right – last man standing wins. Hernandez decided two men were enough. Stripping an activity down to its studs was in slap-fighting’s DNA from the start. At an expo in Lubbock, Texas, in early 2015, Hernandez placed the competitors either side of a folding table and explained the entire rulebook. Slap.

The first man slapped the other across the table without much impact; the second slapped back and knocked his opponent out. Hernandez hadn’t arranged for anyone to catch the falling fighter. “We never thought you could get knocked out by a slap,” he has said. The footage, recorded on a smartphone, went viral. ESPN and Jimmy Kimmel got in touch. Slap fighting was born.

It wasn’t until 2017 that Dana White first became aware of slap fighting. Sitting in a meeting room at UFC’s head office in Las Vegas, White, as CEO, was supposed to be discussing matchups and pay-per-view deals, yet his attention was elsewhere: specifically, on a social media video of two large Russian men taking turns to slap each other. The production value was not high – to White it looked like it had been filmed in a barn – yet it had racked up almost 400m views. At the time, those were Justin Bieber numbers.

At UFC, White had built a reputation on turning violence into entertainment. UFC is a very-few-holds-barred cage-fighting contest that combines kickboxing and wrestling undertaken with minimally padded gloves. In 1995, the senator John McCain labelled it “human cockfighting”. By 2001, UFC was on the verge of bankruptcy when White, along with Vegas casino magnates Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta, bought it for $2m. They codified the rules, received athletic commission approval, and self-funded a reality TV show to promote it. It became a juggernaut. In July 2016, the trio had sold UFC for $4bn, though White stayed on as CEO. Not long after seeing the video of the Russian men slugging each other in a weirdly compelling ritual, White called the Fertitta brothers and asked: “Wanna do it again?” It was a historic moment. “I don’t know another example where this has happened, where you take one YouTube video and you build an entire sport around it,” Lamicella told me.

Owing to the pandemic, it wasn’t until March 2022 that they put together a closed-doors pilot in Las Vegas. It consisted of 25 bouts involving more than 40 fighters over two days, and its aim was, among other things, to firm up the rules. By then, other slap-fighting competitions, with varying standards of safety and showmanship, had formed in Poland, South Africa and the UK. There was even an American upstart called SlapFight Championship. Power Slap, with more buying power, snapped up the best fighters.

The rules boiled down to three main fouls. No stepping – meaning no heel lift, feet square, to reduce a strike’s power. No clubbing – meaning no striking with the heel of the palm and no contact anywhere but the cheek. And no flinching. They also limited the number of rounds. At SlapFight Championship, they initially went on until someone won, which usually meant a knockout. One fight lasted 27 rounds before doctors stopped it. One man’s eye had swollen shut.

For Lamicella, the pilot event in Vegas brought home one major realisation: they were going to need a hell of a lot of cameras. More than 30, he reckoned, to capture the full majesty of the sport. “You have the shot, the slow-mo, the super slow-mo, the aerial shot, the shot of the feet, every which angle,” he told me. “It looks simple, but the production budget is huge.”

White followed the same formula as UFC. After obtaining regulatory approval from the Nevada State Athletic Commission, he launched a reality TV show to promote it, Power Slap: Road to the Title, to air on basic cable network TBS. The show did not last long once footage emerged of White, in an irony that was lost on no one, slapping his wife in a nightclub. TBS cancelled the show after the first season.

There is no typical route into “slap”, as those in the sport call it. Robinson, who had never previously competed professionally in any combat sport, discovered it online during lockdown. Then and there, he decided, for reasons he finds hard to fully articulate, to become the best slap fighter in the world. His podcast co-host, Kenny, had been making $30 a match in Canadian wrestling when a recruiter asked him: “You wanna get slapped?” After asking how much it paid – $5,000 with another five if he won – it turned out that, yes, in fact, he did.

Some journeys are more colourful. Peter “the Alligator All G” Truchlik, a former international arm-wrestling champion, was talent-spotted by Power Slap promoters who came across YouTube videos of him bending nails, tearing books and slapping watermelons into oblivion. Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii, who competes in the super-heavyweight division, found the sport by chance. At a strongman festival years before, the Siberian farmer had entered both a slap-fighting and a dumpling-eating contest, won both, and got a new side-hustle and a new nickname to go with it. His first Power Slap paycheque was $25,000 and three goats.

No one I spoke to slapped full-time. Even reigning heavyweight champion Dibbell, who sells slap-based merch (phone cases, hoodies, T-shirts) on the side, has a day job as an air-conditioning repairman. Robinson is a lift engineer by trade. He enjoys the work. It teaches him a lot about people. Surprisingly often, he says, he’ll attend a broken lift only to find those stuck inside have ended up fighting, breaking it further still. “A different type of cage match,” he laughs.

Robinson is short and sturdy, with a trim beard and a seriousness only punctuated by a laugh that seems to arrive by accident, as if he’s been caught off guard. He is a man easily obsessed, and his obsessions make him easy to like. Before slap fighting, his passions flared and burned out. As a younger man, he compulsively collected things such as coins and cards, before moving on to driving simulators, buying everything from the chair to the steering wheel to the gearstick. By his mid-20s, he was on to chess, setting up two monitors at work, one permanently on chess. com, playing four or five hours a day (he has since left that job), before moving on to darts, joining leagues, spending hundreds on the exact type of board and arrow, “trying to work my way up”.

Each time, what ended the obsession was the dispiriting realisation he would never be the best. Chess came to an abrupt halt when he realised he was 20 years late, having failed to start aged five.

His gift for Power Slap had been staring him in the face the whole time. He grew up on a rough estate in Stalybridge, was punched and slapped his fair share, yet he never so much as bruised. His party trick as a teen: to let people punch him as hard as they could. This was not his proudest hour, yet he eventually realised it was his superpower. When he saw slap fighting on YouTube in lockdown, he thought: where can I do this?

He contacted Josh Skeete, who by 2022 was just getting a UK slap-fighting scene, which would later be called BritSlap, off the ground in Liverpool. Skeete had encountered his fair share of resistance. At first, the fighters and wrestlers he contacted to take part told him to get lost; slap fighting wasn’t a sport. Others seemed interested. He hired refs – who could ensure the fighters’ feet didn’t move and the striker’s aim for the cheek was true – and a medical team, yet soon realised he needed to hire catchers, too. At early events, fighters brought along a friend for the job, but they would often get so wrapped up in the action, they’d forget to actually catch the falling fighters.

For his first slap fight, at BritSlap 3 in early 2024, filmed without an audience in a TV studio in Liverpool, Robinson competed in jeans. Looking back, he reckons his technique was all over the place, his body motion all wrong. Still, by the judge’s decision, he won. He was hooked. “I was all in. I was addicted. That was it for me. I thought: now I’m gonna conquer the world.”

He had only told his partner, Shannon Hilton, that he was taking part a few hours before. She spent the intervening time watching YouTube videos, becoming ever-more horrified. “She was livid,” Robinson told me. When he returned and told her he’d won, she had been so angry, she’d already decided to deny him victory, and had told everyone he had lost.

Slap fighting is so new that nearly every aspect of training and technique must be invented. Prior to his second BritSlap fight, in October 2024, Robinson prepared mostly with regular gym work, while also honing his technique by slapping pads held by a friend. He got some odd looks in a PureGym while those around him did pilates. He won his fight, knocking his opponent out with the very first slap. But to become the best in the world, he needed more.

The demands on the slap fighter are particular. Unlike boxing, the rules dictate that competitors cannot place one foot behind the other to help generate force. So Robinson sought out a sport in which competitors throw while seated, and found one: Paralympic discus. He found a Paralympic discus trainer who taught him how to generate torque from his hips. The motion suited him: unlike taller US slap fighters, who prefer horizontal bear-claw swipes, Robinson, at 5ft 7in, is mostly slapping upwards.

His feet weren’t allowed to lift – but what, he wondered, if they could roll? Other slap fighters wore cowboy boots to aid this. Power Slap has no rules regarding footwear. Under the guidance of his personal trainer, James Reed, Robinson began studying the heel-to-toe rolling techniques that surfers use to change direction. He realised the tendon in his slapping arm, his right, was more important than the muscles. In his van, any time he was parked, Robinson pumped a hand-grip with his right. To strengthen that hand, he looked to rock climbers, who do finger exercises with their hands submerged in uncooked rice. “The burn you get off that is insane,” says Robinson, who mostly does it while watching Netflix. When he saw an actor deliver a slap on screen, he’d think: amateur.

At the gym, he’d slap a punching bag. At night, in his garden, he’d practice by slapping the head of a boxing mannequin. At first, his neighbours thought the sound was gunfire. By BritSlap 5, in May last year, now at Boxpark in Liverpool with a crowd of more than 1,000, Robinson knocked another opponent out with his first slap. Power Slap soon came calling. Skeete became his manager.

To fully appreciate the power of a well-honed slap, I attended the Resilience Training Centre in Stalybridge, a small gym in a former factory that recently became the first in the UK to offer dedicated slap-fight training. I held a pad at head height as a slender young man, who was competing in a forthcoming BritSlap, practised his slaps. With each, my arm was almost wrenched from the socket. I declined Robinson’s kind offer to receive his slaps next, but I can confirm: Robinson’s slaps do sound like gunfire.

When it comes to brain injuries, just how dire is Power Slap? The bad news is that participation virtually guarantees head trauma. But its defenders note that this trauma comes in limited portions: five scheduled blows for title fights. Robinson points out that he might take more than 100 blows in a boxing match. In Power Slap, the most common injuries happen to the slapper – pulled biceps, fractured wrists, even broken arms, because, unlike boxing, where your gloves cushion the blow, the combatant is putting all their force into connecting with a solid object.

Still, the solid object in question happens to be the opponent’s face, and the unabashed aim is to render that opponent unconscious. It is this that drives online views. Power Slap offers $10,000 bonuses for knockouts, typically doubling a fighter’s purse. Robinson has honed his technique to this end. He slaps upwards, making the head move quicker, the brain deforming inside the skull. “The science of knocking someone out isn’t how hard you hit them,” he told me. “It’s how fast you can make that brain accelerate.” Robinson has yet to be knocked out, but notes the “flashes” of white light he gets each time he is struck.
