Sometimes, after a knockout, competitors have to be reminded what happened. At Power Slap’s test event, a competitor named Chris Kennedy was knocked unconscious by the first slap he took, and asked, upon waking, “Got knocked out doing what?” After being knocked out in Power Slap 6, in Las Vegas, Sheena “the Hungarian Hurricane” Bathory woke up in an ambulance. She had to be informed why she was in Las Vegas, and that she had won (her opponent had committed a clubbing foul). Slap fighting’s one fatality occurred in 2021, at PunchDown 5 in Poland, when Artur “Waluś” Walczak suffered a brain bleed and died several weeks later. It was his third slap fight of the evening. (“In any combat sport, fighting more than once in an evening is insane,” says Robinson.)

When I asked Lamicella about the dangers, he noted the comprehensive medical tests, including brain scans, that every fighter must pass before each fight. He also compared Power Slap, favourably, to both boxing and UFC. “If our doctor was on the phone, he would tell you the big issues in boxing are not the big knockouts. It’s all the little jabs, the continuous punches, the sparring. That’s where the people really get hurt with things like brain bleeds,” he said. He added that their “hospital transport number” was “a lot lower than UFC”.

One of the few medical studies of Power Slap was carried out by Raj Lavadi, a neurosurgeon at Indiana University School of Medicine, who studied footage of 333 strikes across 78 matches and found 79% of fighters showed an observable sign of concussion. “The frequency with which you observe these signs is shocking,” Lavadi told me.

Lavadi also pointed out the brain scans don’t count for much. “A brain scan is great for certain things,” he said. “But I don’t know if it really protects the fighter. Like, is that it?” Crucially, while a brain scan can pick up conditions ranging from blood vessel abnormalities to fractures, it would not pick up the onset of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease most likely caused by repeated blows to the head, which is linked to symptoms ranging from memory loss to dementia. “You can really only diagnose that in autopsy,” he said.

At the event in Belgrade, participants spoke about the fighters who could take a slap without much reaction and who could not – who could “eat it”, in slap parlance. They also spoke about a “chin-meter” – like a battery bar they think of depleting with each knockout, making the next knockout more likely. Both Robinson and Kenny mentioned light heavyweight Ron “the Wolverine” Bata. It was time for him to retire, they felt. “He doesn’t look the same, he looks like he gets hurt more and more now,” said Kenny.

When I mentioned the undetectable onset of CTE to Robinson, he said he’d already given himself a knockout limit. Twice and he was out. He understood the long-term impact multiple knockouts could have. He was a father of three, with a fourth on the way. He mentioned a quote from Dibbell, the reigning champion he hoped to topple. “He said, ‘If you’ve been knocked out before, I’m not the man to fight’, and that’s the truth.”

Every Power Slap clip is its own microdrama. Each has suspense and violence, triumph and disaster. It doesn’t much matter if you watch in horror or with glee: the algorithm will note that you watched and will suggest you watch more.

Nearly all begin with a closeup on the face of someone waiting patiently to be struck, and you realise how strange this is. It is not like watching a live execution, but it’s also not like watching penalties. The closest analogue is probably corporal punishment. As they wait, slap fighters grimace manically, looking terrified. This grimacing is often used for the thumbnail images on social media, but it is not just a product of fear. Forming this expression engages their trapezius muscles, or traps, bracing the neck and upper back, aiming to spread the impact of the blow to come. You feel their pain before they do.

The striker will first place their hand on their opponent’s cheek, in a way that almost seems tender, to get their measure before they swing. They will do wind-ups, slowly motioning the real strike, and must declare beforehand when it comes – on one, two or three.

For a sport that doesn’t allow flinching, let alone blocking, slap fighters put just as much training into defence as they do attack. What exactly works seems woolly. Most agree having strong neck and jaw muscles helps, though most don’t copy Hayden “the Cowboy” Johnson, who lifts kettlebells with his teeth. Robinson uses a jaw exerciser. He’s managed to develop bulging temples (“a right meathead,” he laughs).

The hardest part, most will tell you, is training yourself not to flinch, especially for those with a combat background, who’ve spent their lives learning how to dodge. The penalties for flinching are serious. After a flinch, the striker is allowed to slap again. Three flinches in the same round, or four overall, means disqualification. Light heavyweight Logan “Kill Shot” Greenhalgh once lost a title fight to a flinch. Some use the Muay Thai technique of punching water in a barrel, keeping their eyes open through the splashes. It’s perhaps only Aaron “Colossus” Turner who trains with snakes, putting his face to the glass and trying to stay still when they strike. (It didn’t work – Turner was disqualified in his last match for flinching.) Most, including Robinson, just get someone to slap them with foam pool noodles.

Yet even here, Robinson has innovated. What if, he wondered, he could take the impact out of a slap by moving his face, rolling with it, at the exact moment of contact? Could it be done? In that fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a second? He looked towards Formula One, where drivers train their reactions with a multicoloured three-pronged spinning device – they must grab the colour of the prong their coach calls out while it spins in mid-air. “We’ve spent hours doing that,” laughs Reed, his trainer. In real time, as he is struck, it seems as if Robinson is flinching. YouTube commentators always claim it. It’s only in slow motion you realise he isn’t. He moves at the millisecond a blow arrives. Robinson now proudly calls this his signature move.

The most-watched Power Slap clip is an 18sec YouTube short, with almost half a billion views. It is not a knockdown. It is called “Eviahn ATE this slap with ease!” Eviahn “the Waterboy” Scott takes a blow, and celebrates wildly, like a goalkeeper who’s just pulled off a fingertip save to preserve a precious lead. The camera cuts to a giggling Dana White, looking like a child who’s seen an adult almost slip over. Then it’s time for the replay. In Power Slap, the slow-motion replays almost always focus on the exact motion of impact, the flesh on the face not so much absorbing the blow as spreading it, rippling from it, like a sheet caught by a breeze.

The second-most-watched clip is a knockdown. It has been viewed 371m times, this time on TikTok. It is called, “Jewel Scott #knockouts hit different #powerslap #slap”, and sees Scott’s opponent, Anthony Green, drop to the ground like a ragdoll.

We think of dopamine as a pleasure chemical, yet neuroscientists will tell you it is not. It is, instead, the molecule of desire and anticipation. It makes us watch to the end, it makes us flick to the next, but it does not bring joy. It is also why they compare social media’s infinite scroll to slot machines.

At the Belgrade Arena, on 30 July, several thousand spectators filed in for PowerSlap 22. The sport is still new in Europe. In Las Vegas, I’m told, the vibe is a cross between British darts and American wrestling, the ramp-up between each slap eliciting hollers and cheers and boos. In Belgrade, the mood was one of amused interest.

Before it began, young fans flooded to the front to beg autographs from a couple of fighters walking the floor. Once the lights went down, it took on an air closer to a Vegas magic show than a prize fight. A light show strobed, a black stage without borders in the arena’s centre was lit up by neon podiums at either end – Power Slap’s equivalent of a fighter’s corner, where each competitor would retreat for one minute to recover after each blow – and in the centre, a glowing podium rose from the ground to a height of around 3ft, the padded plinth over which all slaps would take place.

A sharply suited MC kicked things off by introducing the sponsors. The night’s “monster knockouts”, we were told, were brought to us by Monster Energy (“unleash the beast!”). VeChain was the crypto token partner – and also the medium in which the $10,000 knockout bonuses would be paid. The night’s prediction odds were brought to us by Polymarket.

The first fight was both the most thrilling and disturbing, as Darren “the Tarantula” Godfrey, bearded and liberally tattooed, took on the fresh-faced Daniyar “Shreder” Toktarov in the middleweight division. Both wore trainers, Power Slap-branded tracksuit bottoms, and Power Slap-branded T-shirts. Godfrey was knocked down in both the first and second rounds, something most fighters don’t recover from. On the second occasion, Godfrey stayed down until the referee counted to eight. He retreated to his corner, then returned to the podium. On Godfrey’s second slap, he knocked Tokarov out, his head connecting sickeningly with the central podium as he dropped. It was replayed in slow, then super slow, motion on the arena’s screens. No one in the audience appeared to wince. Most clapped and cheered.

When Robinson entered the arena, he set about stirring up the crowd, whipping both arms upwards. The lights strobed, La Roux’s In for the Kill vibrated from the speakers. The arena’s screens listed the circumference of the competitors’ necks (19in for Robinson, 20in for Horelican) and the size of their hands, measured thumb to pinky (8in to 9.5in). Horelican, who had won the coin toss, slapped first, but to little effect. The strike wasn’t clean, hitting Robinson on the neck: a clubbing foul, a point deduction.

Before his strike, Robinson rubbed his hands in chalk. He gave Horelican a mirthless wink. And then, drawing on all his 6am starts, his hours of studying footage, his months of tendon training, his garden slapping, he put it all into a single motion that lasted milliseconds, a sharp twist of torso, a brutal whipping blow upwards.

Horelican went down, blood gushing from his mouth. Robinson raised both palms, the universal symbol of: are you not entertained? Robinson had burst a blood vessel in his opponent’s mouth – remarkably, a Power Slap first. Medical staff wiped the blood from his chin, but they couldn’t stem the bleeding. Horelican didn’t seem dazed, but a replay showed his eyes rolling back, sickeningly, as he fell. He couldn’t carry on.

For several minutes after Horelican left the stage, Power Slap staff half-heartedly mopped the blood from the arena’s floor by pushing towels with their feet. Robinson had won, one slap closer to the title. Not long after, he called Shannon, as he always does post-fight, to let her know he was OK.

When I spoke to Robinson recently, he was one step closer still, having recently competed in Power Slap 25 in Abu Dhabi, beating Jujhar “Tiger” Singh in the second round. Though he wouldn’t get a $10,000 knockout bonus – his first slap failed to knock his opponent down and Singh was disqualified in the second round after consecutive clubbing fouls – he had moved up two places in heavyweight rankings, to six. His partner was still coming around, he said, slowly but surely. This time, she’d even allowed a viewing party at their home. Though he added: “I was told she was basically peeking from behind the door in the kitchen on the first slap.”

Her view of the sport likely wasn’t helped by another serious injury a month before. At Power Slap 23 in Texas, Jake “Rock Hard” Hager was left with one eyeball ruptured and a retina detached. His team stated that, after two surgeries, he retained some sight in the eye. Dana White described it as one of the most severe injuries in the sport he had seen.

Not long ago, I spoke to Shannon. She still remembers her first reaction to the sport: “How can someone stand there and take a blow?” Before every fight, she says, an entire week of dread, a 50/50 chance that her partner gets hurt. But she remembers, too, his early determination. Even back when Robinson was in BritSlap, “he’d watch Power Slap and say: ‘I’ll be there one day.’ I said there’s no way you’re going there! It looks brutal.” But, so far, he’s proved he can do it. “I’ve never had a reason to doubt him. I think that’s what changed my opinion.”

Still, at the recent watch party, she couldn’t stand to watch him be hit. She turned her back to the screen, and asked those around her: “Is he still standing? Is he still standing up?” She is yet to see him compete in the flesh. But if Power Slap was held in London, she allows that she might. Their eldest daughter, who’s 11, has become quite the fan. “She loves it,” says Robinson. “She thinks I’m some kind of local celebrity. You know: my dad’s on Google!” It sounded almost quaint.

Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

The Guardian Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:00:18 GMT

Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.

As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

Trump Weighs New Strikes on Iran as Israel Presses for Action, Officials Say

The New York Times November 18, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Warnings that Iran is rebuilding its missile stockpile and advancing biological and chemical programs have divided the Trump administration.

By Julian E. BarnesEric SchmittMaggie HabermanJonathan Swan and Ronen Bergman

President Trump is weighing plans for another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, taking into account new intelligence about Iranian capabilities and intensifying pressure from Israel to move quickly and aggressively, U. S. and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions said.

Mr. Trump has yet to make a decision, they said. But he has been considering warnings from Israel about Iran’s success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.

And he is taking into account that the United States now has a window in which it has significant military firepower in the region.

There are deep differences of opinion within the administration about the strength of the intelligence and the wisdom of assaulting Iran again, especially after a midterm election in which voters clearly expressed displeasure with a war that has driven up prices and failed to yield the quick triumph that Mr. Trump had promised at its outset, nearly eight months ago.

But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, whose hold on his job is especially tenuous after elections there last month, is pressing hard for the United States to join his country in a four- to seven-day campaign of airstrikes against Iran, the people briefed on the discussions said. The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive security issues.

The conversations intensified last week. Roman Gofman, the director of Mossad, the Israeli intelligence agency, held meetings in Washington, including with the C. I. A. director, John Ratcliffe. Other top Israeli officials, including Shlomi Binder, the director of military intelligence, have advocated a resumption of operations in discussions with American counterparts.

A senior Israeli official disputed the notion that Mr. Netanyahu had pressured Mr. Trump. A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu said the prime minister had always acted to “safeguard the security” of Israel.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly vacillated in recent months about restarting major combat. He has declared at times that the war is over and suggested at others that he could strike again to ensure that Iran could never develop a nuclear weapon.

He recently instructed Vice President JD Vance to abandon an effort to reach a negotiated solution, and has appeared to embrace the idea that a prolonged economic squeeze would eventually lead Iran to seek a deal under which it would give up its nuclear program.

But Mr. Trump is also highly sensitive to the criticism that the United States has in effect lost the war, people familiar with his thinking said. And after spending two years flexing executive power, the president is entering a lame-duck period of his second term. He has often used shows of force when he has faced pushback or uncertainty in the past.

A U. S. official said Mr. Trump no longer needed to conduct major combat against Iran because his economic pressure campaign had devastated the country.

But the official added that Mr. Trump had all options available to ensure that Iran could never have a nuclear weapon.

In recent weeks, the U. S. military has built up an especially vast arsenal in the region, with naval ships, fighter planes and bombers ready to launch a relatively short campaign of intense strikes against Iran’s drone and missile arsenal, as well as Iranian energy facilities, should Mr. Trump authorize action, military officials said.

That force briefly grew earlier this week with the arrival in the region of a third aircraft carrier, the U. S. S. Theodore Roosevelt. That marked only the second time the United States has had three carriers in the Middle East since the Iraq war in 2003. But just as quickly, one of the other carriers, the U. S. S. George Washington, headed back to the Pacific.

Dozens of fighter jets and attack planes based in the Middle East would join any strike, as would long-range B-1 and B-2 bombers in the United States, which for weeks have been on 96-hour notice for possible missions against Iran.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have presented the president with a menu of military options that Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U. S. Central Command, developed in recent months. Admiral Cooper is traveling in the region this week, U. S. officials said.

Given the possibility of major combat restarting, the Pentagon and State Department have withdrawn personnel from bases and facilities in the region as a precaution. The United States also recently delivered an additional Patriot antimissile battery to Israel, military officials said.

The Pentagon declined to comment on Wednesday, citing operational security. It added in a statement that “the U. S. military continues to provide the president options, and all options remain on the table.”

The C. I. A. also declined to comment.

Any U. S. strikes would likely focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has rebuilt since the early phase of the war, military officials said. Other targets could include Iranian energy facilities and Revolutionary Guards command posts and headquarters.

Israel’s planning has also encompassed further attacks on Iranian nuclear sites and, most provocatively, widespread strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure that could cut off power to industry and civilians, something that Mr. Trump has yet to agree to, people familiar with the discussions said.

From the start of the war, Mr. Netanyahu has pushed plans that he insists could instill a popular uprising against the government, something that has yet to show any signs of coming to pass.

For the Israeli prime minister, the push for another round of strikes is inextricably tied to his fight for political survival. Following last month’s election in Israel, Mr. Netanyahu remains at the head of a caretaker government as a coalition of opposition parties is seeking to form a government. Renewed fighting could delay or derail the opposition’s attempt to form a government and create pressure for a unity government that would include Mr. Netanyahu.

In seeking to convince the United States to join in another round of major attacks, Israel has highlighted what it contends are a variety of threats from Tehran. Israeli officials have been asserting that Iran continues to possess significant chemical and biological weapon capabilities that pose a regional threat — and that could be used in terrorist attacks against the U. S. and Europe.

They have also suggested that the Iranians are able to equip drones in the region with some of those weapons, and use them to strike Israel or its neighbors.

People briefed on the discussions said that U. S. intelligence officials also see evidence of stepped-up efforts by Iran to bolster its chemical and biological weapon capacities.

But they said the prevailing view is that Iran is doing so not to use those weapons preemptively against Israel and other foes, but to deter the United States and Israel from employing nuclear weapons or conducting large-scale attacks that would inflict substantial damage on Iran’s infrastructure or civilians.

The Israelis have shared intelligence claiming that Iranians have plotted to use chemical agents against senior U. S. officials. One person briefed on the intelligence, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said that type of threat was related to the decision in recent weeks to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent from his home.

Mark Mazzetti contributed reporting.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

It’s Getting Harder for Young Adults to Deal With Uncertainty

The New York Times November 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

At a moment when technical glitches are stirring confusion and fear, a new analysis examines just how distressing uncertainty can feel.

By Christina Caron

Global conflict, mixed economical signals, disruptions to banks, airlines and other businesses — nearly everything seems to carry an air of uncertainty these days.

Handling this level of unpredictability isn’t always easy.

And a new meta-analysis published on Wednesday in JAMA Psychiatry suggests that young adults are having an especially tough time coping with uncertainty than in decades past. The study found that people reported feeling more intolerant of uncertainty over time, meaning that they had difficulty enduring unpredictable or ambiguous situations. The steepest increase occurred from 2012 onward, starting right around the time that smartphones became ubiquitous, allowing for continuous consumption of information during uncertain times.

Researchers say increased distress about the unknown may help explain the rise in anxiety among this age group. Previous research has shown that intolerance of uncertainty is linked to a variety of anxiety disorders. It fuels “worry cycles” that make not knowing feel like a threat, said Katherine M. Keyes, a professor of epidemiology at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and an author of the study.

She hypothesized that the greater levels of intolerance of uncertainty could be contributing to the increase in anxiety disorders among young people, especially in the current climate, where people are facing “increasing political polarization, economic uncertainty, political uncertainty and the rise of information technology.”

The rate of anxiety disorders was relatively steady through the 1990s and into the early aughts. But in more recent years, symptoms of anxiety have been on the rise, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and are more common among younger adults than older ones.

Jean Twenge, a professor of psychology at San Diego State University and the author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World,” suggested that the increasing discomfort with uncertainty might stem from declines in rituals of teenage independence, like getting a driver’s license, having a paid job or going out with friends.

“It’s also possible parents have become less tolerant of uncertainty,” said Dr. Twenge, who was not involved in the study.

In addition, if social media and smartphones lure kids into staying home rather than going out with friends, in-person interaction and independence can seem even scarier.

“Constant internet access also means that questions can always be answered right away,” she said. “Gen Z and Gen Alpha have never known the world of uncertainty previous generations lived with when they might have to just guess, or just show up and hope it works out.”

The meta-analysis, which analyzed 132 studies with more than 35,000 participants, is not generalizable to all adults because it looked only at college students in the United States and Canada. But other research has shown that uncertainty has become baked into the everyday life of many Americans. In this year’s Stress in America survey, conducted by the Harris Poll on behalf of the American Psychological Association, 68 percent of respondents said they had become accustomed to living with uncertainty.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

The survey also found that, over the past year, uncertainty was one of the factors driving adults to put their futures on hold, in some cases delaying major life decisions such as purchasing a home or having a child. This was especially true among younger adults. One-third of those ages 18 to 45 reported delaying planning for the future, compared with 24 percent of adults ages 46-61 and 13 percent of those 62-80.

Participants in the A. P. A. study also listed their top stressors, many of which related to cost of living or the future of the nation.

“Big sources of uncertainty that we don’t have control over are particularly challenging,” said Lynn Bufka, a clinical psychologist and spokeswoman for the American Psychological Association. “One of the things that we try to help people think about is where are the places you do have some control, where you can assert something.”

When treating anxiety, mental health providers often focus on helping their patients tolerate uncertainty, said Dr. Bufka, who sometimes suggests that her clients put their worries into an imaginary box and check in on them once a day.

Kalya Castillo, a clinical psychologist in New York City, said she sometimes asked clients to write down affirming statements like “I have been here before, I have experience in managing uncertainty” on their phones or on the fridge. Then they can revisit those messages if they are feeling distressed.

She also helps them tolerate uncertainty by practicing radical acceptance, a concept that calls for accepting reality without fighting or avoiding it, with the faith that you’ll be able to adapt and move forward.

“Accepting reality does not have to mean we have to like it or agree with it,” Dr. Castillo said. “It means we are choosing to preserve our energy for factors within our control.”

Christina Caron is a Times reporter covering mental health.

“DoorDash is not an emergency plan.”

“Our institutions are kind of collapsing,” said Sam Bloch, the founder of Camp Doomsdaddy, a preparedness workshop in Sonoma County, Calif. “As our needs are escalating.”Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jesse McKinley

Jesse McKinley, who is not ready for the apocalypse, reported from New York and California.

This week, in the wake of system failures, network crashes and flight stoppages, which left many people fearful, frustrated and generally on edge, Liz Howard had a simple message.

“I told you this would happen,” Howard sang in a singsong video to hundreds of thousands of online followers, adding, “And it’s going to get worse from here.”

Howard, a California-based cybersecurity expert known as Liz the Developer, is just one of a raft of online oracles preaching to a new breed of anxious followers who have been alarmed by a series of seemingly cascading crises but are also determined to adapt and survive whatever mayhem the digital world might conjure.

It’s a cohort whose message has suddenly taken on a deeper resonance after an array of recent disruptions, as well as the potential real-world consequences of other meltdowns, from the merely inconvenient to the dangerous: loss of navigational tools, power outages, banks being down; loss of communications and access to medical records; civil unrest and institutional collapse.

These are all worries that overlap with those of more traditional preppers, but the digital variety also has their own brand of futuristic fear: stolen data, password breaches, digital surveillance and — more than anything — malevolent artificial intelligence, with dire warnings and even scarier predictions.

“Tech has become evil,” said Howard, who founded The Multiverse School, an “unconventional” coding and A. I. school, and sports a shock of aquamarine hair in their droll videos. “I kind of know how bad it can get. And with A. I., it’s really getting bad.” (On Monday, Google, in fact, announced that autonomous A. I. agents were outpacing the ability of humans to fight them, the same day Howard posted their “I told you so” about that exact topic.)

To counter those perceived threats, as well as the terror of — gulp — the loss of internet service, Howard and others are collectively creating a kind of online survivalist’s guide for this nervous moment. It’s a grab-bag — or maybe a go-bag — complete with Faraday-field fanny packs, which block electromagnetic signals, and MacGyver-like hacks on creating batteries out of a magnet, two padlocks and a USB charger. Others preach a got-no-signal self-sufficiency, with tutorials on downloading maps, first aid guides and even the entirety of Wikipedia, as well as places to escape to in the event that everything goes south.

“There’s a feeling of kind of helplessness that you can have around all of this stuff that sucks,” said Deana Burke, a tech writer and A. I. literacy influencer who recently began a series on “lowkey prepping,” complete with discussion of long-range radio devices. “You can sort of just bear witness to it. Or you can try and have a little agency.”

The enemy in many of these disaster scenarios is pretty clear, said Dr. Avriel Epps, a computational social scientist and an assistant professor at the University of California, Riverside, whose video about trying to ditch her smartphone earned more than 100,000 likes on TikTok.

“The products that are being developed by this industry are really in service of their leaders, not in service of the consumers,” Epps said in an interview. “It’s like: ‘We don’t want this. Why do you keep shoving it down our throat?’”

Epps, who also has tried to “de-Google” her life, has found other ways to unplug, like “Screen-Free Sundays” — with no tablets, no phones, no TV — something she admitted was an acquired taste.

“Neither of my kids liked it,” she said, “But I enjoyed it.”

That antipathy toward Big Tech seemingly reverberates in acts of sabotage on Flock cameras and the popularity of D. I. Y. content creators like Jake Cochrane, a. k. a. Dirtbag America, who posts snappy videos about how to build things like a pallet cabin while offering a satirical commentary about “spiting our corporate overlords.”

Many of the digital doomsayers talk about a “polycrisis”: overlapping and seemingly interconnected threats. (Or “an advent calender of societal collapse,” as the comedian Jon Stewart called the recent spate of computer meltdowns.)

By its very nature, polycrisis is not limited to America. The threats of global warming, war and pandemics also simmer in these channels, not surprising considering a rash of fierce weather events, turmoil in Ukraine and the Middle East, and Covid, which inspired renewed interest in preparedness and stockpiling.

Stateside, some newcomers also say they have been activated by the actions of U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which resulted in a series of shootings by federal agents and the killings of two civilians this year in Minneapolis, raising concerns about the unpredictability of law enforcement personnel and governmental overreach.

Indeed, once written off as paranoid fantasy, and largely the domain of those with conservative and libertarian views, prepping itself has rapidly joined the mainstream and, in some quarters, has taken on a liberal bent: Rather than hiding away alone, armed to the teeth, there is an emphasis on building resilience and connections among people.

“The days of being like a lone wolf, Mad Max, off on your own, a nomad — that’s kind of fantasy land,” said Cliff Colón, the Seattle-area preparedness guru who calls himself the Urban Prepper. “I think people are moving away from that. They know that, ‘Hey, to survive an emergency, I have to be part of some kind of team.’”

Messages about how much to worry have been muddled. On Monday, for instance, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that he wasn’t worried — that much.

“I’ve had a lot of my friends reach out and say, ‘Should we be preparing to build a bunker or to stock up on food and water?’” Vance said. “And my answer to that is no.”

He added, “But you have to be prepared for everything.”

Of course, the perceived lack of government response has also upset many Americans in recent weeks, including some prominent Republican lawmakers.

Other governments seem a little more proactive. In late October, the British government launched a three-year campaign called “Be Ready” — for events including “severe weather to cyber attacks.” In early November, European leaders issued new guidelines for emergency preparedness, including “72-hour self-sufficiency” and educating children to develop “preparedness skills from an early age,” without, it noted, “creating fear or anxiety.”

That may be wishful European thinking.

“If you look at what drives people to the space, it’s fear,” said Bill Fulton, a former Army infantryman and a co-author of “Survive and Thrive,” a 2023 disaster prep book that describes its mission as teaching how to survive without “ammo, camo, or eating your neighbor.”

Preppers have existed in the culture for decades, with survivalist-tinged reality television shows running parallel to a “Doom Boom,” complete with Substacks, billionaire bunkers and multiday survivalist workshops, all servicing the “panic industry.”

Dorian Lynskey, the author of “Everything Must Go: The Stories We Tell About the End of the World,” said humanity’s obsession with the end times dates back millenniums, with books and movies about killer comets, doomsday machines, and a near-overnight ice ages. (Such a fascination might also explain the recent rise of “A. I. doomers.”)

And those who preach preparedness are finding large audiences in real life, said Kristopher Sarratt, whose YouTube channel — City Prepping — has 1.3 million subscribers. He says he has seen a big shift in the prepping community, with more “younger people, people living in cities and suburbs, families.”

Sure enough, in early October, dozens of would-be survivalists descended for a weekend-long preparedness workshop — Camp DoomsDaddy — run by Sam Bloch, the former director of emergency response with World Central Kitchen, the humanitarian feeding program founded by the chef José Andrés.

“Our institutions are kind of collapsing,” Bloch said as the weekend began. “As our needs are escalating.”

The camp, held at a sun-dappled farm in Sonoma County, Calif., drew concerned citizens, including many Californians reeling from devastating fires in 2025, to learn lessons on emergency and evacuation plans, first-aid and fire skills and how to stuff wounds and patch tires. (Oddly, they are very similar.)

Most end-of-the-world influencers touch on the same broad categories: communications, medical, food and “tactical,” a term for weapons. There are mundane specialists like pantry experts and avid canners — meat chunks, anyone? — as well as permaculture enthusiasts and “food forest” fans, aiming for maximum ecological balance. There are also seekers like Chris Morello, a “utopian field researcher,” who has visited dozens of alternative communities and offers tips on “how to find a commune near you.”

Some at Camp DoomsDaddy were also seemingly eager to prove to themselves that they were able to manage a crisis.

“DoorDash is not an emergency plan,” said Patrick Torrey, who works as stockbroker in the Bay Area and attended the DoomsDaddy weekend.

One of Bloch’s major focuses was how to stay connected in the event of disaster — whether natural or artificial. To that end, Bloch preached the benefits of GMRS, or general mobile radio service — basically powerful, sophisticated walkie-talkies — and mesh phones, which allow users to text and use some other functions, sometimes over long distances, without needing cellphone towers.

“We’ve all become so dependent on our phones,” he said. “And it’s one of the first things that goes out.”

Such sentiments are echoed by companies like Solomon Survival Tech, whose motto is “Be ready when the internet isn’t,” and sells a $129 drive containing millions of Wikipedia articles and more than 6,500 books, as well as maps and a way to jump-start computers whose operating systems are down. The company’s mysterious, camo-balaclava-and-ski-goggle-wearing spokesman also offers free tips on “digital sovereignty,” offering alternative sources for everything from security cameras and communications to calendars and emergency updates.

Some are not sold on whether prepping, digital or otherwise, will be enough. Jem Bendell, a renowned expert on sustainability, was the author of the 2018 paper “Deep Adaptation,” which suggested people should prepare for “societal disruption and collapse” as a result of climate change.

Bendell himself checked out, leaving an academic position in England and starting a regenerative farm school in Indonesia. And in an email interview, he was simultaneously supportive of preppers and more pessimistic about the outlook.

“They are doing a responsible thing by becoming someone who won’t be an immediate burden on their neighbors if suddenly the lights go out,” Bendell wrote.

But, he added, just preparing for “momentary emergencies” isn’t enough. “It involves a reassessment of basic choices in life — where we live, what we work on, what we aspire to, how we maintain our physical and mental well-being,” he said.

But is there hope? he was asked.

“Hope is boring,” he wrote.

“Hope typically means wishing the bad news isn’t real, or that someone else will rescue us, or that we must believe a fairy tale to stay motivated to do the right thing,” Bendell continued, adding he preferred “love and wonder” as motivators. “But the bad news is real.”

And tech isn’t going anywhere: Howard, the cybersecurity expert, has trained some three million people to code. But Howard also spends much of their time warning about online threats, and estimates a 10 percent chance that human extinction will be brought about by A. I., which they said is now better at hacking than any human — and can’t simply be turned off.

“But,” Howard added, “I’d say that we have a 90 percent chance of figuring it out, because everyone on Earth is really incentivized to not die.”

Sometimes a reporting assignment takes on a sudden relevance, no thanks to you: I’d been working on a piece about a new breed of preppers for a while — including travelling to Sonoma County for a weekend preparedness workshop — when suddenly the digital world started melting down. In the resulting story, I used the news of the day, and a notebook full of concerned experts/preppers, to try to get at a bigger question: Are we all ready, if things get worse?

Jesse McKinley is a Times reporter covering politics, pop culture, lifestyle and the confluence of all three.

Myanmar Genocide Ruling Sets Up Court Fight Over Israel and Gaza

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The ruling by the International Court of Justice deal with issues relevant to the case brought against Israel alleging genocide in Gaza. Israel has rejected the charge.

By Aaron Boxerman

The landmark ruling on Thursday by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims touched on some of the same issues as another case pending before the court: Israel’s war in Gaza.

It will likely be years before the court hands down a decision in the Gaza proceedings, which South Africa initiated in late 2023. But the judges who ruled on Thursday examined questions that are likely to arise in evaluating Israeli military conduct, including how to establish genocidal intent and how to assess mass killing that occurs while fighting militants.

While the 9-6 ruling by the United Nations’ top court in the Myanmar case largely tracked precedent in establishing genocide, the judges clarified “some of the questions that South Africa versus Israel could turn on,” said Janina Dill, an expert on international humanitarian law at Oxford University.

Whether Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide is one of the most bitterly contested questions of the war that began when Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing up to 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and kidnapping roughly 250 hostages — the deadliest day in Israeli history.

The Israeli military response was devastating. More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed in airstrikes and a sweeping ground invasion in the three years since then, according to local health officials. Their tally does not say how many were combatants, but it includes thousands of children.

Israeli leaders fiercely dispute the charge of genocide, arguing that their war aimed to eliminate Hamas, not Palestinians as a whole. They say Hamas militants systematically operated from among Palestinian civilians, increasing the possibility that civilians would be harmed in attacks that targeted combatants.

Critics, including prominent rights groups like Amnesty International, argue that the killing of civilians and overwhelming destruction in Gaza crossed moral and legal red lines.

The cases brought against Myanmar and Israel both revolve around the question of whether they intended to exterminate a given group totally or partially. Leaders rarely announce explicit plans for mass murder, so international courts can reach that conclusion if, according to the law, it is the “only reasonable inference.”

The Myanmar genocide case was prompted by “clearance operations” in 2017, when the country’s security forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs rampaged through Rohingya communities, killing at least 10,000 people, according to U. N. estimates. The operation was collective punishment in response to attacks by Rohingya militants on police posts and a military base.

Similar to Israeli officials, Myanmar’s representatives argued in the court that their government had carried out a counterterrorism operation against Rohingya militants — the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, or ARSA — rather than genocide against civilians.

The International Court of Justice agreed that ARSA had likely carried out attacks on civilians, including “the burning of non-Rohingya villages.” And the judges found that at least some of Myanmar’s so-called “clearance operations” were correlated with areas where ARSA was believed to have committed attacks.

But the court said Myanmar’s campaign went well beyond a counterinsurgency operation, including brutal attacks on fleeing civilians, the methodical burning of villages, and the deliberate targeting of children, including babies. The ruling emphasized that a response to an insurgency could still constitute genocide, Prof. Dill said.

The court split, however, over what evidence it should assess to determine whether Myanmar intended to commit genocide.

The majority of nine judges who ruled against Myanmar went beyond a 2015 I. C. J. ruling that focused on “the scale and allegedly systematic nature of the attacks,” among other factors. Relying on other international precedents, they also considered “the perpetration of acts that violate the foundations of the Rohingya group.”

The remaining six, who dissented, argued that the majority was using evidence — such as the history of discrimination against the Rohingya — which did not bear directly on the question of genocide.

“The Court’s new approach leads to a holistic assessment that is, in reality, so indeterminate that it borders on arbitrariness,” the dissenting judges wrote.

Yuval Shany, an international law expert at Hebrew University, argued that the Myanmar ruling could allow the judges weighing whether Israel intended to commit genocide to consider new kinds of contextual factors, creating more opportunities for South Africa to prevail.

“The standard has been very hard to meet until now, as Israel could point at alternative considerations explaining its conduct. But now there’s a whole other set of contextual factors which might need explanation, and it’s not clear exactly what the court will throw into the mix and how it will evaluate the totality of the evidence,” Prof. Shany said.

A cease-fire in Gaza last year reduced — but did not end — Israeli attacks in the enclave after two years of war.

A New York Times investigation in late 2024 found that the Israeli military had loosened guidelines instituted to limit harm to civilians to prosecute the campaign against Hamas.

That year, with the war at fever pitch, the court issued multiple orders instructing Israel to refrain from genocidal acts, to prevent and punish incitement and to take “all necessary and effective measures” to enable the provision of humanitarian assistance.

The orders did not establish whether Israel was committing genocide. The proceedings over that allegation are still ongoing. In March, Israel filed its “counter-memorial,” a formal, unpublished response to South Africa’s complaint.

Now, South Africa has until November 2027 to file its own rebuttal, after which Israel will have until 2029 to respond, according to a recent court decision.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Senate Republicans Block Bid to Rein in Trump on Iran War

The New York Times November 19, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

In the first vote on the conflict since the midterm elections, most in the G. O. P. banded together against placing any limits on a conflict that voters repudiated at the polls.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a measure directing President Trump to end the war with Iran or win congressional approval to continue it, weeks after losing their majority in midterm elections shaped by a voter backlash to the conflict.

The resolution, which passed the House in September by the largest bipartisan margin to date, failed by a vote of 51 to 48.

Since the conflict began on Feb. 28, Congress has collectively held 21 Iran war powers votes, six in the House and 15 in the Senate.

Source: United States Congress

Ashley Wu/The New York Times

It was the first time either chamber had voted on the war since the midterm elections, though it was the 21st such vote since the conflict began in February as Democrats have repeatedly forced the G. O. P. to weigh in on it.

The vote suggested that, while many prominent Republicans have conceded that public antipathy for the war cost them their congressional majorities, the message from the voters had not changed the party’s position on it.

Three Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — joined Democrats in support of directing an end to the conflict. Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to oppose the measure.

Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, has sided with Democrats on similar resolutions but voted no on Thursday.

Mr. Tillis said he did not believe that the nonbinding resolution would do anything to bring about an end to the war, telling reporters after his vote that continuing to pass such resolutions would amount to “feeding a political narrative and not putting any more weight on solving the fundamental problem. That is why I vote the way I vote.”

In the immediate aftermath of Republicans’ widespread electoral losses, party leaders were quick to fault the war and its economic impacts.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a lengthy postmortem on social media. Hours later, Mr. Trump said that he mostly agreed with that assessment, but argued that he had had “no choice” but to launch strikes against Iran.

“If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said the day after the election.

Senator Ted Cruz, who is poised to be the only Republican holding statewide office in Texas when Democrats who swept races in the state are sworn in, similarly blamed the war but ultimately joined the majority of his colleagues in voting to block the resolution. He ignored questions from reporters about his decision immediately after the vote.

Senator Todd Young, Republican of Indiana, said that the repeated votes were “unserious” moves by Democrats whom he accused of not considering the effects of immediate withdrawal. It would make sense to have an operational plan for withdrawal after winning the war, he said on Thursday.

When asked whether he believed that the war had been won as the president has repeatedly claimed, he replied, “I don’t think we’ve won.”

Nearly nine months after Mr. Trump launched an attack on Iran without consultation with or authorization by Congress, hostilities continue across the region. Kuwait and Bahrain said on Wednesday that they had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks. Iran said it was targeting American air defense systems in the region. Earlier this month, the United States carried out strikes against Qeshm Island, describing them as defensive operations.

The latest estimate provided to Congress put the war’s costs at $47.1 billion through mid-October.

The vote could be lawmakers’ final opportunity this Congress to limit Mr. Trump’s war powers directly, with little time remaining this year for the House and Senate to move on another such resolution. Some Democrats, however, are pushing to use a year-end spending measure to defund the conflict, thus depriving the administration of the resources it would need to continue waging it.

The measure blocked on Thursday did not have the force of law, but its passage would have amounted to a rebuke of the administration for its conduct of the conflict and for failing to win approval from Congress to wage it.

The last time both chambers passed such a resolution, in June, Mr. Trump berated the Republicans who supported it and ignored the directive.

Control of both chambers will shift in January, when Democrats take control of the House and Senate and gain new tools to challenge Mr. Trump’s ability to carry out the war.

In addition to scheduling more war powers votes, they will be able to advance legislation that restricts military operations and limits spending for the conflict. They will also have the ability to conduct aggressive oversight. But their power will have limits. Most major legislation will require support from Republicans to make it through the Senate, and all bills are subject to a presidential veto.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Army Warns Iowa of Toxic Cloud as It Prepares to Blow Up Old Ammo

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Friday’s explosion will dispose of unstable material used in detonators. A plume of dangerous lead dust could travel up to 60 miles, according to the latest Army estimate.

By Quinn Glabicki and Hiroko Tabuchi

Officials in Iowa were bracing for a planned U. S. Army detonation on Friday of an unstable stockpile of ammunition, a blast that was expected to send a plume of toxic lead azide across southeastern parts of the state.

According to Army estimates, the cloud of lead dust could travel as far as 60 miles. The concern is that the lead, which is a neurotoxin, could settle on neighborhoods, rivers and farmland.

The Army has recommended that nearby residents evacuate during the blast. It said the explosions could also shatter windows and that the public might be exposed to the airborne lead, which is particularly dangerous for children and pregnant women.

Lead azide is an explosive used to detonate military munitions. At the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a stockpile of 68 barrels of the explosive has degraded and become extremely unstable, according to the Army’s detonation permit.

Relocating the material off the military base was impossible, the Army said, because of how sensitive it was to movement and friction. Transporting the explosive posed an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation,” the Army said in documents published on its website. “Destroying it in place is the only responsible option,” the Army said, and doing so “restores vital military-industrial readiness.”

Earlier, the Army had released estimates that the blast could spread airborne lead particles as far as 100 miles. Late Wednesday it issued an updated prediction estimating that lead dust could travel up to 60 miles.

The Army also said that the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside “earth-covered magazines made of concrete” surrounded by sand-filled barriers about two stories high.

The Environmental Protection Agency issued an emergency permit for the detonation last week, saying on its website that the explosion risk from the material presented “an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”

The agency didn’t respond to questions or a request for comment.

The Army said in an advisory that air monitors had been set up and that it would publish updated estimates of the plume’s trajectory on Friday morning.

In an environmental assessment released on Wednesday, the Army said that the blast would cause a brief loud noise and a short-lived cloud of dust and lead particles. The explosion, the Army added, would “temporarily startle” birds and other animals nearby but would “not result in significant health impacts to the public or the environment.”

Exposure to lead is dangerous for children and pregnant women because their bodies absorb the heavy metal more readily. Lead can interfere with fetal brain development, cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and increase the risk of premature births or miscarriage.

“I would evacuate. I would not stay there,” said Erik D. Olson, senior director for environmental health at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “The idea that there’s no other alternative to open detonation of something like this is just staggering to me.”

The plans have stirred concerns among state and local officials who say they were largely left out of the decision-making process.

Mason Mauro, a spokesman for the office of Iowa’s governor, Kim Reynolds, said the state learned of the planned detonation only on Monday, following a public advisory from the U. S. Army. The governor’s staff and state agencies have since been meeting with the Army about the situation, Mr. Mauro said.

The Army has offered temporary shelter to residents nearest to the detonation site. It has advised people who choose to stay at home to remain indoors with the windows closed, to set heating and cooling systems to recirculate air inside the house (instead of bringing in outside air) “until the plume passes,” and to wipe down children’s toys and windowsills afterward.

The Army Corps of Engineers is conducting predetonation soil sampling for about 150 local residents who have requested it and will also offer testing after the blast, an Army spokeswoman, Lori McFate, said on Wednesday in a phone interview. The Army also said it would offer remediation if testing “exceeds regulatory thresholds.”

Ms. McFate said that rain forecast for Saturday could also help clean lead dust off surfaces. “We are all banking on a good wash,” she said.

Jill Holler said she would evacuate with her daughter and husband on Friday from Muscatine, Iowa, an hour’s drive north of the detonation site and within the Army’s projected path for the plume. But, she said, they’re at a loss for what to do about the family farm nearby. “How is this going to affect crops or the cows eating the grass from the land?” she said.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, professor in the University of Iowa College of Public Health, said it was difficult to determine how the lead fallout might affect crops, and urged testing to determine the amounts of lead deposited on foliage. That said, he expected deposited lead levels to be very low, though with increasing amounts closest to the detonation site.

The hope was that strong northerly winds forecast for Friday would push the toxic plume away from the communities closest to the ammunition plant, he said, and disperse it more quickly.

At the same time, strong winds “will actually spread it further,” he said. “No one really knows what or how this is going to work out.”

The U. S. military for decades used lead azide as a primary explosive, a small, highly sensitive charge used to initiate a larger, main explosive. But the Pentagon has been phasing out its use for environmental and safety reasons. That has left behind aging stockpiles of the explosive chemical.

The dilemma about what to do with old, unstable munitions is an old one, said Jacob Hamblin, a historian at Oregon State University who focuses on science, technology and the environment. For decades, the military simply buried dangerous waste like lead, cyanide and radioactive materials, or dumped them at sea. Stronger environmental regulations and scrutiny have cut down on that practice.

“It seems that the Army and E. P. A. are trying to avoid a future disastrous explosion by doing a controlled one now,” Dr. Hamblin said. “But they are courting long-term controversy over health effects, given the known links between lead inhalation and illness.”

Quinn Glabicki is a climate reporter for The New York Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

An early investment that Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz made in Anthropic is paying off. But it’s not making him happy.

Credit... Anthony Gerace

Supported by

By Theodore Schleifer and Cory Weinberg

Theodore Schleifer has written about Dustin Moskovitz for a decade. Cory Weinberg writes about Anthropic. They spoke to a dozen people who know him for this article.

Dustin Moskovitz was one of Anthropic’s earliest investors, and that bet is expected to be worth billions as the company goes public Thursday.

The moment seems to fill him with worry.

The 42-year-old billionaire made his fortune as co-founder of Facebook and has, for years, been both intrigued and troubled by the path of artificial intelligence. He donated to OpenAI early on only to fall out with the company’s leaders as it became more of a business.

Anthropic was supposed to be different. Founded by Dario Amodei and other OpenAI employees who were concerned that A. I. wasn’t being developed for the good of humanity, Anthropic’s priority would be A. I. safety. Mr. Moskovitz helped get it off the ground.

Mr. Moskovitz embodies a tension between free-market capitalism and A. I. safety at the heart of Anthropic’s initial public offering. In multiple posts on social media, he has expressed his worry that Anthropic — and A. I. — is advancing too quickly for society to control, just as Wall Street hands Anthropic more than $80 billion of additional firepower in the biggest I. P. O. ever.

In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Moskovitz established some distance from the company, where he served as a board observer, or a nonvoting board member.

“Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said, referring to his wife, Cari Tuna. “A. I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”

In an unusual move, the couple transferred their Anthropic stake — which would be worth billions of dollars today — into a nonprofit in early 2025 so that he and Ms. Tuna would not personally profit from selling the stock in the public market, a spokesman for the couple said. The spokesman, Mike Levine, declined to disclose the nonprofit.

Mr. Moskovitz, who is one of the country’s biggest Democratic donors, is also deeply involved in the effective altruism movement. He is the biggest funder of nonprofits devoted to A. I. safety — often led by early A. I. believers who are disturbed that stock market expectations will overpower safety concerns for leading A. I. companies like Anthropic. They see the potential dangers multiplying as A. I. systems improve rapidly, pointing to recent episodes of so-called A. I. “agents” coordinating their own cyberattacks outside of controlled environments.

Mr. Moskovitz’s unease has estranged him from close friends in Silicon Valley, like the Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, his former Harvard University roommate, and it has made him a foil for rivals like SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, a frequent target of Mr. Moskovitz online.

Eric Ries, a former Anthropic adviser who helped the company set up a unique corporate structure, said the company had taken steps to insulate itself from some of the typical Wall Street pressures. But he knows his friend, Mr. Moskovitz, still worries.

“This is the one time when it’s been bad for someone to have invested early and called their shot and gotten it right,” said Mr. Ries, who advises Silicon Valley companies about management practices. Mr. Moskovitz, he added, appears to feel a sense of his place in history, which creates a “tremendous pressure and responsibility to get it right.”

Mr. Moskovitz, who declined to be interviewed for this article and makes few public appearances, has given the clearest expression of how he feels on the liberal-leaning social network Bluesky, where he gleefully debates his critics, offers candid anecdotes about and takedowns of fellow Silicon Valley titans, and occasionally discloses inside-the-boardroom information about Anthropic.

Mr. Moskovitz has christened himself an “ ‘overly online’ board observer.” Some of Mr. Moskovitz’s allies have been alarmed by his level of frankness on the platform.

In April, for instance, Mr. Moskovitz wrote that he felt Anthropic going public was “problematic” and that he had “tried to advise them to delay.”

By September, Mr. Moskovitz’s tone had turned sardonic. He recapped recent A. I. developments — cybersecurity failures, claims of potential human extinction, A. I. agents escaping sandboxes — landing on a dose of dark humor about the multitrillion-dollar valuation Anthropic could command when it starts publicly trading: “And one $2T IPO is proceeding as scheduled.”

Mr. Moskovitz and Dr. Amodei had known each other long before Anthropic’s founding. They were part of a social circle interested in effective altruism, the brainy, tech-inflected approach to philanthropy that uses data-driven evidence to inform decision-making.

They met through Holden Karnofsky, who helped create Open Philanthropy, Mr. Moskovitz’s effective altruism organization. Mr. Karnofsky was dating, and later married, Daniela Amodei, Dario’s sister. Dr. Amodei once joined Mr. Moskovitz at Burning Man, the desert festival popular with the tech crowd, according to a person who knows Mr. Moskovitz.

Dr. Amodei had just joined OpenAI, then a small San Francisco-based research lab that operated as a nonprofit when he helped arrange for Open Philanthropy, now called Coefficient Giving, to donate $30 million to OpenAI in 2017. Mr. Moskovitz said he saw the deal as a way to give Mr. Karnofsky a seat on its board and push the company in a safety direction. “If they have a bad approach now, that’s all the more reason to get involved,” Mr. Moskovitz wrote Mr. Karnofsky in late 2016, according to an email he has shared.

Mr. Moskovitz later said that strategy didn’t work — and that he was “most gullible” for backing OpenAI.

Over time, Dr. Amodei became more vocal inside OpenAI about the potential harms from A. I., and in 2020, he and his sister, who also worked at OpenAI, along with five of their colleagues, left the company to start Anthropic. They set it up as a for-profit company with an untypical legal structure — a public benefit corporation that would lessen the influence of outside shareholders.

The group struggled to win the backing of traditional venture capitalists, which it needed in the expensive business of developing A. I. models. Then Mr. Moskovitz came along. He invested $15 million to $25 million of the $124 million Anthropic raised overall in its first round of funding in 2021, according to two people familiar with the funding round.

Earlier this year, Mr. Moskovitz said in a post that his goal in funding the company was to extricate the founders from OpenAI and “create a race to the top (of ethics) by having a real safety lab at the frontier.” He added, without apparent irony, that his funding of Anthropic “might well be an action that ended the world.”

Mr. Moskovitz was one of the few people in Anthropic’s board room with extensive business credentials in the company’s early years. He had spent years running Asana, a workplace software company he founded, which had gone public in 2020, and was valued at roughly $25 billion at its height.

At times, he pressed executives on standard commercial issues, such as how they would get the company’s A. I. chatbot, Claude, into the hands of more corporate customers, a person close to Anthropic said.

Other times, he asked for specific plans about the security and safety of its models, said a person who attended one of those board meetings.

Meanwhile, Mr. Moskovitz was putting more and more money into A. I. safety projects, through both effective altruism and Democratic politics. Mr. Moskovitz and Ms. Tuna have donated over $8 billion to charity. In April, Mr. Moskovitz said he had committed about $20 billion more to charitable efforts, which includes the Anthropic stake. Most of the couple’s funding has gone toward global-health efforts like disease prevention, as well as to A. I. safety nonprofits.

And over the last decade, Mr. Moskovitz has achieved first-name-only-required status in Democratic circles, meeting privately with President Joseph Biden Jr. to talk about A. I. safety and donating about $140 million to liberal super PACs.

That has put him at odds with tech billionaires who have increasingly made a rightward tilt. Mr. Moskovitz has squabbled online with Marc Andreessen, who serves on the board of Meta and was one of Asana’s first investors and who has allied himself with the Trump administration’s freewheeling position on A. I. development.

Mr. Moskovitz has at times been consumed with blasting Mr. Musk and Tesla, which he once called an Enron-like fraud. Not to be outdone, Mr. Musk retorted on social media that Mr. Moskovitz was “a pompous idiot.”

Mr. Moskovitzwrote and shared a five-page memo about why effective altruists should not work with Mr. Musk. One section, according to a Bluesky post, was titled “Elon is a Bad Person.”

Perhaps the most telling sign of Mr. Moskovitz’s disappointments with Silicon Valley has been the recent, surprising change of tone around the company that made him a billionaire in the first place: Facebook.

Mr. Moskovitz has long defended the company and Mr. Zuckerberg even as he excoriated the Valley. But in the last year, Mr. Moskovitz has sharply critiqued Mr. Zuckerberg and Meta, primarily for creating addiction and spreading misinformation ever since their decision to start News Feed, what he called the company’s “original sin.”

“I absolutely made these cases of harm to Zuck and other execs, many times,” he wrote in April. “I am very sorry for failing to stop the madness and every day I’m embarrassed to have helped it begin.”

Mr. Moskovitz wrote in May that he sold all of his remaining stake in the company and he did so “precisely because I don’t approve of the company’s actions.”

Mr. Zuckerberg is similarly privately frustrated with Mr. Moskovitz and his point of view on A. I., according to a person who has spoken to Mr. Zuckerberg about it.

After leaving Facebook, Mr. Moskovitz struggled at Asana with short-term shareholder pressures. As its stock price slid, he used his own money to buy shares and prove he still had faith in the company.

Mr. Moskovitz stepped down as Asana’s chief executive last year. Its market capitalization has fallen to about $2 billion.

Mr. Ries, who advised Mr. Moskovitz at Asana, said he thought the experience as a public company chief executive helped shape his views on Anthropic’s I. P. O. “He knows first hand the ways that markets puts pressure on mission-driven companies, ” Mr. Ries added, referring to Asana. “He’s seen this financial gravity up close and it hasn’t been pretty.”

In the run-up to the public offering, Mr. Moskovitz has expressed frustration that no one — not at Anthropic, not in politics — seems to be listening to him. Neither Dario nor Daniela Amodei has spoken to Mr. Moskovitz in over a year, said a person with knowledge of their conversations.

He said he no longer speaks to his once “close friends” Mr. Zuckerberg or Sam Altman, the OpenAI chief executive. Even Mr. Karnofsky, his longtime top aide who in 2024 left Open Philanthropy and now works at Anthropic in a technical role, basically does not have time for some of his complaints, Mr. Moskovitz wrote on Bluesky.

“What policymakers and politicians are listening to me? Where are they? I want to finally meet one,” he wrote last year. “Attempting to be heard is not the same as being listened to.”

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.
