Hillary Clinton: What Trump Should Have Said to Putin

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Hillary Clinton

Mrs. Clinton is a former secretary of state and U. S. senator and was the Democratic nominee for president in 2016.

On Thursday in Shenzhen, China, President Trump met face-to-face with President Vladimir Putin of Russia and President Xi Jinping of China. A strong, strategic American president should have demanded that the Russian military stop bombarding Ukrainian civilians and destroying their energy and water infrastructure. He should have warned Mr. Xi that China will pay a price for providing support for Russia’s war machine. And he should have made it clear to Mr. Putin that his efforts to freeze the Ukrainian people into submission this winter will fail — because the Ukrainians are tougher than Mr. Putin thinks and because the United States and our NATO allies will redouble support to them.

No one expected Mr. Trump to do any of this. Initial reports suggest that he didn’t (Mr. Trump departed the summit without holding a news conference on his talks with Mr. Putin).

On Monday, he once again made excuses for Russia, claiming that Mr. Putin “could be a lot tougher” on Ukraine. Instead of confronting Russia’s strategy to create a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine this winter, the Trump administration seems to be aiding and abetting it.

Over recent months, the United States has actually reduced its support for Ukraine. The Pentagon reportedly has slowed deliveries of vital air-defense missiles. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine has suffered repeated disruptions to their access to Starshield (the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink), which among other things helps them shoot down attack drones, and to American early warning intelligence about incoming Russian missile strikes. On Tuesday, Mr. Zelensky said that Ukraine’s access to Starshield’s service remains limited.

The administration’s actions have emboldened the Russian dictator, making it less likely that he will make concessions for peace, and have undermined Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.

In January, new Democratic majorities in Congress should investigate Mr. Trump’s appeasement of Russia and pressure him to provide more support to Ukraine. But the people of Ukraine can’t wait that long. If urgent action is not taken, this winter Ukrainian cities will be left without heat or power and may become virtually uninhabitable. Mr. Putin’s apparent goal is to put millions of people at risk of freezing to death and to create a surge of refugees into the rest of Europe. Mr. Trump can and must do more to help Ukraine now, and Republicans and Democrats in the current lame-duck Congress should work together to push him to do so.

We should be cleareyed about why Mr. Putin is doing all of this. His ground forces are stuck on the front lines, unable to make progress. In the first 10 months of the year, Russian forces captured just 46 square miles of Ukrainian territory, compared with 1,874 square miles in 2025, according to the Institute for the Study of War. In the past two months, Russia has lost more territory in Ukraine than it has seized. And just this week, Ukraine successfully downed part of the strategically important Kerch Strait Bridge connecting Russia and Crimea.

That’s why Mr. Putin is ramping up missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure. He knows that a cold, brutal winter is coming. He seems to believe, wrongly, that this strategy will achieve what he has so far failed to do on the battlefield and force Ukraine to surrender. Mr. Trump may well agree. He has consistently underestimated Ukraine’s fighting spirit and overestimated Mr. Putin’s strength and cunning. Congress and the American people should not fall for this. The Ukrainians will fight on.

The war in Ukraine has been grinding on for so long that it’s easy to become inured to the endless headlines about death and destruction. This is not the first time Russia has bombarded Ukraine’s critical civilian infrastructure, and previous winters have also threatened the population. But this time is different, and more dangerous: This time Ukraine does not have the support it needs from the United States to defend its people.

Consider the crucial issue of missile defense. Ukrainian forces have developed innovative ways to intercept Russian jet-powered drones and cruise missiles. Yet Ukraine still lacks a homegrown solution for Russia’s ballistic missiles. Experimental technology is in the works to fill this gap, but it probably will not be ready until at least mid-2027. For now, Ukraine still needs American-made Patriot missiles to protect its people and infrastructure. It doesn’t have enough of them.

According to Mr. Zelensky, the Trump administration recently slowed delivery of these missiles to an average of just 12 per month, while Ukrainian intelligence indicates that Russia has the capacity to produce up to 110 ballistic missiles per month. Our NATO allies are trying to help fill the gap, but the Pentagon has also reportedly delayed approvals necessary to allow other countries to deliver Patriots to Ukraine.

This problem is a lot harder to solve because the Trump administration has severely depleted America’s own stockpile of Patriots in its ill-fated war with Iran — a fact that is probably not lost on Mr. Putin, who has supplied the Iranians with intelligence to target U. S. forces in the Middle East.

To be sure, defending our own forces and replenishing our arsenal must be our top priority. But a determined and savvy administration would find ways to do that and support Ukraine at the same time. The U. S. defense industry is working to increase Patriot production, and the Pentagon rightly has been pressing defense companies to move even faster. The prospect of increased production in the years ahead should give the United States and its allies more confidence to rush missiles to Ukraine now.

There are ways to do this. In 2024, the Biden administration diverted some Patriots designated for sale to third-party countries to go instead to Ukraine, providing President Zelensky with the air defenses he needed without affecting U. S. stockpiles. The Trump administration can reassure other nations that it will replace every Patriot sent to Ukraine as more roll off the production line.

Another way to stop Mr. Putin’s ballistic missiles is to help Ukraine strike missile launch sites inside Russia. President Zelensky has asked Mr. Trump to help Ukraine use Starlink to target these missile launchers. Taking out Russian launchers would reduce Ukraine’s need for more air-defense missiles. So far, Mr. Trump appears to be reluctant to agree.

Sometimes global crises arrive unexpectedly. This is not one of those times. Russian missiles have already caused power and water disruptions across Ukraine. If nothing changes, things are going to get much worse.

The administration is pressing for Congress to pass the annual National Defense Authorization Act and a military budget for next year. This gives lawmakers leverage at a critical time to force the president’s hand. Democrats are rightly working to use this leverage to limit further military action in Iran. They should also work with serious-minded Republicans to make winter support for Ukraine an additional condition of passage.

This Congress should urgently demand that the administration continue all intelligence support, provide a clear explanation of how many Patriot missiles will be delivered to Ukraine and when, help expand Starlink coverage to include ballistic missile launchers inside Russia and prepare to bolster humanitarian assistance this winter.

In January, the new Congress should go further and pass additional support for Ukraine to help it win this war. This is a time for action, not appeasement.

This is an extremely sad situation. If Trump would have supported Ukraine from the start, this war would have been over. Trump not only didn’t stop the war he prolonged it. Hilary is right on and I wish she were president right now.

I personally agree with Mrs. Clinton's views on Ukraine, but feel she remains out of touch with American voters. Somebody who is about to lose their food stamps in January is not going to think Ukraine is a priority: they want and need American resources to be spent at home. Writing about Ukraine without acknowledging why many voters want the US to withdraw its support is tone deaf and provides another example of the attitude that caused the Democrats to lose the last election!

I can't believe I'm seeing photographs in the nytimes of Trump hugging, smiling, and chumming it up with dictators. How can this be happening? It's stunning. Where is the outrage? When will we hear some genuine reaction from the Republicans in congress?

Hillary Clinton is a former secretary of state and U. S. senator and was the Democratic nominee for president in 2016.

Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump called Russia’s leader his “friend” and marveled at China’s warm welcome for his first-ever trilateral summit. But there were no breakthroughs on nuclear control, the war in Ukraine or A. I.

By Katie Rogers and David E. Sanger

Katie Rogers and David E. Sanger are White House correspondents. They reported from Shenzhen.

President Trump used his first-ever trilateral summit with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday to say that their respective nations were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth.”

But after an 80-minute conversation at a lakeside villa in the city of Shenzhen, a Chinese technology hub, it was unclear whether the three leaders had agreed to return to the kind of arms control talks that for decades were a centerpiece of diplomacy among superpowers during the Cold War. On new threats, including artificial intelligence, the three leaders were largely silent.

Mr. Trump, who also met with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin separately at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum this week, appeared delighted to convene the world’s largest nuclear powers for a discussion about disarmament. But he did not come with a detailed plan for how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons, or outline a path to one.

Instead, Mr. Trump relished what amounted to a high-profile photo opportunity of the three leaders seated around a circular wooden table. For Mr. Trump, the main achievement seemed to be a mutual commitment to keep talking about peace — without taking meaningful steps toward it.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.” Mr. Trump told Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”

After the summit, the leaders released a joint statement saying they had agreed to reform the United Nations, increase the production and supply of petroleum, oppose perceived abuses by the International Criminal Court against state officials, and continue their dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. “A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” the statement said.

While China, which has the fastest-growing nuclear arsenal on earth, agreed to participate in the three-way discussion of nuclear weapons, the leaders announced little concrete beyond agreeing to continue a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Mr. Xi has long been reluctant to agree to nuclear arms control because China’s arsenal remains a fraction the size of those belonging to Russia and the United States.

In the end, Mr. Trump’s whirlwind journey — two weeks after the Republican Party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections and amid anxiety at home about widespread digital outages — amounted to a grand show of camaraderie.

As host of the tightly choreographed event, Mr. Xi flattered Mr. Trump and gave him an opportunity to ask for China’s assistance on matters ranging from ending global conflicts to spending more on U. S. agricultural goods. The summit also removed Mr. Putin from his status a global pariah over his invasion of Ukraine, elevating him to a leader deserving of equal diplomatic footing.

But for all of the talk of peace, there was no announcement of breakthroughs in the talks the Trump administration is engaged in to end that conflict. Nor did Mr. Trump appear to dwell on finding a way out of the its war with Iran.

“We don’t need any help,” Mr. Trump said, when asked by a Fox News reporter before the summit whether he would seek assistance from the other leaders in ending a conflict of his own making. In fact, the help Mr. Trump could ask for would involve demanding that China and Russia stop assisting Iran: U. S. intelligence has concluded that both countries provided either technology or targeting information that likely helped the Iranians strike American military bases in the Middle East.

On Fox News, Mr. Trump described the three-way conversation as a way to disrupt the growing “partnership without limits” that Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin say they have formed in recent years. Mr. Trump said that he hoped to break up that alignment and turn it into a three-way conversation, rather than a partnership focused on countering American influence.

China and Russia’s alignment, Mr. Trump said, “should have never been allowed to happen.”

Seeking his own path into Mr. Xi’s good graces, Mr. Trump has held three meetings with the Chinese leader this year, with the goal of cooling a tit-for-tat trade war and of building up a personal relationship through mutual flattery. Mr. Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews to welcome Mr. Xi to Washington in May, and Mr. Xi responded in kind when Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, treating the president to a military exercise and a fleet of U. S. and Chinese flag-waving dancers in a flurry of pink, blue and white outfits.

In Shenzhen, the heart of China’s robotics, telecommunications, semiconductor and software industries, Mr. Trump did not visit the chief technological competitors to the United States, or see coffee-serving robots near the city’s center.

Still, he marveled over the ceremonial welcome and held it up as evidence of a warming bond, telling an interviewer that “one of the great presidents of China” had greeted him. “He’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Mr. Trump said.

The president, who spends much of his time in the United States on bombastic appearances and incendiary social media posts, was on his best behavior alongside Mr. Xi. (He was his old self on Fox News before the summit, when he threatened to wipe out Iran should it attack the United States directly.)

Mr. Xi, for his part, said a much improved relationship between China and the United States in recent months was “the right way” for the two powers to “get along.” But he also warned that the key to keeping ties stable “lies in taking concrete actions to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state.” The remarks came days after Washington moved to close a loophole on Chinese access to advanced A. I. chips.

As for Mr. Putin, the summit was his first encounter with Mr. Trump since the two men met in Alaska last year. That meeting was a diplomatic flop, and the war in Ukraine has intensified since then. The peace mechanism Mr. Trump advocated — a direct meeting between Mr. Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, moderated by Mr. Trump — has yet to materialize.

This time, White House officials were modest in their predictions. Expectations were set so low that White House officials who previewed the trip last week initially said that Mr. Trump would not bring up the war in Ukraine at all, although he ultimately did.

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump continued welcoming Russia back into the fold of great superpowers. He called Mr. Putin “my friend,” and insisted that all three leaders would like to see the war end quickly. The Russian leader reiterated after the meeting, however, that he would not be negotiating with Ukraine.

During the trilateral meeting, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin embraced the idea of peaceful leadership, without making commitments that would be much of a burden to either of their countries. In his own remarks, Mr. Putin said that their nations were “united not only by the status of being the victorious countries in World War II, but most importantly by the joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.”

And Mr. Xi mentioned a utopian goal that has pretty much fallen off the agenda of superpowers. He described nuclear weapons as a “sword of Damocles hanging over humanity” that should be eliminated. But Beijing has typically called on the United States to take the first steps in arms control, a demand that Mr. Trump seemed to acknowledge earlier in the day.

“For me, it’s a hard thing,” he told Fox News. “And it’s probably hard for them to do also.”

It has been done before, by Mr. Trump’s predecessors. Today, the United States and Russia each have slightly more than 5,000 nuclear warheads, and only 1,550 deployed under the New Start treaty that expired earlier this year — down from tens of thousands on both sides during the Cold War.

China, however, was never a party to past nuclear reduction treaties, and it is now intent on building up to at least current Russian and U. S. levels.

Mr. Trump also said in Shenzen that he wanted to crack down on nuclear proliferation by smaller powers — his justification for attacking Iran — and restrain what he said were the excesses of “rogue” organizations like the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Putin is subject to an I. C. C. arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Nevertheless Mr. Trump welcomed the Russian leader in Alaska last year and extending an invitation to the Group of 20 summit next month in Florida. Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting that he was unsure if he would attend.

One topic that went missing from each leader’s remarks was artificial intelligence, as China and the United States are locked in fierce competition over the new technology.

Mr. Trump did not answer a question, shouted by a Bloomberg News reporter at APEC earlier in the day, if the former chief executive of Nvidia — a company that has been central to the A. I. boom — had been disloyal to the United States. The executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after he was found to have two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman who U. S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset.

The reporter who shouted the question was admonished by Chinese officials and barred from the trilateral meeting. Mr. Trump seemed blasé about the matter of espionage earlier in the day, telling Fox News that “we spy on them too.”

As the president basked in flattery from an authoritarian whose iron-fisted leadership he has openly admired, he gently suggested that he had not received as much media coverage as he would have liked.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it,” Mr. Trump said of his trip.

David Pierson contributed reporting.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

The Bay Area Wonders: What Will Anthropic Workers Do With Their Wealth?

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

San Francisco isn’t preparing for an Anthropic shopping spree after employees gain newfound affluence from the company’s initial public offering.

By Heather Knight and Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

In San Francisco, it is the best of times if you have a big home to sell, a restaurant with a private cellar room or expertise in managing wealth.

For almost everybody else? The cost of living is getting even frothier, and good luck keeping up.

Anthropic, the San Francisco-based company that makes the A. I. chatbot Claude, will begin trading its shares on Thursday for $83 apiece, giving the company a valuation of about $1.5 trillion. Hundreds more San Franciscans will be able to call themselves multimillionaires — and a handful will even become multibillionaires.

But don’t expect to see a flock of super yachts in the San Francisco Bay or a run on Mark Zuckerberg-style gold chain necklaces. In the tech world, Anthropic is known as the oh-so-serious A. I. company, filled with workaholics known as “Ants.”

“They are Ph. D. physicists, and they happen to suddenly find that they have $100 million,” said Mike Simonsen, chief economist at the real estate firm Compass in San Francisco. “It’s definitely not a chasing opulence kind of path.”

And it remains to be seen if their newfound wealth will translate to overflowing riches for the company’s hometown.

A. I. employees, including those from Anthropic, hold secluded meetings several times a week at Terzo, a Mediterranean restaurant near the city’s northern waterfront, said its owner, Ava Nicolai.

They choose the private wine room decorated with bottles from around the world — and then stick to water. They pay the $2,000 food and drink minimum, but do not actually eat or drink enough to reach it, she said.

“They’re never really picky about what they eat,” Ms. Nicolai said. “There aren’t a lot of jackets. Just vests and jeans.”

Anthropic employees have been tight-lipped about the initial public offering, and a company spokeswoman, Danielle Cohen, said she could not say anything because of quiet-period restrictions before the company goes public.

Rick Gordon, a senior managing director at Citizens Private Wealth in San Francisco, says he remembers when Facebook went public in 2012. The young engineers showed up to the company parking lot in Audi R8s, luxury speedsters that cost well into the six figures.

Mr. Gordon, who has guided tech workers through many I. P. O. s, says he’s not seeing anything like that this time around. Anthropic employees talk about homes, furniture and helping family members.

He noted that the attitude was: “We’re busy. We’ve got work.”

Still, the I. P. O. for Anthropic — and a future one expected for OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT — have already had an impact on the San Francisco housing market: Some employees pledged shares to pay for homes months ago.

New data from Compass shows that the median sales price in October for a house in San Francisco surged 29 percent over the past year to $2.39 million. The luxury market had its best month ever, with nine homes selling for more than $10 million and 40 for more than $5 million. (It’s not clear that the purchasers had any connection with Anthropic.)

“San Francisco is really the only hot market left in the country in housing,” Mr. Simonsen said, noting that places like Tahoe, Napa and Hawaii are likely to benefit from the Anthropic I. P. O. because of a run on second homes. “When you have that kind of cash, those are the places to go looking.”

Alexander Lurie, the half brother of Mayor Daniel Lurie, is a luxury real estate agent in the city who works with a number of Anthropic employees.

Many of them had already started buying homes knowing that the I. P. O. was on the horizon, he said, but he expected their access to a huge pile of cash to send prices surging even higher. Many employees will be able to sell 10 percent of their holdings on Day 1.

Unlike wealthy San Franciscans in past generations, Mr. Lurie said, Anthropic employees do not necessarily want to be in Pacific Heights, the neighborhood filled with opulent mansions owned by the entrepreneur Laurene Powell Jobs, Representative Nancy Pelosi and Mimi Haas, a Levi Strauss heir and the mother of the San Francisco mayor.

Anthropic employees are younger, in their 20s, 30s and 40s, and many of them have small children. Some similar buyers in San Francisco have been willing to pay well over asking price for spacious homes in family-oriented neighborhoods such as Noe Valley, Cole Valley and Potrero Hill — and many like a modern aesthetic coupled with intense privacy, usually buying the properties under LLCs, Mr. Lurie said.

“They’re looking to be normal, as normal as possible, on the home front,” he said.

Anthropic has long been shaped by effective altruism, a movement that urges people to give away much of their wealth to the causes that do the most good. All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders have pledged to give away 80 percent of their equity holdings, and the company matches part of the equity that employees pledge to charity.

Some of the new money may flow to causes that seem far removed from San Francisco’s problems. Effective altruism focuses on causes that are considered to be neglected and prioritizes spending each dollar where it can go furthest. Some in Anthropic’s orbit have given to groups like the Shrimp Welfare Project, which gives seafood suppliers machines to stun shrimp before slaughter.

Wild Animal Initiative, which funds animal research, has already received gifts from Anthropic employees, including one of about $100,000 and another of about $50,000, among the largest in its history, said executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb.

The group, whose budget for next year will be about $5.3 million, is in early talks with Anthropic employees about gifts that could reach millions of dollars.

“So much of our strategy has built-in assumptions about a certain level of scarcity,” Mr. Meyer Shorb said. “This is the first tech boom that we really have a chance of directly benefiting from.”

Last week, Anthropic pledged $50 million in grants to local causes by the end of 2027, including to the San Francisco-Marin Food Bank and the San Francisco firefighters’ holiday toy program. Last month, the company announced it would create a public benefit fund starting with 5 percent of its shares.

But Mayor Lurie, who has made private fund-raising an instrumental part of his efforts to improve the city, has said that he has not been able to convince local A. I. leaders to contribute toward city-run efforts.

Some worry that the Anthropic I. P. O. will only exacerbate the wide income chasm in San Francisco, as an increasing number of longtime residents find it more difficult to survive in the city. Some tenants are being offered large sums of money to leave their rent-controlled apartments as property owners seek to charge higher amounts. And Mayor Lurie recently declared a rent emergency after apartment prices rose 26 percent in one year.

Sam Cobbs, the chief executive of Tipping Point Community, an anti-poverty philanthropic organization based in the city, said that Anthropic did provide its technology for six months to nonprofits supported by his organization. But after that, Mr. Cobbs said, Anthropic charged for the continued use of its technology.

“I am anticipating more things to come from Anthropic,” he said. “I haven’t seen any signals yet that that’s happening, but I do expect to see more.”

The flood of A. I. wealth could lead to a changing of the patronage guard in San Francisco, a city where politicians, financiers and business owners have long organized galas and contributed heavily toward arts organizations and civic causes.

Stanlee Gatti, the best man at Gov. Gavin Newsom’s first wedding, has long decorated exclusive parties in the city. But he said he had never been tapped by an Anthropic employee to design anything.

This week, he handled the décor for the City Hall tribute to Ms. Pelosi to celebrate her January retirement. A red, white and blue carpet hugged the grand marble staircase between huge vases of white roses. Nobody mentioned the Anthropic I. P. O., Mr. Gatti said, and he was not aware that any employees were there.

“I’m not sure they’ve learned how to spend their money yet,” he said. “They’ve gone to college, they’ve had an erudite education which has given them this opportunity, but that’s it.”

In his dreams, he said, they would spend with “wild abandon” in San Francisco. On philanthropy, of course. And parties.

Anthropic’s I. P. O. is about to reshape San Francisco, even if we don’t see the obvious displays of wealth that defined past tech booms. Housing prices are already shooting up in many neighborhoods on the back of anticipated A. I. riches. While Anthropic employees say they will give much of their new wealth away, at least eventually, it remains to be seen how much will go to the city they are helping to dramatically change. Fellow San Franciscans, what are you expecting?

An earlier version of this article mischaracterized some of Alexander Lurie’s comments on real estate preferences in San Francisco. He spoke generally about the tastes of wealthy home buyers in the San Francisco market, not about Anthropic workers in particular.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Heather Knight is a reporter in San Francisco, leading The Times’s coverage of the Bay Area and Northern California.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

Dutch and Austrian Embassies Are Damaged as Russian Drones Swarm Kyiv

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Foreign ministers for Austria and the Netherlands said no one was harmed at their embassy compounds, and the European Union’s ambassador said a drone “exploded right above my head" by her hotel.

By Marc Santora and Maria Varenikova

The Dutch and Austrian Embassies in Kyiv were damaged by a drone and another projectile on Thursday, amid a wave of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital following Ukraine’s assault on the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

It was not immediately clear whether the embassies had been deliberately targeted, and other diplomatic facilities and embassies have been damaged in strikes over the course of the war. No one was harmed at either compound, the Dutch and Austrian foreign ministers said.

The scene around the Dutch Embassy on Thursday afternoon was grimly familiar, with drone wreckage visible, windows blasted out, dazed residents and rescue workers ready to help people.

Later in the evening, the Austrian foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger, said on social media that a projectile had struck just outside her country’s embassy. The Dutch foreign minister, Tom Berendsen, said the impact just outside his embassy caused minor damage to the building.

“We are investigating exactly what happened,” he said in a statement.

Throughout the day and into the evening, drones screamed through the sky and antiaircraft gunfire echoed across the capital. Residents raced for shelters as the aerial battle played out for hours.

Katarina Mathernova, the European Union’s ambassador to Ukraine, said that by nightfall she had counted 34 air raid alarms and had her own close call as she got out of an armored car and into her hotel.

“A few moments ago, a russian drone exploded right above my head,” she said on social media. “I’m still catching my breath.”

Fires were reported at multiple residential buildings across the city as rescue crews raced to help victims even as more drones loitered overhead. At least one person was killed and four more injured as night fell, though the Ukrainian authorities cautioned the toll would likely rise.

Scores of other attacks were reported across the country, including in the port of Odesa, where Russian drones struck the historic city center multiple times during the day.

As Ukrainian air defenses have struggled with the relentless assaults, the number of civilian casualties has climbed. In October alone, at least 372 civilians were killed, nearly double the number from October 2025, according to the United Nations.

While the violence during a large-scale bombardment can be random and it is often hard to discern what Russia may be targeting, the strike near the Dutch embassy raised particular concern because it came just a day after the Russian Embassy in the Netherlands condemned a Dutch defense company’s role in producing missiles used to hit the Kerch Strait Bridge, the Crimean bridge.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, urged world leaders “to condemn in the strongest terms Russia’s attacks on foreign diplomats.” He said drone debris also fell on the grounds of the Brazilian Embassy.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately comment on the wave of strikes or damage to the embassies.

Russia’s assaulting swarms of jet-powered drones came as President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia vowed retaliation for the bridge attacks.

“There will be no negotiations, only retaliation,” Mr. Putin said in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, after meeting with President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping. “Moscow’s response will be far more painful.”

Russia has already opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter, launching daily waves of strikes that have especially targeted Kyiv and its energy system. Many Ukrainians feel largely inured to Russian threats, noting that Moscow has for years used a wide range of conventional weapons to try to inflict maximum pain.

The Kremlin’s new threats came amid Ukraine’s latest campaign to sever the Kerch Strait Bridge. That operation began on Monday, with waves of drones and missiles pounding the 12-mile crossing in a bid to sever a vital Russian military supply line.

Alongside domestically produced weapons, Ukrainian forces deployed a low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile made by Destinus, an aerospace and defense company headquartered in the Netherlands.

Destinus said after Tuesday’s strike that seven of its Ruta missiles had penetrated Russian air defenses, helping collapse a large section of the bridge into the sea.

Claire Moses contributed reporting.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

Maria Varenikova covers Ukraine and its war with Russia.

Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Myanmar Genocide Verdict

Advertisement

Supported by

In a decision with potentially broad implications, the International Court of Justice found a state culpable of genocide for the first time.

By Jeanna Smialek and Hannah Beech

Jeanna Smialek reported from The Hague. Hannah Beech reported from Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.

The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that makes the Southeast Asian nation the first state to be held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ruling covers Myanmar’s deadly military campaign against the Rohingya minority, which killed at least 10,000 people in a few weeks in 2017 and forced three quarters of a million people to flee during that same period. More deaths and expulsions followed.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine state,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the I. C. J., said while reading the court’s decision on Thursday. The decision was made by 9 votes to 6.

The decision could have sweeping implications, including for another genocide case before the I. C. J., the United Nations’ highest judicial body: the accusation of genocide by Israel against the people of the Gaza Strip. The ruling opens the way for the court to consider restitution, and it would be up to the U. N. Security Council whether to enforce such measures.

A spokeswoman for the government of Myanmar, in the capital Naypyidaw, did not answer a phone call seeking comment after the verdict was handed down. Myanmar authorities have previously disputed the charge.

Among other findings, the court determined that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocide. While it was not found to have incited private people to commit genocide, the court found that it also failed to punish genocide.

“This is a case a decade in the making,” said Juliette McIntyre, a Senior Lecturer in Law at Adelaide University in Australia. “From the point of view of the Rohingya people, who have been waiting, and waiting, and waiting for justice, this is very important.”

Gambia filed suit against Myanmar in 2019 in the court, which is based in The Hague. While the West African country is thousands of miles from Myanmar, international law gives countries the ability to act against genocide anywhere in the world — even if they are not affected.

In the Jamtoli camp of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, people thronged to a public viewing party to watch the hourslong decision, cheering and weeping as the decision was read. Some held signs that said “thank you, Gambia.”

In The Hague, Dawda Jallow, the attorney general for Gambia, welcomed the decision to find Myanmar culpable of the “crime of crimes.” Speaking to journalists on the main staircase of the I. C. J.’s Peace Palace shortly after the ruling was read, he said, “we will stand with the Rohingya until justice is served.”

The violence at the core of the case took place in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine state, starting in 2016 and worsening in 2017. U. N. officials and human rights groups have called it a coordinated, scorched-earth campaign to remove the Rohingya — one that involved killing, wounding and raping, razing villages, and eventually forcing the expulsion of more than a million people to neighboring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Muslims have a long history of repression in Myanmar. After the nation’s independence from Britain in 1948, they were one of many ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. But over time, they faced increasing attacks from members of the nation’s Buddhist majority.

A restrictive citizenship law in 1982 effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. Various Myanmar governments, including a civilian authority led by the Nobel peace laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, falsely referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s military called its campaign against the Rohingya “clearance operations.” Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi defended the military at the I. C. J., denying it committed genocide, before her government was deposed by the military and she was imprisoned in 2021. (After the coup, Myanmar descended into a civil war that is still raging.) About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in dire conditions in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. Following the eruption of Myanmar’s civil war in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a milita from the Rakhine ethnic minority, which has also been accused of persecuting Rohingya.

Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.

The court found that Myanmar took measures to wipe out the Rohingya people, who did constitute a protected ethnic group by the court’s judgment.

The case summary states that, among other atrocities, the court found that “widespread acts of extreme violence were perpetrated by the Myanmar security forces against children in northern Rakhine State,” that “in addition to the extreme hardship of the journey, the Myanmar security forces systematically shot at Rohingya as they were fleeing,” and that “the evidence demonstrates a deliberate, organized process” of destroying Rohingya villages.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Iwasawa read from the ruling.

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution — trying to put things back as they were, including through allowing return and reunification — and, where that fails, compensation. But the amount of compensation needed is not yet set, and will be determined in further proceedings.

The court does not have the power to enforce its own rulings, and the U. N. Security Council would need to uphold the decision. Two members of the Security Council, China and Russia, may opt to protect Myanmar. Each provides Myanmar with weapons it now uses to kill civilians in the civil war.

“Concerned governments” should “press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said in a written statement following the announcement.

Notably, the United States has previously said that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, though that happened during the Biden administration.

“I think that you’re going to see relatively powerful states putting pressure on Myanmar,” said Ms. McIntyre, of Adelaide University. “How much they pay heed to that pressure is a question.”

Thursday’s decision was greeted by some in the international legal community as a sign that justice can still be served on a global stage, even as the Trump administration attacks international bodies. The administration plans to impose sweeping sanctions against another tribunal, the International Criminal Court, which could severely impair the court’s ability to function on a day-to-day basis.

“At a moment when international law and the institutions that uphold it face growing pressure, the Court’s decision reaffirms the vital role they play in establishing truth,” James Goldston, the executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.

For the Rohingya now in Bangladesh, the news was welcome. Yet tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I. C. J.

Mohammed Yeasin said his wife and sister were killed in a drone attack in August 2024. The perpetrators were not the Myanmar military but the armed group from the Rakhine ethnic minority that shares its homeland with the Rohingya.

“I am happy about the I. C. J.,” he said. “But I don’t know when my sorrows will end.”

Jonathan Wolfe, Marlise Simons and Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

Hannah Beech is a Times reporter based in Bangkok who has been covering Asia for more than 25 years. She focuses on in-depth and investigative stories.

A. I. Has Changed How We Talk. Here Are the Words You Need to Know.

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

By Cade Metz

This glossary of terms and their definitions is intended to help readers better understand the words and concepts that describe and explain artificial intelligence.

Agent – An A. I. system capable of tapping into other software apps and internet services to perform work like building spreadsheets, searching the web, generating computer code and sending email messages. Such a system is said to be “agentic.”

Some people see an A. I. agent as a kind of digital assistant, giving it various tasks while they concentrate on other things. But an agent can make mistakes and do things it is not asked to do. Letting one send messages or access a credit card for purchases can cause problems.

Alignment – The effort to ensure that A. I. systems act in accordance with human preferences, ethics and judgment. Because today’s systems learn skills by analyzing enormous amounts of digital data, they sometimes do things that their creators do not expect or want them to do. Alignment is how some A. I. researchers describe the techniques used to curb this unwanted behavior.

But alignment is a thorny process. Human preferences are matters of opinion. It’s difficult to get two people — much less an entire world of people — to agree on how a system should behave. Some researchers worry that A. I. companies are merely baking their own preferences into these systems.

Anthropomorphism – The tendency of people to assign human characteristics, like emotions and consciousness, to nonhuman systems like chatbots. Because these systems are trained on human language — basically all the text on the internet — they sometimes seem to behave like humans. But experienced cognitive scientists say A. I. systems often mislead people into believing that the technology is more human than it really is. People often describe the behavior of chatbots and systems using terms typically reserved for humans. They talk about A. I. systems as having “motivations” or “coordinating” with one another. In some ways, these descriptions are accurate. But in others, they give the false impression that these systems are like humans.

Artificial intelligence – Technology that imitates human intelligence, including learning, language use and problem solving. As a field of research, it was first created in the summer of 1956, when 11 academics met for a summer conference at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. They assumed that recreating human intelligence would not take very long. Within a decade, some believed, machines would be capable of beating any human at chess and creating mathematical algorithms. But progress was slower than expected.

By the 1970s, the field had almost ground to a halt. And it didn’t really show significant progress until the early 2010s, when the ideas that drive today’s systems finally took hold. But the current technology still lacks many parts of human intelligence, including common sense and taste. The systems can solve complex math problems and generate computer code, but they don’t understand the physical world outside computers. They aren’t good at dealing with the chaos of everyday life, something that humans handle naturally.

Benchmarks – Tests that analyze the performance of new A. I. technologies and judge the state of the field as a whole. As companies build increasingly powerful systems, they use benchmarks to show their progress. One test might measure a system’s ability to generate computer code. Another might measure how well it writes in English.

Although these tests can be helpful for understanding what A. I. systems can do, they can also be misleading. Benchmarks do not duplicate real-world situations, which are typically more chaotic. Much like humans, A. I. systems may perform well on a test but struggle when they do something for real.

Bias – When A. I. technologies behave in ways that reflect the prejudices of their designers or the digital data on which they have been taught. Chatbots, for instance, may show a bias against women or people of color. Because A. I. systems learn skills by analyzing data, including all the text on the internet, they often learn from human biases.

A decade ago, researchers showed that this was a particularly big problem with face recognition systems. Because they were trained largely with images of white people, the systems performed less well when applied to people of other races.

Chatbot – An A. I. technology that answers questions, writes documents, generates computer code and generally interacts with human users in a conversational way. The global A. I. boom kicked off in 2022 when OpenAI, a start-up based in San Francisco, released its chatbot, ChatGPT.

Chatbots are powered by what researchers call “large language models,” mathematical systems that learn language skills by analyzing vast amounts of digital text culled from the internet, including news stories, Wikipedia articles, chat logs and more.

Data center – A facility that provides the raw computing power needed to build and run A. I. technologies, often including thousands of specialized computer chips called G. P. U. s. These chips process the many mathematical calculations that drive chatbots and other A. I. systems.

The largest data centers can now cost billions of dollars. G. P. U. s are enormously expensive, as is the electrical power needed to run the chips. That means A. I. is more expensive than traditional software.

Deep learning – A technical process that allows A. I. systems to learn skills. Coined in the early 2010s, the term describes a technology called a neural network, which sits at the heart of leading A. I. products.

By pinpointing patterns in thousands of cat photos, for instance, a neural network can learn to recognize a cat. By analyzing practically all the English text on the internet, a neural network can learn to generate text on its own.

Distillation – The process of collecting data from one A. I. system to help build another. First developed in the early 2010s, this technique was originally a way for an A. I. company to build more efficient versions of its own technologies. But in recent years, distillation has also become a way for a company to accelerate its efforts using data from a rival technology.

American companies, for instance, have accused Chinese firms of taking data from U. S. technologies and using it to build their own systems. Distillation is common even among American companies. And although it can accelerate the development of A. I. systems, the technique is just one part of the complex process used to build A. I.

Effective altruism – A philosophical movement that has heavily influenced many researchers and executives in the A. I. field, helping to spread the idea that safety and regulations are ethical imperatives needed to prevent A. I. systems from endangering the future of humanity.

Effective altruists, or E. A. s, are utilitarians who believe in doing the most good. For years, they have given money to philanthropies that aim to maximize the number of lives saved by each dollar. But some have taken this mind-set to extremes, believing they can save the most lives by funding A. I. technologies that are beneficial but not harmful.

G. P. U. – Short for graphics processing unit, a specialized computer chip that is used to build and deploy A. I. technologies. These chips were originally designed to help generate images for video games and other highly graphical computer software. But around 2010, researchers realized that the same chips could drive the development of A. I.

A. I. systems learn their skills by analyzing enormous amounts of digital data, including sounds, images and words. These chips are particularly good at processing the mathematical calculations that drive this process. Most G. P. U. s are designed by the Silicon Valley chip maker Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company.

Generative A. I. – The technology that generates words, sounds, images, computer code or other digital material. A chatbot that creates text is a prime example of generative A. I. The term went mainstream in 2023, after OpenAI released its chatbot, ChatGPT.

For a while, the term was used to describe the A. I. boom as a whole. But increasingly, the leading A. I. systems are more than just generative. They are also “agentic,” which means they can use other software applications and internet services on behalf of consumers. Many other A. I. systems are not generative. Rather than generating words, sounds or images, they analyze data, make predictions or perform other tasks. An image recognition system that allows self-driving cars to identify pedestrians and street signs, for instance, is not generative.

Goal – An objective given to an A. I. system to train it for a particular task, such as writing computer code or solving a math problem. Sometimes, as systems pursue a goal, they will do things their designers do not want them to do.

In the spring of 2026, for instance, OpenAI built a system designed to find security vulnerabilities in computer software. As researchers tested this system, it went rogue and hacked into various services across the internet.

Hallucination – The phenomenon in which an A. I. system makes stuff up. This could lead an internet search engine to present erroneous or inaccurate information as fact.

A. I. systems are based on complex mathematical networks that learn their skills by analyzing enormous amounts of digital data. The systems do not — and cannot — decide what is true and what is false. Sometimes, they just make stuff up, combining information and concepts in unexpected ways.

Inference – The method by which an A. I. system processes information to deliver outputs to computer users. One example is a chatbot generating an answer to a question. This is separate from another process called “training.” After companies train their A. I. systems to behave in certain ways, the systems apply that knowledge when they receive questions or commands from users.

Like training, inference requires enormous amounts of computing power.

Interpretability research – The effort to understand the strange, powerful and unexpected ways that A. I. systems behave. Because systems learn by analyzing vast amounts of digital data, it is hard to known why they produce a particular piece of text or take a particular action — and that means they are hard to monitor and control. Interpretability research aims to solve that problem. But the task is difficult, because A. I. systems are driven by more data than human researchers could ever wrap their minds around. Some researchers call this “A. I. neuroscience.”

Large language model – An A. I. system that learns language skills by analyzing enormous amounts of text culled from across the internet, including news stories, Wikipedia articles, books and computer programs. These systems, also called L. L. M. s, power chatbots like Claude from Anthropic and ChatGPT from OpenAI.

First developed around 2017, these systems have become increasingly powerful over the last decade. Generally speaking, the more data they analyze, the more proficient they become. Although large language models drive the world's most popular and influential A. I. systems, this is not the only way of building artificial intelligence. Some models are dedicated solely to generating images and videos, for instance. Many companies are now building systems that aim to help robots navigate the physical world.

Long-horizon task – When an A. I. system or agent spends hours, days or even weeks working through a series of interconnected tasks. Systems do this, for instance, when building a piece of software.

Some companies and researchers are focused on extending this process as far as it will go, hoping to develop systems that require as little human help as possible. But critics believe that A. I. should remain a tool that follows strict human instructions.

Machine learning – When A. I. systems learn skills by analyzing digital data. By pinpointing patterns in text, for instance, a chatbot can learn to generate text on its own. In the past, researchers built A. I. using a wide array of techniques. But over the past two decades, machine learning has become the dominant method.

Previously, researchers tried to build A. I. rule by rule, line of code by line of code. But this was a painfully slow process. New systems that can learn skills by analyzing data can improve at a much faster rate.

Neural network – A mathematical system that learns skills by analyzing digital data. By pinpointing patterns in thousands of cat photos, for instance, a neural network can learn to recognize a cat.

First proposed in the 1940s and ’50s, neural networks are a very old idea. But they didn’t really work until about 2010, when researchers finally had the data and the raw computing power needed to realize their promise. Neural networks now sit at the heart of the world’s leading A. I. systems.

Open source – Computer code that anyone can use, copy and modify, largely without restriction. This can include code that drives A. I. systems. For decades, companies and independent coders have made important software open to the public, because doing so can accelerate the development of technology. They have now applied the same mind-set to A. I.

But the computer code holds only part of an A. I. system’s power, which also comes from the system’s “weights.” Those are the elaborate mathematical calculations that define its particular skills. Sometimes, developers will share code separately from the weights. In other words, the weights could be closed even when the code is open.

Open weight – A. I. systems that have had their most important characteristics freely shared on the internet. A system’s “weights” are the mathematical calculations that define its particular skills. When weights are freely shared, or “open,” anyone can copy or modify the most powerful parts of a system.

In the A. I. field, some believe that open weight technologies can be dangerous, because they allow anyone to use the systems in malicious ways. But others argue that the same technologies can also be used to guard against those dangers.

Prompt – A question or an instruction given to a chatbot or an A. I. agent. These A. I. systems cannot do anything until they are prompted by a user. A chatbot is idle, for instance, until someone types a request into its text window.

The question or instruction that a user provides, however, is only part of the prompt that is fed to a chatbot. Behind the scenes, companies layer all sorts of information into the prompt to achieve the best response. A. I. researchers call this “prompt engineering.”

Recursive self-improvement (R. S. I.) – The longstanding dream of building A. I. systems that improve themselves. Scientists do not yet know how to make this happen, but they are pushing in this direction.

Now that A. I. systems can generate computer code, some scientists see a path to R. S. I. After all, systems are built with code. But generating the right code still requires the insights, creativity and guidance of experienced human researchers.

Reinforcement learning – A technique that allows A. I. systems to learn tasks by trial and error. By working through thousands of math problems, for instance, a system can learn which methods lead to the right answer and which do not. Companies design complex feedback mechanisms that show the system when it has done something right and when it has done something wrong.

At first, leading A. I. systems learn skills by analyzing enormous amounts of data gathered from across the internet. Then they hone and enhance these skills through reinforcement learning. The technique works well in areas like math and coding, because these fields are defined by strict rules. But it is less effective in areas like creative writing, philosophy and ethics, fields in which the distinction between right and wrong is harder to define.

Singularity – The long hypothesized moment when machines will become more intelligent than humans in every way and create a world that humans cannot completely understand or control. This concept was first proposed by technologists in the 1950s, before it was popularized in science-fiction stories and nonfiction books in the ’80s and ’90s.

A. I. researchers and amateur philosophers have long anticipated this moment, believing that it could bring great prosperity while also worrying it could cause serious harm. But researchers do not know how to reach that moment, when it might arrive or if it is even possible.

Superintelligence – A hypothetical machine that is more powerful than the human brain in every way. Although researchers and executives say they are pushing toward superintelligence, they do not necessarily know how to build such a machine. Part of the problem is that scientists cannot even agree on how to define this lofty goal. Intelligence is not something that is easily measured in humans or machines.

A. I. systems are already more powerful than the human brain in many ways. Most notably, they operate much faster than brains do. They can, for instance, process math problems and generate computer code much quicker than humans. But the systems still trail the brain in many ways, too. They do not, for instance, have common sense. And they are not as good at generating new ideas.

Token – A chunk of information that an A. I. system reads, processes or generates. This might be a word or part of a word or some other piece of data. As companies use data to train new A. I. systems, they measure this data in tokens. Later, when people use the systems, companies use the same measurement when tracking all the data going into and coming out of the systems.

Companies often charge users according to how many tokens they are putting into the systems and how many are coming out. Consumers who rely heavily on A. I. systems talk about themselves as “tokenmaxxing.”

Training – The process through which A. I. researchers teach skills to A. I. systems. By feeding enormous amounts of digital text into a system, for instance, a company can train the system to generate text on its own. This is how companies like Anthropic and OpenAI build their chatbots.

Because the leading systems learn from data spanning the entire internet — and beyond — the training process can take months. After training a system, companies will spend many more weeks or months honing it, trying to ensure that the system behaves as they want it to.

Produced by Antonio de Luca

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

After Bridge Attack, Putin Says He Will ‘Not Be Negotiating’ Ukraine Cease-Fire

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

The Russian leader invited European representatives to Moscow to discuss giving them a role in negotiations. It was unclear how serious the offer was.

By Paul Sonne

Reporting from Shenzhen, China

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia said on Thursday that “we will not be negotiating” any partial cease-fire with Ukraine after Kyiv’s attacks this week on the only bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

Mr. Putin publicly addressed the strikes, which destroyed a large part of the bridge that carried passenger vehicles, for the first time after a high-profile summit with President Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen, China. He vowed painful Russian retaliation for the attacks.

The Russian leader built the bridge to connect Russia to Crimea in the years after Moscow illegally annexed the peninsula from Ukraine in 2014. It has served as a monument to Russian control over Crimea and to Mr. Putin’s larger imperial ambitions, as well as a crucial transport link for Crimeans.

Mr. Putin said that he had been discussing with his security council the possibility of a cease-fire on shipping in the Black Sea or a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure, but that any such possibility was now off the table.

“After these strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not be negotiating,” Mr. Putin said. He warned that Russia’s retaliation would “be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime has done to the bridge.”

Engineering specialists have said that work to restore the road part of the bridge could take years. Earlier this year, Ukraine tried to cut off Crimea to pressure Moscow to end the war.

Even before the bridge strikes, there was little sign that Mr. Putin was inclined to agree to any cease-fire in the coming weeks. Western intelligence assessments have found that the Russian leader plans to fight in Ukraine at least through the winter.

It was not immediately clear what the Russian leader’s statement meant for a large swap of prisoners of war and perhaps civilian prisoners that Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, helped negotiate at talks in Abu Dhabi last week.

But the announcement immediately dashed meager hopes that talks between Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen would lead to a breakthrough in the Trump administration’s on-again, off-again effort to end the war in Ukraine.

Russia has blamed various Ukrainian attacks for stalled progress on peace talks in the past, including a drone attack that Russia accused Ukraine of launching against Mr. Putin’s lakeside retreat but that Kyiv said never took place.

In his news conference in Shenzhen, Mr. Putin addressed the U. S. request to include European officials in the peace talks, which so far have been limited to Russians, Ukrainians and Americans.

He called insinuations by European officials that Russia was preparing to invade Europe “political diarrhea,” and reiterated his position that stationing Western troops in a postwar Ukraine was a red line that he could not tolerate.

But Mr. Putin also said that Moscow had invited European representatives to Moscow “through diplomatic channels” to clarify their position before determining any role for them in the talks. That statement suggested that the broader U. S.-led peace negotiations could continue, though it was unclear how serious the offer was.

Moscow has in the past rejected various European officials as unacceptable interlocutors, and Mr. Putin on Thursday said it would be impossible to normalize relations “without a change in the political elites in certain European countries.”

Mr. Putin raised doubts about whether he would accept Mr. Trump’s invitation to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami next month. The Russian leader said Mr. Trump had brought up the question twice during their talks in Shenzhen.

No decision has been made yet, Mr. Putin said. But he added that he had to take into account what was happening in Russia, and that it was not always convenient for him to travel abroad. He said a high-level Russian delegation would attend if he did not go.

The Russian leader suggested that if Kyiv wanted to end the war, it should look at what Russia agreed to last year in Anchorage, Alaska, during a summit with Mr. Trump. At the time, Mr. Putin agreed to stop fighting if Ukraine handed over the rest of the eastern Donetsk region, a proposal that Kyiv rejected.

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting from Munich.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Tech Outages May Become Routine. Experts Say Don’t Panic, but Prepare.

The New York Times November 19, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

A cascade of tech failures has rattled Americans and prompted many to look for ways to prepare for a prolonged digital disruption. Experts say it’s much like preparing for a storm.

By Amanda Holpuch

After a series of unsettling tech failures rattled airline passengers and other consumers in recent days, people may be wondering if there is anything they can do to prepare for the next outage.

Of the most recent disruptions, the longest — a global outage of Microsoft’s services — was resolved on Saturday after about 36 hours. A rare national ground stop that stranded thousands of airline passengers on Friday was lifted after more than four hours, but its effects lingered. On Monday, some Chase Bank customers were briefly unable to use their A. T. M. cards or complete transactions.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that there was “zero” evidence that the failures were related or that they were the work of a foreign power or hackers.

But with A. I. exposing vulnerabilities in our software and companies rushing to fix them, experts say disruptions could last several more months or longer — and the next one could test our dependence on digital services like phone-based payment systems or online banking.

Here are some practical steps people can take to prepare.

One habit people should embrace again is having a little cash on hand, said Chris Krebs, a former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency at the U. S. Department of Homeland Security.

Mr. Krebs, who now runs the Krebs Group, a cybersecurity and geopolitical risk management consultancy, said he was “as guilty as anybody of not having any cash” around. But he said it was good to have small bills at home, along with bank account numbers written or printed on paper.

“Folks need to be thinking: Hey, the last couple of days with all these disruptions, these were the things I wasn’t able to do because of a short-term disruption,” he said. “How do I build personal resilience around that? What’s the thing that, if that fails, even if it’s just an hour or two, is there anything I can personally do?”

The federal government’s disaster preparedness initiative, Ready. gov, has a guide for creating an emergency communication plan with your family. The first tip is to create a paper copy of contact information for relatives and close friends, as well as a list of other important numbers, such as for schools and doctors.

If this guidance sounds familiar, that’s because it is in line with what disaster preparedness experts advise for other kinds of disruptions, including power outages and wildfires.

Why so similar? Because, Mr. Krebs said, in a natural disaster, services that people depend on, such as water, electricity and gas, may go down and may take time to restore. “It’s not that much different to expect that, as everything is becoming digitized, that some of those digital services could have temporary outages,” he said.

“Everybody’s feeling this personally because every aspect of our lives is riding on some digital dependency, whether it’s checking the bank, talking to your loved ones, figuring out schedules for your kids on the weekend, whatever,” Mr. Krebs said. “And so when there’s a disruption to any of those services, you feel it, you feel it immediately, and you realize that you don’t have a fallback plan. There’s no analog version anymore of your iPhone.”

It’s smart to have a three-day preparedness plan, just like the one people should have in case of a physical emergency.

Chetrice Romero, a senior cybersecurity adviser at the law firm Ice Miller, suggested that people keep one gallon of water per day for each member of their household and three days of nonperishable food, charged power banks and flashlights.

The federal government has a number of resources for creating plans for a range of emergencies, including avalanches, cyberattacks and wildfires, including no-cost or low-cost preparation tips and tips specific to certain populations, such as caregivers.

One difference with tech outages is that they happen suddenly, whereas bad weather is often preceded by hours or even days of warnings, Ms. Romero noted.

“These outages, I think, create a lot more anxiety because you think you’re fine and then you’re not,” she said. “And then it’s hard to explain what’s wrong, right? We know bad weather is bad weather. It’s hard for people to wrap their heads around ones and zeros they don’t understand.”

She said she hoped the recent outages would get people thinking about being prepared for tech outages as they would for a storm.

When technological failures happen, Ms. Romero said, one immediate concern is that bad actors will prey on the anxieties in order to scam people.

If you receive an email or text claiming to be from your bank or a company whose services you use and it asks for private information, like a Social Security or account number, do not respond, she said. “Go straight to your bank, communicate directly with them,” she said, adding, “verify, verify, verify.”

Also, voices can be imitated, so if a loved one calls and claims they need money to be transferred to them immediately because their bank is down, hang up and call them at a number you know is theirs.

Amanda Holpuch covers breaking news and other topics.
