Connections Coach

The G. T. A. series is more than just a crime simulator — it’s a cartoonish sendup of our country. What happens when reality outruns the joke?

Credit... Illustration by Daukantė

Supported by

By Joseph Bernstein

Joseph Bernstein traveled to Scotland to meet with Rockstar executives and played dozens of hours of G. T. A. VI.

A few months ago, when I started to brag to people that I might be getting an advance copy of Grand Theft Auto VI, an unusual thing happened: Grown men started to invite themselves over to my house for play dates. Some of these men were my friends — but not all. Others were co-workers, acquaintances, the dads of my kids’ classmates. Nor were they necessarily gamers. Some had aged out of the hobby, some had never started and some considered gaming a waste of time. Among them were married men and carefree bachelors and guys leading several other early-middle-aged lifestyles besides.

To understand just how rare it is, in 2026, for one early-40s straight man to ask another for a one-on-one hang in his home, to do something other than watch a ballgame, in the absence of at least an implicit understanding that getting drunk is the point, I suggest a thought experiment: Try to imagine two such men in your life making plans to binge Netflix’s handsome new adaptation of “East of Eden,” sober. You can’t! Yet I felt there was nothing strange at all about these men wanting to come over to partake in G. T. A. VI. It’s just that big of a deal.

As you may have heard, the game was released today. G. T. A. is the Super Bowl of video games, in the sense that it is an extravaganza that attracts even the most casual fans and, out of curiosity and/or obligation, their loved ones. Also like the Super Bowl, it features Bad Bunny (he hosts one of the in-game radio stations). But unlike the Super Bowl, it doesn’t happen every year. Far from it: G. T. A. VI is the first new entry in 13 years.

Let’s take a moment to distinguish between 13 years in the abstract and the 13 years that have just occurred. The presidency went from Obama to Trump to Biden to Trump again; the phone went from bringing long-lost high school classmates together through viral dance crazes to tearing recently reunited high school classmates apart via gamified arguments about, inter alia, Russian intelligence, Chinese laboratories, Honduran migrants and American bathrooms. All that stuff.

Because G. T. A. has been gone for precisely this period — the Gulf of America? — the new game arrives with a rare perspective. What might this visitor from our coherent past tell us about our incoherent present? Long delayed, Grand Theft Auto VI has achieved a messianic status among gamers: a great force that has occulted itself during a time of disarray, whose reappearance has the chance to make the slop-worn present worth living, or at least more legible.

If you care about this game, you are probably already playing. If you don’t care about it, just so we’re on the same page, it’s the one that involves zipping around a meticulously rendered three-dimensional simulation of an American metro area, committing crimes. Sometimes it’s New York, sometimes Los Angeles; in the new game, it’s Miami.

There’s a story to follow, but many gamers opt for the extracurriculars, things like dirt-bike racing, weight lifting and eating hot dogs. Others, in a time-honored G. T. A. tradition, simply cause as much chaos as possible before being killed by the police. It’s this invitation to murderous rampage that has made the game controversial since the first one came out in 1997.

Conspicuously missing from the hype this time around has been much tut-tutting, if any. For years, the games were a symbol of what was wrong with the state of young people and their morals. But over the intervening decades, the nation reconciled itself to G. T. A., or at least developed more pressing concerns. In September, Miami Beach commissioners approved a marketing proposal that would see Vice City (G. T. A.’s version of Miami) logos festooned around town, and last night, the Miami Heat wore special Vice City uniforms in their game against the Milwaukee Bucks. The best outrage Fox News has mustered in the run-up to the release was to lecture men that they should not be gaming past the age of 40. (Disagree.) In other words, G. T. A. now falls into that category of hyperpopular things that many Americans deep down sense might have poorly understood side effects, but that we have resolved to shrug our shoulders at, like dating apps or legal weed.

I like to think of Grand Theft Auto as two different but complementary experiences. The first is more or less what its critics accuse it of being: a hunk of nasty pulp. The second — much less appreciated — is a satire that pulls the nastiness into quotation marks. If most violent video games are grim and airless, the Grand Theft Auto series is in the madcap tradition of Looney Tunes: dumb done smart, lousy with references high, low and in between. Importantly, the experiences don’t work without each other. In the absence of the satire, the playable mayhem would be sort of indefensible. In the absence of the playable mayhem, the satire would find its way to no one.

It is a persistently underappreciated fact that the Rockstar team behind every Grand Theft Auto game is based not in any of the American cities it reproduces, but in Edinburgh. Today the staff is international, and the work is spread among Rockstar studios around the world, but the games retain a donnishly screwy sensibility that owes at least as much to Monty Python as it does to Michael Mann. What I mean is, the feeling of moving through a Grand Theft Auto world is not simply sitting down with an interactive version of “Heat.” It is also inhabiting a quasi outsiders’ fun-house take on the American image.

But which image, exactly? The bulk of the series lines up closely with the global war on terror. Those years gave us “The Daily Show With Jon Stewart,” “Team America,” “Borat” and “American Idiot”: satirical critique of America and Americans, but not a loss of faith in the national project. You can see this in the targets of G. T. A.’s satire between 2001 and 2013, which are all very “What’s the Matter With Kansas?” by way of “South Park.” There’s the gun store, Ammu-Nation (Americans are violent); the burger, the Heart Stopper (Americans are fat); the right-wing news network, Weazel News (Americans are gullible); and so forth.

Those G. T. A. games made the ugly subtext of American life text through puerile exaggeration, a useful register for a product aimed at young men. But the issue today is that there is no longer much subtext to extract from America’s derangements, no distance between the way the country presents itself and any number of acid jokes you could make about it.

Brainstorm the consumer goods released since 2013 that could have been invented for an over-the-top satire of the United States. There’s Ozempic. Liquid Death. Gwyneth Paltrow’s jade egg. Juicero. NFTs. Those big red cartoon meme boots. Or what about the celebrities? MrBeast? Clavicular? Andrew Tate? Rockstar, meanwhile, has placed physical versions of its parodies of Burger King and KFC (Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell) in Miami, where you can actually go and eat a meal.

That shadow you see on the ground? It’s a giant cartoon eraser descending from the cosmos, rubbing out the line between reality and satire, to a slide-whistle glissando. The situation now is that the United States resembles a Grand Theft Auto game. How do you represent a world that’s already so detached from reality?

The nondisclosure agreement I signed in order to access Grand Theft Auto VI three weeks before its commercial release stipulated that I was not allowed to let anyone else watch. This meant I had to renege on several homosocial encounters I had really been looking forward to. But it also meant I got to tell my 6- and 4-year-old boys that Daddy was one of the only people in the world who had the coolest video game ever, but they couldn’t watch, because it was against the law.

For Rockstar, mystery has been more than a good P. R. strategy. It has also allowed it to play with audience expectations. For example, you might go into a game called Grand Theft Auto VI — one with a 30-year legacy of letting players immediately perform acts of boisterous criminality — expecting that it will be trivial to steal whichever car you like. But it is not so. You are not playing a simulation of criminal excess. You are playing American Underclass: The Game.

Rockstar’s version of South Florida is a cultural statement in itself, a Boschian landscape of hierarchy enforced by money and technology. The player starts the new game with almost nothing, not a slim jim for cracking doors nor a key-fob cloner to steal something German. Even if you do manage to get inside a nice car and start it, omnipresent tracking devices mean you’ll quickly draw the police. Instead, you might wander around looking for a beater and bust out a window with your elbow. But good luck losing the cops in something that old, and anyway, you’ll have to fill it up with fuel. Try to stick up a convenience store for gas money, and you’re likely to end up on CCTV: police. Or customers will record you on their phones: again, police. Might it all just be easier, as the game seems to suggest, to use the taxi app, RydeMe, on your in-game smartphone?

That is, if you can even afford it. In G. T. A. VI, you play as Jason and Lucia, lovers and partners in crime whose terrible credit disqualifies them from a checking account at the local bank. They must rely instead on BuckMe, a depressingly lifelike mobile payment app. Now in the back seat of your RydeMe, on the way to your destination you may spot a Sahara delivery van. The online retail giant has recently relocated to Leonida (Florida); a decision, we learn in a story on the in-game news app, that “has nothing to do” with the state’s “rare combination of lax regulations on employees’ rights with very tight surveillance of bathroom breaks.” Do not attempt to rob the van. It most likely has armed private security guards. They will light you up.

At night the couple scrolls social media in bed. Jason’s feed is action shots of dirt-biking and brain-rotted political memes. Lucia, the more ambitious of the pair, looks at photos of glamorous yacht parties and yearns for a glossier life. The last G. T. A. set in Vice City was a homage to “Scarface” and, of course, “Miami Vice”; this one is tonally closer to Sean Baker’s “The Florida Project.” You even live, for part of the game, out of a greasy motel. The characters aren’t cartoon supervillains but losers who have turned to petty crime out of necessity.

You can make them snort coke, but this will make you feel like more of a deadbeat. You can make them go to the strip club, but this will make you feel that you are wasting money. You can make them kill civilians, but this will make you feel, weirdly, that you’ve betrayed your fellow prole. One early mission is a quest to find oxycodone that hasn’t been stepped on. One early side activity is laying roof tile. Later, there’s an uncomfortable meeting with a parole officer. No, the setup of G. T. A. VI does not ooze with “gamer thrills” as much as it does “adults coming to terms with difficult things in a crumbling society.”

It all plays as a grim joke: Even the antiheroes of our culture’s foremost purveyor of criminal escapism are no longer having unmediated fun. Their lives, like ours, are shaped by a tech oligarchy that surveils, exploits and narcotizes them. The “South Park” stuff has been dialed way back. Rockstar seems to have decided, in the main, that lampooning the particulars of Trump’s America through exaggeration is like bolding 72-point type. There is no Mar-a-Lago north of Vice City. Though there is an out-of-control Department of Homeland Security: the National Office of Security Enforcement, or NOOSE.

Rockstar has embedded its sharpest commentary in the gameplay. It can’t be an accident how much looser and lighter the game feels after you have cash on hand and can start directing Lucia and Jason toward the old G. T. A. pleasures: picking up a grenade launcher, robbing a bank and escaping on a Jet Ski. Here is Rockstar’s answer to the question of how to capture the American zeitgeist: You can still have the time of your life — so long as you have enough money to put down your phone and engage with the world.

The Rockstar office in Edinburgh is at the foot of Arthur’s Seat, the inactive volcano that looms over the city and that tour guides will dubiously inform you may have been the location of Camelot. But Edinburgh really is a delightful fairy-tale city, actually overlooked by an enchanting castle, whose wee closes (little alleys) helped inspire J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter universe. It’s amusing to think of it as the place where Rockstar employees spend many hours a day piecing together a sun-blistered American underworld.

About a month ago, a half-dozen of these employees, mostly longtime executives, sat with me in a long room there, talking about their creation. None of them wanted to take too much credit, out of propriety, because nearly 5,000 people worked on G. T. A. VI, but also because it’s hard to say any one person speaks for a blockbuster video game in the way a director speaks for a movie.

There are a handful of auteurs in the industry, but they tend to be pseudointellectual egomaniacs, or Japanese. Rockstar’s president, Sam Houser, is a bit different. He was educated at the posh St. Paul’s School and is the son of the actress Geraldine Moffat. In interviews, he has cited Rick Rubin as an inspiration, and he built Rockstar to be a bit like a cool record label. His mission, to give video games the same cultural clout as music and movies, has both succeeded — in the sense that his studio has created a series that does — and failed, because there isn’t anything remotely comparable to G. T. A. In true visionary fashion, Houser no longer gives interviews.

Each new Grand Theft Auto game starts with a map: an abstraction, a series of choices. And it is in these choices — what exactly in that America of the mind to represent and what not to — that Rockstar’s voice is heard loudest. The maps are overseen by Aaron Garbut, a cheerful Scotsman who has worked on the series for 30 years, since he was fresh out of art school. In that time he has made New York (Liberty City) twice, Los Angeles (Los Santos) twice and now Miami (Vice City) twice. He had the slightly disoriented look of a man who has spent a decade peering through a loupe. He was still refocusing on the scale of the real world. “We sort of just refine and refine and refine,” Garbut said. “Forever.”

Because I’ve lived in New York for almost 20 years, my personal favorite is Garbut’s work on Liberty City in G. T. A. IV. It’s accurate to the image of New York you may have gotten from some combination of movies, music, television and real life — with nods to “The French Connection” and “Carlito’s Way,” but also a recreation of Brighton Beach so authentic you can practically smell the stuffed cabbage. The storefronts in the game’s version of Times Square are actual early digital photographs of real electronics and souvenir shops that Garbut took during research trips. A G. T. A. map lets you inhabit a place made up of the media representations that already define it, and that have just as much to do with how you understand that place as the material thing itself.

There is a Nathan Fielder-esque level of obsessive derangement involved in the construction of a Rockstar game. The company is well known for eschewing procedural generation — using algorithms to produce digital objects with superficial differences — in favor of custom detail. For G. T. A. VI, Garbut said, Rockstar created some 30,000 unique NPCs, or nonplayer characters, the digital humans who roam the game. (That’s about one fake person for every 16 real people who live in the city of Miami. Those actual people, by the way, are now subject to the real-world insult “NPC,” meaning an actual person with the nonexistent inner life of a video-game person, in another troubling instance of game reality invading our own.)

On a recent media tour, the chief executive of Take Two, which owns Rockstar, emphasized the fact that no generative A. I. was used in the creation of Grand Theft Auto VI, and that he (the money guy) gave Rockstar (the creatives) as long as they needed to bring their world to life. That’s a sales pitch. But it’s also an honest reflection on an industry staring down existential change. In recent weeks, A. I. advocates have posted footage from their own enormous “open world” games generated by prompting Claude. The games look stupid, like something a dog would make. But that’s not the point; the point is that Rockstar’s bespoke approach may, in a benighted near-future, strike us as a beautiful though inefficient form of artisanship practiced by a lost civilization.

At this level of tinkering exactitude — the Rockstar execs call it “fidelity” — questions arise, like: Should the main characters have their own, interactive, in-game iPhone? (Yes.) And should that iPhone have apps? (Yes.) And should one of those apps be an Instagram clone with hundreds of its own posts? (Yes.) And should some of those posts be one-to-one satires of common meme formats including the one in which Winnie the Pooh wears a monocle? (Yes.) And should those posts have realistic comments, including horny ones and “6-7”? (Yes.) And so on.

This is all possible because Rockstar has multiple teams dedicated to creating mock media. They make the phone and the television with its own fake TV shows and the fake video game system with its own video games, which are, yes, playable. None of this filigree is necessary, perhaps. But it does create an uncanny tingle of mise en abyme, the vertiginous sense that you are staring into a copy of a world that has recreated all the important bits, but smaller.

“Hand-touched, hand-built, every single part of it is thought about and worked through,” Garbut told me. “I think you can feel that.”

As G. T. A. VI got closer to completion, Houser and Rob Nelson, the game’s head of development, rented a hotel suite in Miami Beach for 10 days. There they drew the curtains and played through the most recent build. At night, Nelson told me, the two would stagger outside blinking, noticing wrong details — not enough tourist shops on Collins Avenue; the quality of the streetlights at midnight a little off — and relay them back to Garbut to be fixed. Hearing this, I was reminded of the one-paragraph Jorge Luis Borges story about an empire that builds a map as big as its territory.

Back in the Edinburgh office, Nelson picked up a controller and began to piddle around in the world he and thousands of other people had spent a decade filling in. He rode a bike; he threw a football; he petted a dog. I hadn’t yet signed the NDA, so the company did not want me to witness anything that rose to the level of spoiler. Each time a snippet of plot-related dialogue played, a man sitting behind a desk at one end of the office turned a knob to cut the volume. I realize this sounds boring, so let me be clear: It was not boring. It was orders of magnitude more exciting to see a state-of-the-art virtual man lollygag in a state-of-the-art Florida simulator than it would be to watch a real guy do it in real Florida. It was thrilling, I realized, to see humans create such an intricate and functional world.

I have something disgraceful to confess: As I played G. T. A. VI, I kept looking at my phone. My actual phone. Not for long periods of time, because you can’t hold a controller and a phone simultaneously. More like the way I check my phone while reading a great novel: too often. After all, I was one of the first people in the world to experience what sure seems like the most anticipated entertainment product of all time, a brilliant cultural achievement that somehow overdelivers on more than a decade of hype. Yet I kept updating myself on the Instagram stories of people I don’t even like, and reading memes on X that didn’t even bother to make an attempt at human syntax.

The question of contemporary attention hovers uneasily over Grand Theft Auto VI. As you play, you sense the designers trying to strike a balance between poking fun at our tattered brains and accommodating them. Along the way, you are encouraged to pay close attention to your significant other. This occurs through things like gamified foot rubs, gamified couch time, pressing a certain button to hold hands and so forth. I know how ridiculous this sounds, and I also know that at various times I had to stop to reflect about why I was buying my virtual girlfriend a gold necklace when my family was sulking in the other room. I then had to reflect on why I was ignoring my virtual girlfriend, for whom I was ignoring my real family, so I could check real Instagram to see if my wife had posted anything.

As my mind wandered, I found myself thinking again of the Borges story about the map as big as the territory. The reason I know this story, the reason most anyone really knows this story, is because of a famous interpretation of it by Jean Baudrillard, the French theorist and America obsessive. It’s a little pointy-headed — oh, well. Basically, Baudrillard found the story useful as an allegory for a traditional order of meaning, in which things in the real world can be represented: say, through a painting or a staggeringly lifelike video game.

But in the new order of meaning, Baudrillard’s one, this relationship has been inverted, and representations give meaning to the world. This doesn’t just mean that life sometimes imitates art. It means that all representations, including video games, advertisements, movies, TikTok videos, you name it, work together to create a universe of symbols that feel realer to us than reality. And that in fact subsume reality altogether.

Baudrillard argued that the characteristic mental disorder of this new arrangement was schizophrenia. Because he was a French theorist, he was being edgy and didn’t mean the actual disease. He meant a state of terrified confusion, brought on by the relentless bombardment of contextless signs. Humans no longer have an autonomous inner self that can point our attention at this or that; we are powerless nodes, receiving and transmitting superficial fragments of media that stimulate our emotions and bypass our understanding.

Baudrillard wrote all this in the 1980s, roughly 20 years before the invention of the iPhone, and it describes exactly how we experience reality today — about 20 years since its release. And as a result, there is no single media product that can compete with the world of fleeting and insane impressions that is always a glance away. Certainly, G. T. A. VI can’t. It will be absorbed into the greater world of fragments and sensations through which most of us now experience culture. There it will be regurgitated in often-garbled forms, sometimes by nonpeople, according to rules written by nonpeople, for a human audience addicted to garbled regurgitation. In another 13 years it will be 2039. You don’t have to work for Anthropic to know that the way humans represent and understand their lives is probably going to look different.

This is the paradox of Rockstar’s grand undertaking: It has crafted a working miniature of the United States during a period in which the American sense of reality has almost completely broken down; a period in which the desire for grand attempts at sense-making have been subordinated to the desire for distraction; a period in which American disorder has moved from the outside world to our innermost selves. It is a coherent map of incoherent territory — maybe the last one.

Joseph Bernstein is a Times reporter who writes feature stories for the Styles section.

A Village Burned, Its People Killed or Exiled. A Court Ruled It Was Genocide.

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Myanmar Genocide Verdict

Zammona’s erasure was part of a wider campaign of violence against Rohingya Muslims. An international court found that Myanmar was culpable for the atrocities.

Zammona’s erasure was part of a wider campaign of violence against Rohingya Muslims. An international court found that Myanmar was culpable for the atrocities.

Mustafa Kamal and Toyuba Khatun once had a prosperous life in Myanmar. But for nearly a decade the couple and their family have been living in a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Credit...

Supported by

By Hannah Beech

Photographs and Video by Lam Yik Fei

Hannah Beech and Lam Yik Fei spent a week in the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Hannah Beech has reported extensively on Rohingya, documenting their exodus in 2017 and investigating their continued repression.

As his village burned, Mustafa Kamal somehow kept his family safe.

Husband and wife, three sons, three daughters, a granddaughter, they ran until their breath ran out. They stumbled past bodies of people they knew, shot by Myanmar’s security forces. They slogged through mud that claimed some of their clothes and trekked over jungle passes thick with leeches. Days later, when they finally crossed a river into Bangladesh, they rowed past swollen bodies of other Rohingya Muslims who never made it to the other side alive.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that the atrocities against the Rohingya ethnic minority constitute a genocide waged by the Myanmar state. The killing, gang rape and mass arson reached a furious zenith in 2017, building on years of systematic persecution. Three quarters of a million Rohingya flooded into Bangladesh in a matter of weeks, the most rapid refugee exodus in recent history. And more kept coming.

A judgment in a country half a world away would matter, Mr. Kamal told me. It would acknowledge the fate of his home, Zammona, one of 400 Rohingya villages that were obliterated by Myanmar security forces nine years ago.

Agnes Chang/The New York Times

But sitting in the dark, cramped shelter that is now his home in Bangladesh, part of what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, Mr. Kamal said that the trauma did not end nine years ago. For the Rohingya, he said, misery never ends.

International aid to the camps has plummeted. Hunger and disease are rampant. In May, Mr. Kamal’s 18-year-old son was killed by militants who have unleashed a reign of terror in the refugee camps. Human traffickers roam the narrow spaces between tarpaulin shelters, grabbing men, women and children. One of Mr. Kamal’s daughters was kidnapped by a militant, who forced himself on her. She had no choice but to marry him, and they now have a baby boy.

“Oh, Allah, why is there no justice for the Rohingya anywhere on earth?” Mr. Kamal said, weeping as he clutched a photo of his dead son.

Mr. Kamal, now 66, grew up in Zammona, a fertile collection of hamlets in Myanmar’s far west, dotted with fish ponds, well-stocked groceries and mosques with graceful arches. His father was a teacher at a government school. Mr. Kamal learned Burmese, the language of Myanmar’s Buddhist Bamar majority, and took a job as a trader, ferrying goods from one town to another. His wife, Toyuba Khatun, was educated, too.

The Rohingya had long faced repression from the military, which ruled Myanmar for decades and preserved power for the Bamar. In the 1980s, the Rohingya lost their legal status in Myanmar, their citizenship essentially stripped from them. Babies rarely were issued birth certificates. There was also occasional tension with the Rakhine ethnic group, with whom the Rohingya shared Rakhine State.

Still, Mr. Kamal said he had easy relations with Rakhine villagers who lived nearby. After all, he had gone to school with them; his father had been their teacher.

A store owner in Zammona, Mohammed Yunus said he welcomed Buddhist customers, bantering with them as they haggled over the latest clothes or electronics. (Zammona is called Zin Paing Nyar in the Burmese language.)

In 2012, violence flared between the Rohingya and the Rakhine, inflamed by state media coverage. Gatherings of more than five Rohingya were banned. Mosques were shuttered. Many Rohingya children no longer felt welcome at government schools. Mr. Kamal’s father secretly taught his grandchildren at home, desperate for the next generation to be educated.

When Mr. Kamal’s daughter Rehana Bibi got married, a Myanmar official forbade her from having more than two children. A false narrative took hold across Myanmar that the high birthrate of Rohingya was part of a global Muslim plot to swamp Buddhist lands. Military propaganda inaccurately portrayed the Rohingya as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Never mind that Rohingya had been elected to Parliament, studied at the nation’s finest universities, and once enjoyed government radio broadcasts in their own language, just like any other of the nation’s many ethnic groups. In the 2015 elections, which elevated the party of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace laureate, the Rohingya lost their right to vote.

On Oct. 9, 2016, a militant group led by a Rohingya refugee who was born in Pakistan and schooled in Saudi Arabia launched attacks on Myanmar security outposts, killing nine police officers, according to the Myanmar authorities.

The security forces’ response to the attacks punished an entire ethnicity.

In Zammona, Mr. Kamal locked the door to his spacious wooden house and prayed with his family that the soldiers would not attack.

Over the next few months, soldiers rounded up men in Zammona, accusing them of participating in the militant raids, charges they denied. Their only crime, they said, was being young, able-bodied Rohingya men. One was given a 54-year prison sentence. Soyadul Amin and Abdul Rohim were sentenced to 16 years each. Mr. Amin described how the Myanmar soldiers tied his arms behind his back, threw him on the ground and laughed as they ordered him to lap up his food like an animal. When he and others cried out for water, the soldiers offered urine.

The United Nations said at the time that hundreds of Rohingya were killed and that the crackdown “very likely” constituted crimes against humanity.

“We could not imagine what would happen next,” Mr. Kamal said. “Our people, our Rohingya were finished.”

On Aug. 25, 2017, the Rohingya militants carried out another series of attacks, killing more than a dozen security forces. This time, the military was prepared. Within hours, the scorched-earth retribution began.

Mr. Kamal heard the rocket launchers crescendo from the east. He gathered his family, but there was no time to grab anything, apart from a few precious papers that proved their existence in Myanmar.

Mr. Yunus, the store owner, marshaled his kin. As he left his two-story home, with its spacious garden and surrounding fields, he made sure to lock the door. He would surely be back, he thought.

“I was a rich man in Myanmar,” he said. “I had everything I needed for my family.”

As the soldiers descended on Zammona, Fatema Khatun, the wife of Mr. Amin, one of the men sent to prison, searched frantically for her seven children and thanked Allah that they were all there. She was seven months pregnant with her eighth child. Along their long escape to Bangladesh, a Myanmar soldier grabbed one of her daughters, Sukura Begum, in the forest and raped her, just one horror in what U. N. investigators say was systematized sexual violence. She was 11 years old.

Elsewhere in the village, Morijan, a young mother who goes by one name, searched for her 9-year-old son, Mohammed Omair, who had raced to the west when the artillery began. Two days later, he was found in a rice paddy with a bullet wound through his heart.

At least 10,000 Rohingya were killed by security forces and Rakhine mobs in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 attacks, the U. N. estimated. In Zammona, 10 unarmed men were trussed and killed, then tossed in a mass grave north of the village, said a Myanmar soldier whose testimony, after he ended up in the hands of an enemy militia, marked the first time perpetrators confessed to their crimes. The soldier also said seven Rohingya were shot dead there.

Zammona was wiped from the map, its ruins smoldering for days, visible from a hill in Bangladesh. When he was released from a Myanmar prison four years later, his 16-year sentence commuted, Mr. Rohim returned home before he, too, fled across the border.

“Everything was gone,” he said of Zammona. “I couldn’t recognize anything.”

The Myanmar government soon covered up evidence of the village, building rows of prefab housing on burned earth.

All that was left of Zammona was a large Bodhi tree, sacred to Buddhists because it was the kind under which a prince meditated and gained enlightenment as the Buddha.

In Bangladesh, Mr. Kamal and his family were allotted a tiny shelter with a tarpaulin cover. They could not leave the refugee camps without permission. International assistance allotted each person $12 a month for food, decreased now to $10.

Fatema Khatun’s daughter, who was raped, suffers from debilitating seizures. Three years ago, another daughter, then 18, disappeared for months, then called tearfully from Malaysia, where she said she had been trafficked. She was forced to marry an older man, she said, 50 or 60 years old, she wasn’t sure.

Five years ago, Ms. Khatun’s husband, Mr. Amin, was released from prison a broken man. His kidneys barely work from the beatings. He lies on the floor of their shelter, groaning from an ache that never dissipates. There is no money for painkillers. Occasionally, he repeats the Burmese words he learned in detention: a string of numbers that was his prisoner ID.

“I was supposed to die,” he whispered. “I don’t feel alive.”

On Monday, children crammed into Mr. Kamal’s shelter. His 10-year-old grandson recounted how the boy had been held by the militants, his hands reaching wide to show the size of the blades they brandished. One granddaughter was quiet, but over the hours she leaned against me. Later, she offered a tentative “hello” in English. We practiced sentences.

What is your name? Sadeka Bibi.

How old are you? 13.

Where are you from? Her English faltered. The answer came translated as the block number of her refugee camp. Her mother intervened. Sadeka tried again.

“I am Rohingya,” she said. “I am from Myanmar.”

Mohammed Faisal Arakani contributed reporting.

Hannah Beech is a Times reporter based in Bangkok who has been covering Asia for more than 25 years. She focuses on in-depth and investigative stories.

Google Leaned Into A. I., Hurting Its Core Business

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The Silicon Valley giant’s search advertising has long fueled the company. But its search ad growth is slowing as A. I. becomes more prevalent.

By Kate Conger

Reporting from San Francisco

Marshall Evans, a marketer who works with small businesses, has helped home repair companies, fitness studios and other mom-and-pop companies buy Google search ads for more than a decade.

The ads — which are tailored to show up when people search on Google for a related term — have been effective in helping a business appear at the top of search results, increasing the chances that someone will click on the ad.

But now those traditional search ads often appear much lower, as Google highlights A. I.-written responses to user queries above its usual list of links and ads.

“A. I. takes over such a large amount of the search results now,” Mr. Evans said.

Mr. Evans’s experience is an example of how A. I. has disrupted Google’s core business of search advertising. As the company plows hundreds of billions of dollars into developing A. I. and incorporating the technology across its services, some longtime advertisers are having second thoughts.

Over the last six months, Mr. Evans, who is based in North Carolina, has moved ad dollars away from Google search ads. For one company that sells trophies, he said, he is allocating $500 a month to the search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago, when Google introduced a feature called A. I. Mode. And he is putting more of the money toward streaming services like Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor.

Last month, Google reported for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50 percent of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue. Search ad revenue rose 12 percent, falling short of the 15 percent that Wall Street expected.

In effect, A. I. has become a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies. While Google stands to benefit enormously from the technology, including in its booming cloud computing business, A. I. is also taking a toll as the behemoth adjusts to the technology’s effects.

“Google is trying to take a business that was the best business in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business that doesn’t have the same advantages,” Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing. com, said of the move from search to A. I. ads. “Making that transition is a lot harder than Google’s management thought it would be.”

Google’s executives have said the company wanted to make A. I. search features appealing to users, and would think about advertising later. At the top of its search results page, users often now see A. I. Overviews, an A. I.-written answer to the user’s query. The bottom of the summary also invites users to interact with a chatbot through the A. I. Mode feature. Advertising in its A. I. answers and chatbots has not yet taken off.

“We are focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization,” Sundar Pichai, Google’s chief executive, said during the earnings call.

Google said users were flocking to its A. I. search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years.

“A. I. is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with our A. I. features leading to increased usage and overall query growth, including commercial queries,” said Thomas Schoenfelder, a Google spokesman. “Our ads experiments have shown promising results and we’re confident about our trajectory.”

Advertisers can pay more for the chance to feature their ads in A. I. Mode, but there is no guarantee that the promotion will show up. When ads appear in A. I. results, some advertisers say, people are getting caught up in back-and-forth discussions with chatbots instead of clicking their ad and visiting their websites.

“What we’re seeing is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior,” said Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at VML, a global creative agency in New York. Whether people are talking to Google’s chatbot or other chatbots, she said, they are spending more time in conversation and less time surfing the web.

Advertisers aren’t abandoning Google search, she added, but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system. “Clients are very interested and they want to test new things,” Ms. Schlosser said. “They are interested in ChatGPT and Perplexity, but they are also not totally pulling back from Google.”

Max Anderson, the chief executive of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on the adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said Google search ads had become more expensive in recent years. He has been running search ads for OnlyFinder on Google since 2022 and ran ads there for his previous company, a software start-up, starting in 2014.

“Our ads won’t show on the page at all, or it will show down the page, below an A. I. Overview,” he said. “Our costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.”

The solution was to spend less, he said, adding that he was “gradually and mathematically” pulling back as costs rise and was now devoting about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business. Mr. Anderson declined to discuss specific spending, saying the numbers were proprietary.

Mr. Anderson isn’t planning to abandon Google, but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in A. I. Overviews. Google doesn’t offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in A. I. Overviews.

“We’d love to have a way as a business to predictably play there, but we have not seen one yet,” Mr. Anderson said.

Kate Conger is a technology reporter based in San Francisco. She can be reached at kate. conger@nytimes. com.

Inside the Contentious World of Elite Piano Tuners

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Op-Docs

By Paweł Chorzępa

Mr. Chorzępa, a filmmaker, captured over 300 hours of the International Chopin Piano Competition to make “The Tuners.”

The International Chopin Piano Competition is one of the most prestigious and grueling contests in all of classical music. Every five years, virtuoso pianists from around the world gather in Warsaw to vie over weeks for glory and recognition.

And then there are the piano tuners. Entering the concert hall late at night, after everyone has left, they go to work isolating harmonics, resolving tiny vibrations and shaping the performances to come. Yet their work is almost never acknowledged.

The first time I observed the tuners at the Chopin competition, I realized I was witnessing something much more intimate and artistic than mere craftsmanship. They were not only repairing instruments; they were creating a world of sound. As a cinematographer and camera operator who also works outside the spotlight, I felt a kinship with the strange loneliness of carrying an enormous responsibility, unseen.

In my short documentary “The Tuners,” I hoped to capture the ethereal intensity of the piano tuners’ task as they strive to adjust their instruments so exquisitely that the competition’s leading pianists will choose to perform on them. More than anything, this film is a tribute to people who dedicate themselves completely to helping others shine and whose artistry often remains invisible.

Behind every great achievement are people whose work often goes unnoticed. The piano tuners in our film are extraordinary artists who make extraordinary performances possible, yet rarely step into the spotlight. We all have unsung heroes in our lives. Who are yours?

Paweł Chorzępa is a director and cinematographer based in Poland.

A Data Center Was Coming. The Town Had a Message: Stay Out.

The New York Times November 19, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

The battle over artificial intelligence is unfolding in rural communities, which are deciding whether to embrace resource-hungry computer farms.

The battle over artificial intelligence is unfolding in rural communities, which are deciding whether to embrace resource-hungry computer farms.

The pastoral town of East Fishkill, N. Y., made clear that it had no interest in becoming home to a data center. Credit... Lauren Lancaster for The New York Times

Supported by

By Hilary Howard

This summer, Hilary Howard reported from proposed and established data center sites in New York, including in East Fishkill and the Finger Lakes.

The Appalachian Trail runs through East Fishkill, N. Y., a hilly, bucolic town where people keep to themselves. But this year, residents were activated. Big time. About a data center. And it poured out at a town board meeting, right after the Pledge of Allegiance.

Amid mentions of the Boy Scouts, a fitness campaign and plans for America’s 250th birthday celebration, barks of “We’re here about the data center,” and “When will we discuss the moratorium?” blared from the lobby, where a standing-room-only throng had spilled out from the meeting room.

Similar scenes are unfolding at town halls across the United States. Local governments, better known for spearheading blood drives and playground renovations, are finding themselves on the front lines of the existential crisis of our time: artificial intelligence and the power-hungry data centers that generate it.

After all, it’s small towns that control zoning decisions. And it’s small towns where the battle over large-scale data centers is likely to be won or lost.

That night in late June, five board members sat behind an imposing, wood-paneled dais. The anxiety in the room was palpable. It was time to pass a moratorium on large-scale data centers, or face the pitchforks. But not before the residents spoke.

“East Fishkill has rules about how many chickens you can have,” George Naumann, a retired teacher, said. “That rule is there for a reason, for health and safety.”

His point being: If the town could regulate poultry, it could regulate data centers. The room erupted in applause.

In the end, the town board passed a three-year moratorium. But that didn’t end the tension in East Fishkill.

Residents are clamoring for more transparency from the board, which created a data center task force that many do not trust. And Treetop Companies, which owns the land where the data center would rise, signaled in a court filing that it intends to sue the Hudson Valley town, a tactic that is gaining momentum elsewhere.

“I’ve never experienced anything to this level,” said Marianne Flores, one of the town board members.

No one from Treetop spoke at the meeting, and the company did not respond to a request for comment on its plans for the data center or about the possible litigation.

Dan Diorio, the executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition, a trade association, said that the industry, by creating local tax revenue, jobs and other opportunities, aims to “help build a stronger economic future for every American.”

But most Americans have made clear that they don’t want the buzzing, high-tech behemoths in their backyard. Data centers are full of hard-working computers that propel the A. I. boom. But they are also energy hogs that threaten water supplies, produce noise and air pollution and heat the atmosphere.

Democrats capitalized on this disaffection in right-leaning states such as Ohio and Texas during the midterm elections. And voters approved all but one of 41 local ballot initiatives to limit or stop the development of data centers.

The people of East Fishkill feel similarly. They know something about technology and pollution.

IBM once ran a major manufacturing site in the town, which is about 75 miles north of New York City. Its computer chip cleaning operations polluted the groundwater, the main source of drinking water for the residents, most of whom rely on wells. Many of those wells became contaminated and had to be plugged.

Pamela Henry, who spoke at the meeting, uses water that is shipped to her area from wells in a nearby town. Her bills have doubled to about $235 a month, and she experiences flagging water pressure.

“I’m struggling to pay,” said Ms. Henry, who is retired and lives on a fixed income. And when it comes to a data center? “I want to know where the water is going to come from to generate this system,” she said.

Water quality and quantity in East Fishkill is already precarious. In 2024, a drought dried out a crucial stream and a well at Fishkill Farms, a popular family business that grows fruit and vegetables. The farm had to ship water in by tanker.

Josh Morgenthau, the farm’s owner, fears that between droughts wrought by global warming and the insatiable appetite of computing campuses, his farm will dry up.

Some data centers are investing in closed-loop systems that recirculate cold water to cool computer equipment, which limits the reliance on local water sources.

But the systems are expensive to build and gobble up more power, which brings up problem No. 2: East Fishkill is not equipped for the mammoth amount of electricity that Treetop has said it needs.

According to the New York Independent System Operator, which manages the state’s grid, the amount of energy that Treetop wants would be enough to power up to one million homes. That’s about eight times as many households as in Dutchess County, which includes East Fishkill, 19 other towns and two cities.

It would be a herculean challenge to strengthen the electrical grid for the project — work that residents would subsidize through higher bills. To avoid such an expensive and time-consuming option, many developers are buying old fossil fuel power plants, building new ones or using mobile gas turbines to generate their own electricity. But that exacerbates air pollution and fossil fuel emissions. And often, the data centers still need to plug into the grid.

Hundreds of miles away from East Fishkill, an old coal plant from the 1930s that now runs on gas provides electricity for a crypto mining data center, where computers crunch number sequences to create digital currency, in the town of Torrey. Now, the site’s owners would like to convert it to an A. I. data center.

A. I. computing requires more electricity than bitcoin mining does. Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, which owns the gas plant and crypto facility, has a request pending with the New York Independent System Operator for additional electricity equivalent to what could power 200,000 homes.

Yvonne Taylor, the vice president of Seneca Lake Guardian, an environmental nonprofit, said that the plant had closed when the state phased out coal. It was brought back to life and retrofitted with gas to sell power to the state grid. A few years later, the crypto computers were installed, which meant the noisy and polluting gas turbines would be in continual use.

“Now, we’re watching the next chapter unfold,” Ms. Taylor said. “It will be difficult for Vulcan to make the claim that they’re ‘providing much needed power to the grid’ anymore, now that they’re consuming more power than they generate.”

Dale Irwin, the president of Vulcan, said that the plant would continue to provide electricity for the grid. “We’re simply pivoting what the data center computers will be used for,” he said.

The gas plant has pipes that extend into Seneca Lake, the deepest water source in the Finger Lakes and famous for its trout fishing. The pipes pull in roughly 74 million gallons of water a day to cool the plant, and then return it at hotter temperatures, as high as 98 degrees. Warmer waters are more conducive to algae blooms, and neighbors are concerned.

Laurie Fish, whose parents have a home next to the plant, said the aquatic life in this part of the lake had been destroyed. “It used to be Jesus fishing,” she said. “You put your pole in the water and you pull out a fish.” Now, she said, algae blooms turn it the color and consistency of pea soup.

“Our dogs can’t swim,” she said. “Our kids can’t swim.”

Mr. Irwin said that his company planned to build a closed-loop system for the A. I. operation, meaning that no additional lake water would be needed. He added that his business operates according to its permits and that no studies have linked algae blooms to the discharge from his plant.

Activists and policymakers who would like to stop the proliferation of data centers point to a one-year statewide moratorium on the centers that Gov. Kathy Hochul declared by executive order this summer. They would like the moratorium made into a law. The Responsible Data Center Development Act would do that, plus mandate environmental and financial protections for communities in New York State.

The legislation would increase the number of data centers included in the moratorium, which would be extended upon the bill’s signing; introduce a more stringent environmental review; require data centers to use renewable energy; and establish separate water and electricity rates, with one for residents, and one for data centers.

While the governor considers the bill, Congress is debating federal legislation that would require data centers to pay for their own electricity.

Although the state and federal measures would both help New Yorkers with soaring electricity costs, the state version would slow down and fine-tune the environmental permitting process of large-scale data centers, while the federal version would fast-track it.

Peter Martini, the town supervisor in Torrey, said he would welcome a stronger state law.

“I don’t deal with bitcoin and I don’t like A. I., but it’s a business in my town,” he said. “Sometimes, when the consequences are out of our hands, it makes things easier for us.”

What struck me while reporting this story was the general panic among New Yorkers concerning A. I. and data centers. One guy in East Fishkill summed it up best: “The robots are coming — they are coming for our jobs and for our resources.”A statement like that is tough to handle in Washington, much less in small governments across the country. Navigating these anxieties while planning for the future is a tall order. Most people I spoke with just want to slow data center development down until the country has a better understanding of what it all means.

Hilary Howard is a Times reporter covering how the New York City region is adapting to climate change and other environmental challenges.

Three MAGA Women Who Defined an Era in Congress Are Exiting

The New York Times November 19, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Congressional Memo

Representatives Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert and Nancy Mace embodied a combative, attention-seeking brand of politics that defined the Republican Congress.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

The tableau was emblematic of a coarse and gaudy era in Congress: Marjorie Taylor Greene and Lauren Boebert, two die-hard MAGA loyalists, jumping out of their chairs at the 2022 State of the Union to heckle President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

Their outburst — provocative, combatant, intolerant and crude — set the tone and style of a distinct period of politics under the Capitol dome in which Republicans were in charge, loyalty to President Trump was all that mattered and decorum was out the window.

That time, like the G. O. P. majority that presided over it, is coming to an end, and the women who were its archetypes — Ms. Greene of Georgia, Ms. Boebert of Colorado and a third who eventually joined their showboat ranks, Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina — are headed out as well.

All three women, never friends but always frenemies, were elected in 2020. And all will be gone in January, bringing to an official end a brief but colorful moment in Congress dominated by a trio of women whose attention-grabbing tactics, hair and makeup, and constant feuding drew comparisons to the cult favorite film “Mean Girls.”

There was Ms. Greene, a former CrossFit gym owner who became interested in politics only because of Mr. Trump. Ms. Boebert was the former owner of a gun-themed restaurant and bar who did not graduate from high school. Ms. Mace, who was the first woman to graduate from the military academy The Citadel, started out as a mainstream conservative but soon veered sharply toward MAGA, joining the other two on a path through Washington that had involved attracting the spotlight more than legislating.

There are many ways to be successful in Congress. Some members emerge as policy experts. Others rise because they are talented communicators. Still others understand how to build coalitions to push an agenda.

These MAGA women excelled at behaving so provocatively that they built a level of national name recognition that is rare for rank-and-file members in the House. But seemingly with no plan for what to do with the attention, except to generate more of the same, their antics ultimately wore thin, on colleagues and constituents alike.

“They taught us that shitposting for power has its limits,” said Annelise Russell, an associate professor of public policy at the University of Kentucky. “They flew a little too close to the sun, and no one knew how to come back down successfully. These women showed us that you have to at least feign effectiveness.”

She added: “If you don’t deliver anything — for constituents or party leadership — regardless of who you are, you don’t have staying power.”

They, in turn, appeared to grow bored and restless in Congress.

Ms. Greene, who had been among Mr. Trump’s closest allies in the House, abruptly quit Congress last January, announcing her exit days after the president branded her a “traitor” for breaking with him and helping compel the Justice Department to release its files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender.

Ms. Mace did not run for re-election, placing fifth in South Carolina’s Republican gubernatorial primary. Ms. Boebert, the only one of the group who sought to hang on in Congress, was caught up in the blue wave, defeated even after she switched districts to what had been expected to be a safe red seat.

But she said there was a part of her that was ready to move on.

“It’s almost liberating in a sense,” Ms. Boebert told TMZ just before her race was called. “I want to offer condolences to some of my friends who did win.”

Ms. Greene — who last year experienced a kind of political awakening in which she repudiated Mr. Trump and apologized for many of her statements and antics — was once the biggest heat-seeking missile of all.

“I think your fake eyelashes are messing up what you’re reading,” she said to Representative Jasmine Crockett, Democrat of Texas, during a late-night hearing of the Oversight Committee.

Speaking on the House floor as she filed a censure against a Muslim Democratic colleague, she referred to “Representative Ilhan Omar of Somalia — I mean Minnesota.”

Her legislative accomplishments included introducing the bill to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America,” as Mr. Trump insisted. Her fury was not reserved for attacks on Democrats; at one point, she tried unsuccessfully to oust Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker who she said had betrayed the MAGA movement.

Ms. Mace once paraded through the Capitol wearing a tight white tank top with a scarlet “A” emblazoned over her chest. Why? Well, that was beside the point of the stunt .

Ms. Boebert also needed no help in generating headlines, although hers were more often caused by her behavior backfiring on her. She was caught on a security camera vaping and groping her date before being ejected from a performance of the musical “Beetlejuice” in Denver.

During a closed-door session of the House Oversight Committee, as lawmakers were deposing Hillary Clinton in the Epstein investigation, Ms. Boebert leaked a photograph from inside the room to a right-wing blogger, causing Ms. Clinton and her attorneys to storm out and the entire deposition to briefly devolve into chaos.

(Ms. Clinton reacted online to the news of Ms. Boebert’s defeat with two words: “Bye, Felicia.”)

All three women demonstrated a rare streak of independence when it came to their demand for the release of the Epstein files, which for them appeared to transcend their unwavering loyalty to Mr. Trump. The trio withstood immense pressure from a vengeful White House that lobbied them relentlessly to fall in line and join Republican leaders in blocking a vote on the release of the material.

The dynamics of Congress next year, when House Democrats will preside over the largest majority in decades, would have made their brand of theatrics easy to ignore.

Still, the three women have promised to remain part of the public discourse in some yet-to-be-determined form.

“Our founders expected representatives to serve and go back home,” Ms. Boebert said in a video she posted online after her race was called last week. “So, I’m home, I am happy, I have peace and this is not the last you’ll be hearing from me.”

Ms. Greene has emerged as a vocal Trump opponent and part of a growing band of America First loyalists who have split from the president and may coalesce into a political movement. For now, she has attempted to use her star power to launch her own YouTube channel, “Life with MTG.”

Ms. Mace said recently she wanted to recede from the spotlight. “I kind of want to whittle sticks for a while,” she said at a recent forum. But she is not, in fact, whittling. She has launched a podcast, “Get MACED.”

Stephen K. Bannon, the former Trump adviser and podcast host, who reveled in their chaos, was one of the only people in Washington who said he would miss them.

“They were simply ‘too hot’ for the imperial Capitol,” Mr. Bannon said.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Behind Trump Meeting, Xi and Putin Share a Vision of Usurping U. S. Power

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

President Trump joined the Chinese and Russian leaders for a summit in Shenzhen, even though the two autocrats are trying to reverse America’s victory in the Cold War.

By Edward Wong

Edward Wong has written a book on China and reported from Shenzhen on the historic trilateral summit. He has covered global affairs for more than two decades.

At the end of a visit to Moscow more than three years ago, Xi Jinping, the leader of China, uttered a line to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that has come to define the outlook and actions of the two leaders.

“Right now there are changes, the likes of which we haven’t seen for 100 years, and we are the ones driving these changes together,” he said.

What Mr. Xi meant is this: The two men and their nations are transforming the world order by usurping the role of America as the sole superpower, the undisputed victor of the Cold War.

Both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin share a sense of historical grievance shaped by the expansion and dominance of U. S. power in the more than three decades since the fall of the Soviet Union. But from Mr. Xi’s perspective, that situation is evolving, and, rightly or wrongly, he has embraced a vision of America in terminal decline.

Mr. Xi brazenly used a similar line about historical changes in his opening remarks at a summit with Mr. Putin and President Trump on Thursday. “A transformation not seen in a century is accelerating,” he said at the conclave in Shenzhen, China.

Mr. Xi said the same thing to Mr. Trump when the two met in Beijing in May.

Mr. Putin, for his part, has demonstrated his own eagerness to challenge the United States by continuing his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which he began in February 2022.

The trilateral summit hosted by Mr. Xi in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen was an extraordinary event, since the leaders of the three nations had never met in a formal three-way setting.

Mr. Trump, who has spoken for years with admiration about both autocrats, gushed about being welcomed by the two men. “We are really making history,” he said at their meeting. Earlier, he called each of the men his friend.

But there is no sign that the summit will change the long-running anti-American stance of Mr. Xi or Mr. Putin, nor will Mr. Trump be able to build the same kind of relationship with either of those men that they have with each other.

Mr. Trump has a little more than two years left in his term. Both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin can hold on to power indefinitely, and neither has designated a successor.

“These are two deeply historically minded leaders who view geopolitics through the frame of their own national narratives,” said John Delury, a professor of international politics at the Hopkins-Nanjing Center in China. “They seem to regard themselves as ‘great men in history’ acting on a different plane than mere politicians. Even Trump can be seen as epiphenomenal in their eyes.”

Those two leaders have met more than 40 times. On one occasion, in Tajikistan, Mr. Putin even feted Mr. Xi on his 66th birthday with a champagne toast, cake and Russian ice cream.

More consequentially, China has continued to support Russia through the war in Ukraine. Mr. Xi allows Chinese companies to sell microelectronics and other critical goods to Russian defense companies, helping Mr. Putin continue his invasion despite having lost 400,000 to 500,000 troops in the conflict, U. S. and European officials have said.

China has also bought oil from Russia throughout the war, providing important financial backing to Russia.

R. Nicholas Burns, the ambassador to China in the Biden administration and a former ambassador to NATO, said that he never got any sense of ambivalence from Chinese officials on their support for Russia throughout the war, even though they would insist they were neutral in the conflict.

“It was quite hypocritical,” he said. “I actually think in the course of my time there as ambassador, they doubled down on their support for Russia.”

“It was very transparent that China wanted Russia to emerge stronger and gain an advantage over Ukraine,” he added. “They wanted to see NATO and the United States defeated.”

In Shenzhen, the three leaders discussed the war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin also talked about when they met privately earlier on Thursday. Western intelligence agencies assess that Mr. Putin is not ready to negotiate seriously on a peace settlement, The New York Times reported on Wednesday.

Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin have both been shaped by the breakup of the Soviet Union, which they attribute to American machinations and the weakness of Soviet leaders at the time. In December 2012, the month after he became China’s leader, Mr. Xi gave an important internal Communist Party speech in Guangdong Province in which he said the Soviet Union collapsed because “nobody was man enough to stand up and resist.”

There are other deep historical ties between the two nations that are foundational to the men’s partnership.

Beijing and Moscow fought on the same side in World War II against the Axis nations. Soon afterward, in the Korean War, the two powers sided with North Korea, another communist nation, against American and South Korean forces. That war has not formally ended, and Kim Jong-un, the leader of North Korea — whom Mr. Trump recently said he would like to meet again — has maintained formal security alliances with China and Russia.

Days before Mr. Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he met with Mr. Xi at the Winter Olympics in Beijing, and the two governments announced that their nations had entered into a partnership with “no limits.”

There have been limits, though. Mr. Xi has been concerned about the global economic effects of the war in Ukraine, analysts say, and China generally has avoided sending weapons to Russia. In May, when Mr. Putin went to Beijing after Mr. Trump’s visit, the Russian and Chinese leaders did not finalize an agreement for the construction of a new gas pipeline and energy sales to China from Russia.

At a banquet on Wednesday night in Shenzhen, Mr. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, a former army singer, welcomed Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and other national leaders who were in town for an Asian economic summit. Mr. Xi had Mr. Trump sit next to him at the head table, while Mr. Putin sat farther away with Ms. Peng. Some people have interpreted that as the Chinese leader possibly snubbing Mr. Putin.

But in two years, Mr. Trump will likely be gone from the world stage, and Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi could be dining together again as leaders of their nations and, in their eyes, great men.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

China Bars Bloomberg Reporter From Trilateral Talks for Asking a Question

The New York Times November 19, 2026

Trump’s Trip to Asia

Advertisement

Supported by

The exclusion of the reporter after she shouted a question to President Trump is an example of how tightly China tries to stage-manage events.

By Lily Kuo and Katie Rogers

Katie Rogers reported from Shenzhen, where Chinese officials limited coverage of President Trump’s appearances and speeches.

Seated at a long table across from the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, President Trump had just finished thanking his host when a reporter called out a question: Had Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia, been disloyal to the United States?

The president did not answer. Mr. Xi looked toward the gaggle of reporters and then away as a security guard moved in and blocked a camera that had been recording the exchange.

Chinese officials later barred the journalist, Annmarie Hordern, a Bloomberg TV reporter, from covering Mr. Xi’s next major event, perhaps the most important of the day in Shenzhen: a trilateral meeting of the leaders of the United States, China and Russia.

It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.

When Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia met in the first-ever summit of the leaders of those three countries, the reporter was prevented from entering the room.

A White House official said that the U. S. side had tried to reinstate the journalist but that Chinese officials refused, according to a report shared among television journalists. Reporters at the summit were told that it was extremely rude to shout a question. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to emailed questions about the reporter’s exclusion. A spokeswoman for Bloomberg News declined to comment.

In the United States, it is routine for the president to answer impromptu questions from the press corps. Over the past week, Mr. Trump has spoken about Mr. Huang several times. Mr. Huang is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U. S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy. (China has denied the espionage claims.)

When China hosts official events, it tightly controls the access of reporters, often allowing only state media outlets into major events or giving foreign journalists selective access. Over the years, China has expelled many foreign reporters, including most recently a New York Times correspondent. Chinese officials also try to influence international outlets by threatening to not grant them the accreditation that their reporters need to work in the country.

Looking out and seeing a lack of the usual fleet of American photographers and recognizable reporters who track his every move, Mr. Trump seemed to gently criticize the restrictions. In his remarks to Mr. Xi, the president praised the organization of the summit. “It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” he told the Chinese leader.

Mr. Xi, whose comments reach the Chinese public via speeches and remarks carried in state media outlets and rarely has unfiltered moments, does not hold news conferences or directly engage with reporters.

Previous American leaders have used state visits to China to push Beijing to be more open with the news media. During a joint news conference that U. S. officials forcefully negotiated during President Barack Obama’s trip to Beijing in 2014, Mr. Xi took a question from an American reporter about how the Chinese leader viewed Washington’s renewed focus on Asia. When Mr. Xi visited Washington in 2015, he took another question on cybersecurity from an American reporter.

Mr. Trump broke with that tradition when he traveled to China in 2017 and refused to take questions. When he visited again in May, he answered some questions from journalists but did not hold a formal news conference with Mr. Xi. During his trip to Shenzhen this week, the leaders again did not hold a joint press conference.

Peter Baker contributed reporting from Shenzhen, China.

Lily Kuo is a China correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.
